t: “The caretaker was saying that there is no fan-puller,” I said. “It may get uncomfortably hot during the night.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Thatʼs partly correct. But as you can see, the heat is much less now; itʼs fairly cold outside. And besides, what am I here for? Myself, my sister, and Vasavi will take turns fanning you by hand. And so that you wonʼt be in any kind of danger while youʼre asleep, Iʼll stand watch. The only trouble you have to take is to go to the room. You donʼt have to think for anything else.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: Nilanjan started for the room and I followed after him.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: By the way, there is one thing I should mention about our walk over. My shoes were squeaking as I walked, but Nilanjanʼs movement was absolutely silent. It was as if his feet werenʼt touching the ground at all, or if they were, they were touching it so lightly that no sound was coming. It was quite strange. Like being in a spectral world! There was some moonlight so very few fireflies could be seen. Those few that were there moved aside when they saw me, but when they saw Nilanjan they did not move at all, as if they did not acknowledge his existence. Imagine! As if he was a phantom moving in a phantom world, lost in a magical inner realm.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: I arrived at a large room. Nilanjan really did have a duplicate set of keys. Otherwise how could they have opened the room? I could see from the decaying condition of the earth and brick walls that the house had been built either at the beginning of the British era or at the end of the Mughal era. It was along this road that they used to send the mail from Bengal to Delhi with mounted postal bearers. At points along the way there were arrangements for food and lodging for the riders and their horses.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: As I entered the room, I had a feeling of the strangeness of the situation. There was no light on in the caretakerʼs room, but here they had lit a wall-lamp. Although one could more or less make things out in its dim light, one couldnʼt see very well. From the open door that white apparition from the forest could still be seen indistinctly, the same white apparition that the caretaker had told me he couldnʼt see clearly at night and would inform me about in the morning.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: The bed was laid out. I lay down and covered myself with my eńd́i shawl. The room was fairly warm. Nilanjan pulled up a stool and began fanning me.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Why should you stay awake so late at night,” I said. “You should go to bed. Just let me know which room you are going to sleep in and I will call you if I need to.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “You are the guest tonight and we are the hosts,” he replied.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Even if you tell me a thousand times we wonʼt budge. Who knows how hot it may get? Iʼll keep fanning you and Iʼll make sure you donʼt get too cold either. Do you know? For a while Iʼve been feeling very remorseful. How long was I holding up the mosquito net and letting the cold air from the forest in? It never occurred to me that you were getting cold. Here, let me warm up a flannel for you.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “No, no, no,” I said. “Donʼt put me into obligation like that. You can stay in my room if you like, but you donʼt have to do anything more for me.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Iʼll stay,” he said, “and Iʼll fan you. Besides it wouldnʼt be right for me to lie down now. Who knows when some danger might present itself? The three of us will take turns staying awake. My sister will take the duty after me. Then Iʼll go out on the road to Chauparan. Itʼs also important to see if thereʼs anything dangerous on the road. When youʼre crossing Chauparan itʼll be dawn. I will have to have a word with whoever is going to look after you on your way out of Chauparan. I canʼt come so easily or talk so easily in the daylight as I can at night, you understand. So, after Chauparan, whoever takes responsibility for your care will have to remain very close to you secretly.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Now turn over to the other side. Iʼll fan the back of your head nicely. That way youʼll fall asleep faster. While Iʼm fanning you Iʼll tell you a little story. Youʼll fall asleep quicker listening to a story.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “The region where we are now used to be the far eastern part of ancient Gondwanaland. I canʼt say it was the farthest eastern part because the farthest eastern part was that part of Gondwanaland which people nowadays call Ráŕh. The eastern mountains of Gondwanaland ran parallel from west to east. Only the Rajmahal Hills in the north ran northeast instead of due east, near Sahebganj and away from the Ganges. I say the Ganges although at that time the Ganges wasnʼt there – the ocean was. At that time the Himalayas hadnʼt been formed yet so where could the Ganges come from?
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “This was during the time before the breath of humans had warmed the earthʼs air. All the way south, in the area near Meghasini peak, the mountains ran more or less southeast. The rest of the mountains ran from west to east and their last lofty peak was Sametshikhar, which today is known by the name of Pareshnath Hills. To the east of Pareshnath Hills was the ancient land of Ráŕh and to the west was Jharkhand. Of course this was before human beings came to the earth.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Into the lowest portion of the valley, between these two mountain ranges, ran the melted ice water of Gondwanaland forming the Bansh, Dwaraka, Mayurakai, Himlo, Ajay, Damodar, Dwarakeshvar, Kangsavati, Shilavati, Kaliyaghai, and Suvarnarekha Rivers – these were all very large rivers. When human beings came and made the ancient soil of Ráŕh holy with the touch of their feet, they built their dwellings on the banks of these rivers. Not only humans – those prehistoric creatures who came hundreds of thousands of years before the advent of humans also used to live on the banks of these rivers, because all living beings need water.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Do you know why Iʼm only talking about Ráŕh and not about any other part of Gondwanaland? Elsewhere it was extremely cold and full of snowstorms. There was no proper environment there for human beings to evolve. Ráŕh had the living touch of warmth, so humans came there first. They founded the worldʼs most ancient civilization and culture, which we can call the original Ráŕh culture. ( 3 )
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Nothing is static in this world – neither animate nor inanimate. It is not only that these rivers carried vital force for existence. They also led the irresistible advance of civilization and culture swiftly toward union with the sea. The civilization that is founded upstream in the river reaches its fullness downstream. No two rivers carry identical civilizations. Thus, after two rivers merge, their combined flow carries yet a third civilization.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Take, for instance, a small example. In our Birbhum there are two very small rivers: the Kopai and the Bakreshwara. The flow of these two civilizations and cultures is nearly the same. The spoken language of the people who live on their banks is also almost the same. But notice, I say ‘almost’ rather than ‘the same’ because they are not identical. Afterwards, when they join each other in Melanpur near Indas Village (the famous Indrahása from the Jain era) and become the Kuye River, then its accompanying civilization and culture becomes a little altered. The people who live on the banks of the Kuye River enjoy the blessings of both the Kopai and Bakreshwara Rivers.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Dumka, Suri, Sainthia, and Kandi – these four towns are in the Mayurakshi Valley. Their customs, behaviour, mode of living and spoken language are the same, but the Mandar hill, which is very near Dumka, is situated on the Chandan River, and thus the customs, comportment and language there is different from Dumkaʼs. Kandi is quite far from Dumka, but they are alike in all ways. Kandi is very close to Jangipur, but Jangipurʼs culture is different; its spoken language is Shershahabadiiya Bengali. You will find this kind of history with all rivers. The rivers of Ráŕh did not simply carry sand and alluvium to the sea, thereby creating the Bengal plains; they also brought the verdant riches of civilization and culture to Bengal.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “After the rise of the Himalayas from the ocean, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra brought the flow of civilization and culture with the current of their waters. The Ganges brought the Indo-Aryan culture, but near Sahebganj, where the Ganges turns south, the Gaoŕiya [a portion of Bengalee] influence over the cultural life increased. Similarly, as the Brahmaputra reached the Assam Valley near Sadiya there was a mixture of the Kiḿpuruśavarśiiya [Tibetan] and Suvarńa Dviipiiya [Burmese] civilizations. The triple mixture of these two with the Indo-Aryan gave rise to the Kamarup civilization which a little downriver became transformed into the Bengalee culture.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “The verdancy and artistry of the Bengalee civilization and culture of today has been enriched by the civilization and culture carried by the many small rivers and tributaries of Ráŕh, and with the admixture of the Ganges and Brahmaputra civilizations the Bengalee civilization has achieved its incomparable sweetness.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Nilanjan,” I said. “You have learned so much at such a young age!”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: Nilanjan replied: “Do you know what the funny thing is?” As he said this he was smiling sweetly. “You were thinking all these things yourself and I was only thinking of you. So what you were thinking vibrated my mind. I spoke so that you could enjoy hearing your own thoughts from my mouth. Now you sleep and Iʼll sit here. Donʼt worry about a thing.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: Suddenly, my sleep was broken. Nilanjan was no longer in the room; instead there was a young woman, about twenty-five or twenty-six years old. She greeted me and said, “Iʼm Nilanjanʼs elder sister, Manjula Bhanja. Nilanjan left for Chauparan to make sure that everything is okay on the road. Now Iʼve taken over the duty.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “First of all, I should mention that when Nilanjan left he put that pen on the table there to give to you. He said that if you object, then I should put the pen forcibly in your pocket.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: I looked and saw Nilanjanʼs pen glittering on the table.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “I also leave my wristwatch beside it,” said Manjula. "Whatʼs the use of a wristwatch in this pitch darkness? Indeed, our life is pitch dark in this forested area, isnʼt it? Better these things be free from the darkness of Hades and enjoy the light and air of the free world in your museum.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “I hope youʼre not feeling any inconvenience. If you do, you must let me know. Does the bed feel very hard? A little while ago I changed the bedsheet. The mattress is very stiff. It wasnʼt possible to change it so late at night. All this time Iʼve been busy trying to think of what might help you fall asleep quicker. You didnʼt really have a chance to eat, but it wasnʼt the right time to bring you food. After my duty is finished, Iʼll make you some breakfast and leave it in the car. You certainly have to eat on your way to Chauparan.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Of course, I have a strong attraction for the terrain of Gondwanaland,” continued Manjula. “But I feel more attraction for the different plants and wild animals of this area, in a word, the flora and fauna. In the laterite soil of this land you find mostly, palásh [Butea monosperma], kuśum [Schleichera oleosa], piyál (piyáshál) [Mimosa odoratassima], sal [Shorea robusta], and kendu [Disopros ambriyotres] trees. You also come across wild jackfruit, wild mango and custard-apple trees. Was the tree-life and different birds and beasts of this area the same during the end of the [[Miocene or beginning of the Pliocene]] ages when ape-men first appeared?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Well, keep in mind,” I replied, “that the custard-apple trees you find here in the wild were brought by the Portuguese about 450 years ago. What do you know about palásh?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Well, looking at the colour of the flower and its qualities, it seems to me that rather than the three varieties we have nowadays, white, red and yellow, there was only the red variety. The tree was ten times taller than the palásh trees of today. The flowers were bright red but very big in size, and the fruits were quite small but sweet and juicy.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Your thinking is correct,” I said, “because there are more palásh trees in the eastern portion of Gondwanaland. Where rivers have more or less level land on both sides you get this red soil that the palásh tree favours. The interesting thing is that in all the river basins of that area, especially the Damodar, Ajaya, Ushri, Konar, Barakar, and the Mahanadiʼs central river basin, you get ample amounts of coal – high quality coal. The primary source of material for this coal is decomposed palásh trees. Those palásh trees were not like the palásh trees of today but were the forefathers of todayʼs palásh trees.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “The part of Gondwanaland in which we are now is more or less divided into east and west by the Koyel River. The difference between east and west is not only evidenced in the terrain, but also in the flora and fauna. I would guess that the western mountains which we now call the Vindhya and Satpura Mountains were once much higher. They had peaks even higher than the Himalayas. Flora and fauna could not evolve there in the ancient past due to excessive snowfall, but the eastern mountains, although very high and snow-capped, were not as high as the western mountains. It is likely that the first appearance in the world of both flora and fauna was here, in this area, where we find our ancient Ráŕh and Jharkhand. In the west, the melted ice ran into the Arabian Sea. Although there was water, the soil was unfertile, so there was little flora and naturally little fauna as well. However, in the east, where the water from the melted snows became rivers, the cold was not so severe. So the first expression of developed life was in the land of Ráŕh – this we can be certain of.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Thus we find an abundance of prehistoric fossils in the eastern portion of the Ramgarh Hills, the Dalma Hills, the Meghasini belt, and the southeast portion of the Rajmahal Hills (Pakur and Rajmahal Subdivisions). The small hills of Bankura District, especially the Shushuniya Hills, are also an extension of this Ramgarh range. Fossils of various types of ancient animal have been found near and around these hills. Still, the greatest amount of fossils are lying in the areas closest to the Suvarnarehka, Kangsavatii, and Damodar.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “It is quite clear that the brontosaurus and other dinosaurs lived in this region. Rhinoceroses also used to roam the extremely high grasses of this area. Just two hundred years ago rhinoceroses were living in Birbhum and Kandi Subdivision. Only 125 years ago rhinoceroses were spotted in Rajmahal and Pakur.There were also huge birds of the phiuṋe variety with loose, hanging tails. I would guess that the size of a single bird was about five or six feet. Their tails used to trail on the ground and the sabre-toothed tigers of those days used to catch them easily by stepping on their tails with their paws. But when the sabre-toothed tiger disappeared from Ráŕh about 700,000 years ago, these large-bodied birds also became extinct. The descendants of these huge birds, the phiuṋe and doyel birds of today, are much smaller in size. The hyena (govághá, huŕál, hud́ár, or huńd́ár in rural Bengali – in Madhya Pradesh vighavá) of today is the descendant of this sabre-toothed tiger. Ape-men or man-apes first took birth in this part of the earth.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “There were some differences between the humans that evolved first on either side of the Koyel River in terms of intelligence and other qualities. Such differences still exist today among their descendants. On the eastern side was the dwelling place of the Muńd́á clan ( 4 ) of that primitive age, and on the western side lived the Oráṋo clan. The former belongs to the Austric group – also their language. Many Austric-family words are still used in modern Bengali – kuŕi [twenty], dulál (from dulár [darling child]) and ghád́a [neck], among others.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “The language of the Oráṋo group is kuruka ( 5 ). This family of words [Dravidian] includes pallii [hamlet], miin [fish], and teṋtul [tamarind] (tintiri → teṋturi → teṋtur → teṋtul), among others.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “The Birhorh ( 6 ) community also arose in this area in very ancient times. They are also part of the Austric family. The original home of the Malpaharhiis is in the northeast part of this area. Later they were subdued by others and forced to take shelter in the forest at the far edge of the Rajmahal Hills.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “In those ancient days there was a great deal of fighting between the ape-men and man-apes. The apes did not know the use of fire so they could not use it to burn their enemies. When humans learned the use of fire, they started to burn to death their main enemies, the apes, and eat them. During the British era also, the Birhorhs used to burn apes to death and eat them. But they also had some attraction towards the human beings; however, there is no proof that they ever ate human beings. One can deduce from this that they used to kill the apes for the purpose of eating their enemies.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “There is still another clan from this Koyel River Basin – the Asuras. They originated here and developed their own separate culture. Later they left and headed northwest in the direction of Europe. A few words from their language can still be found among the Gypsies of Central Asia and in the Romansch language of Europe.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “I can see that you really like your subject, so I also like it. How is it you know so much at such a young age?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “A few minutes ago I hardly knew anything about this subject,” she replied. “Whatever you were thinking just came out of my mouth. And whatever you were saying was reflected in the mirror of my mind.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: I continued. “Near the high mountains of this Gondwanaland there were many huge pits. With the passage of time the mountains eroded and became large hills, then smaller hills, knolls and mounds. Today also, Ráŕh and Jharkhand are full of these hills, hillocks and knolls. Thus the land is undulating. What is today the lowest portion of this undulating land was at one time deep pits. And the upper portions were very tall mountains. Although many large pits have filled up, not all of them have. In Ráŕhii Bengali they are called káṋdar (from kandara in Sanskrit). Still there are a few very large pits. You will also find large pits nearby wherever you find a colliery with an open pit.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “When I hear the word ʼpitʼ I tremble and my throat goes dry,” said Manjula.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Why?” I asked.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “It was in a pit that we had our accident,” she replied. “It was a long time ago, during British rule. I was travelling by car from Hazaribag to Gaya with my friend Vasavi and my little brother Nilanjan to do some research about Magadh. As we were approaching Gobhi our car had to swerve to avoid getting hit by a truck and it fell into a huge gorge. Oh! If I think about it even today I lose consciousness. The last thing I heard was Nilanjan crying ʼDidiʼ. I can still hear him. He was driving the car. We all fell into the gorge and were severely hurt but no one died. We remained unconscious for a long time.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: Listening to Manjula, I gradually fell asleep. Two or three times I said to myself: “Even today the three of us become afraid if we hear the word ʼgorgeʼ.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: I donʼt know when Manjula left. When I woke up again I saw a girl about Manjulaʼs age sitting in the room. I took a good look at her. It was the same Vasavi Basu that I had seen a few years before in Magadhʼs Pahariya Village. What a passion she had for archaeological research!
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: Then Vasavi started talking. “I canʼt tell you how long Iʼve wanted an opportunity to talk to you, but I never got the chance. But first, before we start talking, I have to take care of one thing. I want my locket to stay in your museum along with Nilanjanʼs pen and Manjulaʼs wristwatch. I wonʼt take ʼnoʼ for an answer. And just to be sure that you wonʼt get a chance to object, Iʼve put them in your suitcase in the car.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “What are you saying?” I replied. “The key to the suitcase is in my pocket. How did you open the suitcase? You live here so I can see how you might have a duplicate key for the room, but thereʼs no question of having a duplicate key for my suitcase.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: She replied, a little embarrassed. “Oh yes, youʼre right. How did I open it?… how did I open it?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: To save her from an embarrassing situation I asked, “Do you remember your research into eastern Magadh and your investigation of the idols and images?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Ye-e-s indeed. Most of all, your words left a strong impression on me. You really helped me so much! Do you expect that the results of cultural research throughout Magadh will be the same?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Magadh culture can be divided into four branches,” I replied, “according to river valleys: 1) Shon-Punpun, 2) Naeranjana-Mohaniya-Phalgu, 3) Kiul Valley and 4) Kśuri Valley.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “While it is certainly true that the Ganges flows through Magadh and that the civilization the Ganges brought with it from North India took on a new form when it came to Magadh, Magadh was in no way founded on the Ganges civilization. The heart of these four branches of culture was in Girivraja or Rajagir. ( 7 )
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Today the rivers of Magadh have all but dried up, but it was not always so. At one time the source of its rivers was in the deep forest. There was a great deal of rainfall in those days and the rivers used to flow twelve months a year. Today, as a result of senseless destruction of the forest, Magadh is gradually being turned into a desert. The village where we met was a little outside the Kiul valley. It falls within the jurisdiction of the Kśuri Valley. Today the Kśuri River ( 8 ) has dried up, but at one time it was a very big river. This can be ascertained by measuring the width of its source.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “It is true that, at that time, the Maháyánii Buddhist god Máriici was popular among the people. Some people used to do Maŕiici Pújá [worship] and others used to throw sand in the idolʼs face to make the god leave the village. Háriiti was also popular in Magadh, but one would not usually see both Máŕiici and Háriiti in the same place. At one spot in the Kśuri Valley we found idols of both Máŕiici and Háriiti. But these things Iʼve already told you. You took notes also.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “I did take notes, but I lost them at the time of the car accident.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “How did it happen?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “The gods live inside people,” Vasavi continued, “and the demons also build their homes inside people. Manjula certainly must have told you how we fell into a gorge and were gravely injured. We were stunned; our life-force was paralysed. Nobody lived in that area and no one came to rescue us. But one or two hours after the accident some dacoits arrived and robbed us of all our possessions. They took my notebook and whatever money and other property we had with us, but they didnʼt bother to call a doctor or try to save us by taking us to a hospital. The only things the thieves overlooked were Nilanjanʼs pen, Manjulaʼs wristwatch, and my locket, so weʼve given them to you. What good will it do if they remain in this dark underworld? Let them stay in the open air and light of your museum.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “A little while later, an English gentleman was passing by on the same road and noticed our situation. He took our three bodies in his car to a nearby health centre. Fortunately, we were still alive though our life-force was paralysed.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: I kept listening to what Vasavi was saying.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “But how long shall I go on talking about us?” she said. “You were talking about Háriiti?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Háriiti was also a Maháyána Buddhist goddess,” I continued. “The difference between Máriici and Háriiti was that Háriiti was worshipped by both the Maháyána Buddhists and the Shvetámbara Jains. We found both Háriiti and Máriici in the Kśuri River basin. One can deduce therefrom that in this part of Magadh, both Buddhism and Jainism existed side by side. Whether as enemies or friends, they lived together.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “It may also be, moreover, that this river basin was the original centre of Maháyána Buddhism. It should not be forgotten that Rajagir-Nalanda, Barhgaon, Mahavihar (Biharsharif), Paharhiya (the village of Maharshi Saiṋjaya, the philosophy teacher of Lord Buddha), and Pavapurii (the place where Vardhaman Mahavir died) are all in the Kśuri River Valley. At one time, the river had a very sharp, ( 9 ) strong current. Thus in Sanskrit its name became kśuriká. Later that became kśuri in Bengali. Here it should also be remembered that the current dialects of the Magahi language have been spread through the river basins.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Magadh also has very clear, fixed natural boundaries: The Ganges in the north, the Shon River in the west, the Ramgarh Hills in the south, and in the east Sametashikhara or Pareshanath Mountain, ( 10 ) Cákái Hill (Cakravartii Mountain, that is, Cakravartii → Cakkavatii → Cakkavai → Cákái/Cakái), Grdhrakút́a Hill (Grdhrakút́a Gidhdhkúd́a → Gidhdhaud́a → Gidhaoŕa) and Kiul River Valley. In the direction opposite Grdhrakút́a Hill is Angadesh and opposite Cakravartii Mountain is Ráŕh.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “How very interesting,” said Vasavi. “About a month after we met that time, I went back there to do some more extensive research into the Máriici and Háriiti idols, but this time I was unable to find any. Brokers who dealt in idols had stolen them and smuggled them out of the country.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “This kind of sad occurrence is a daily event in Magadh,” I replied. “So much archaeological wealth has been and is being smuggled out of Magadh that in the near future Magadh will become destitute and empty. There is no dearth of educated people in Magadh nowadays, but it seems that they are not paying proper attention to this. What the universities are doing about it I canʼt say, but I will say that both the educated people of Magadh and the universities should come forward without delay in this matter. It is unthinkable that that part of the world which is richest in archaeological wealth should be deprived of everything it has.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: Again I started falling asleep.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: The sound of the caretaker approaching woke me up. When I looked up, I saw Vasavi getting ready to leave. “The caretaker is coming so I have to go now,” she said and then left rather hastily. At first she went like the wind, then even faster . . . she went near that white object in the distance and disappeared somewhere. The next moment the caretaker entered my room.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: When the caretaker entered my room he said: “Sir, you moved into the room last night! If you had told me that you were going to move into the room in the middle of the night, I would have made all the necessary arrangements. Ah, I see youʼve laid out your bedding yourself. The bedding has also been cleaned up. And I see that the deyálgii ( 11 ) [wall-lamp] has been lit. That was being kept in the storeroom. Why did you take the risk of going into the storeroom in the dead of night like that for the wall-lamp? What if you had had an accident?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: I kept silent. If I had said anything at all it would mean having to say something about those three people. I pointed in the direction of the door and drew his attention to that white object in the distance. Then I said: “Last night, when I asked you what that white object in the distance was, you told me that you couldnʼt see properly in the darkness. Now itʼs time for me to leave. Please tell me.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: The caretaker answered as if he hadnʼt heard my question. “Oh sir, you have to leave now? Before you go, let me tell you a story of mine.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “It took place quite some time back, during British rule. Three people were travelling by car from the direction of Chauparan. For what reason, I donʼt know, they had an accident. Their car ran into a deep gorge. The three of them didnʼt appear too badly injured but they were all knocked unconscious. Whether they were killed or not is difficult for anyone to say in my opinion. One of them was a gentleman and the other two were mishibábá ( 12 ) [ladies].
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “A little while after the accident, it seems, some rogues robbed them of all their valuables, but they made no attempt to save them or bring them to a health centre. Just see what kind of brutes they were! Sometime after, an English gentleman was travelling on the same road from Gaya to Catra (Hazaribag District). He noticed the damaged vehicle, stopped his car and went down into the ditch. When he examined the three bodies, he couldnʼt tell whether or not they were dead or had had their life-force paralysed.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “One by one, he carried the three bodies to his car and drove them to a nearby health centre. At that time the clinicʼs doctor had been absent for about a month. His wifeʼs aunt was suffering from cough and cold, it seems. The English gentleman told the compounder: ʼPlease examine them and see if they are alive or not. If there is any chance at all of saving their lives, you must arrange it. Whatever the expense is, Iʼll cover it.ʼ
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “How much could a compounder know about medical science? To relieve himself of any responsibility, the compounder moved and shook the bodies a little, then pronounced them dead. The English gentleman brought the bodies straightaway to this rest-house and kept them in this room. Within a short time he arranged for their last rites and cremation.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: As soon as the caretaker left the room, Nilanjan quickly stepped in. Needless to say, this time also he had not made a sound. “How come you are in such a hurry and looking so tired?” I asked.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Just now Iʼve come from Chauparan,” he replied. “The road is all right now. In one place a banyan tree had fallen. As you know, there are quite a lot of banyan trees in Magadh. Not only nowadays, during the Buddhist era also there used to be banyan trees ( 13 ) outside many villages. One of these very old banyan trees had fallen in the road. What was I to do? I couldnʼt move it myself. You know, my body is now very light. I influenced the minds of a few elephants in the nearby jungle and brought them to where the tree was lying, and with their help I moved the banyan tree just enough so that the road was clear for a car to pass. Now your vehicle can pass freely through there. But you should still drive carefully. I will also accompany you.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Do you have a motorcycle?” I asked.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “No,” he replied. “I donʼt have a motorcycle. How I will go still isnʼt fixed. When we get to Chauparan Iʼll tell you how I will go. The ladies also insist on coming.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “If they go with you and also come back with you,” I said, “then what objection can there be?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Iʼll let them know that youʼve given permission then. I also informed those who have taken responsibility to look after you after you leave Chauparan. Their bodies burn in the hot daytime sun so even if they want to come they wonʼt be able to do so. But theyʼll come with you secretly. They gave me their word that they wonʼt allow any harm to come to you before you get to Ranchi.”

chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Do they move throughout the building?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Yes, they go everywhere, but it was in this room that the bodies were kept, and probably for that reason they seem to frequent it a little more.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Have you seen them yourself?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “I havenʼt seen anyone clearly face to face, but sometimes in the evening, when it gets completely quiet everywhere and I start feeling drowsy, I feel as if someone is passing by me, going into the room, then going out of the room.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Do they ever disturb anyone or cause anyone any harm?”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Not at all, absolutely not. They are very civilized. But when people see them they get dizzy with fear.”
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: “Then how is it they are like humans?” I asked.

Then I saw that this gentleman had brought a pillow from the room and set it down next to my head in such a way that when I turned over, my head would come to rest on the pillow.”
