t: Another name for the Nagpuri language is Sádánii or Sadarii. This language belongs to the Occidental Demi-Mágadhii family. The other languages of this Occidental Demi-Mágadhii group are Magahi, Bhojpuri and Chatrishgarhi. The Oriental Demi-Mágadhii-derived languages are Maethili, Angika, Bengali, Assamese, and Oriya. These are the nine chief languages derived from Mágadhii Prákrta that are spoken today.
chapterTitle: Gondwana and the River Civilizations of Bengal

t: Human life is the most developed and final stage of animal life. The speciality of human life is that it has dharma. In animal life there is no dharma.
Civilization is a collection of usages, manners, etiquette, formalities, ideologies and love. The culture of the entire humanity is the same, but civilization varies from society to society.

Human civilization is created in, and moves along, river valleys. Like a river, human civilization also has three stages – hill stage, plain stage and delta stage. From the hill stage, it moves to the plain stage and from the plain stage to the delta stage. A civilization starts in the hill stage, develops in the plain stage, and matures in the delta stage.

Why are civilizations created in, and why do they move along, river valleys? In ancient times, up until the Stone Age, humans could not dig wells and depended upon natural sources of water. As such, human habitation started from springs, fountains, waterfalls, rivers, etc. Animals also select such places for habitation; only birds do not follow this rule. Thus, human habitation started near valleys, fountains, waterfalls, springs, and particularly near rivers. Due to the assemblage of humans in the river valleys, the first stage of civilization started there.

The relation between man and man, man and woman, individual and collective requirements, individual and collective responsibilities – how to move singularly and collectively – the collection of all these is civilization. It has already been said that civilization starts in the hill stage, develops in the plain stage, and attains maturity in the delta stage. Naturally, the delta stage is the finality of a civilization.

The hill stage of the Gauṋgá (Ganges) River Valley civilization in India started from the Garwal and Kumaun ranges of Uttar Pradesh (UP). The rest of UP and Bihar is in the plain stage, and the delta stage starts from Maldah in West Bengal. The hill stage of the Brahmaputra Valley civilization starts from Tibet and Arunachal. Its plain stage lies in Assam and its delta stage starts from the districts of Goalpara, Mymensingh, and Rangpur (now in Bangladesh).

The delta is that stage where the river starts to merge into the sea by the shortest route. In the delta stage, tributaries have no prominent role. In the hill stage, tributaries play the dominant role, and there are hardly any branch rivers. In the plain stage also, tributaries have the dominant role in the growth and manifestation of civilizations, but branches also have some importance. However, in the deltaic stage, branch rivers have a more important role than the tributaries.

Original civilizations (maolik sabhyatá) and blended civilizations (vimishra sabhyatá) are the two basic characteristics of civilization. A particular civilization changes in a particular way as a river moves and merges with other rivers, thus giving rise to sub-civilizations.

The Mandakini and Alakananda river civilizations emerged in the plain stage. We find the blending of these two civilizations. At the hill stage, after passing through so many mountains, hills, fountains, etc., these two rivers, Mandakini and Alakananda, come in contact with each other at the hill stage. They merge near Hardwar, and there the two simple river civilizations, Garwali and Kumauni respectively, combine to produce a blended Gauṋgá civilization, which comes up to Prayaga.

Now, another river valley civilization, the Yamuna civilization along the river Yamuna, is also a collection of several sub-civilizations comprising many customs, costumes, manners, etc. It also comes up to Prayaga. The blended Gauṋgá civilization and the blended Yamuna civilization merge at Prayaga, and a blended Gauṋgá-Yamuna civilization occurs after the river confluence at Prayaga and moves towards Varanasi. Prayaga is the second blending of manners, customs, etc., of the Gauṋgá and Yamuna civilizations.

After Prayaga we find another blending of civilizations. Therefore, there are variations in the manners, customs, languages, intonations, physical structures and economic conditions of eastern UP and western UP. A further blending occurs in the blended civilizations of the Gauṋgá and Yamuna when the Gomati, Rapti, Sone and Saraju rivers bring new trends from the northern portion of the Himalaya and Chambal-Ghaghdra River from the Vindhya ranges. Thus civilizations vary and sub-civilizations, branch civilizations, emerge at different stages of the movement of a river and its blending with other river-civilizations.
The Bundela sub-civilization emerges due to the blending of the Yamuna and Chambal civilizations. The Bagheli sub-civilization emerges due to the blending of the Yamuna and Sone.

After Káshii [Kashi] there is another blending of civilizations where several other rivers merge. Thus in this plain stage, tributaries and branch rivers play an important role in the emergence of new civilizations.

After Máldah in West Bengal, the Gauṋgá enters the delta stage – a stage where branches have the dominant role. The blended civilization of the Gauṋgá attains maturity in Bengal. Daha means the circular movement of water in a river; so it is called “Máldaha” (Maldah). At Maldah, the Gauṋgá turns to the right. The blended Gauṋgá civilization is in its highest form in the deltaic stage in Bengal.

Now it is clear that the hill stage of Indian civilizations occurs in the hill area of UP, and the rest of UP and Bihar are in the plain stage, where the Baghali, Bundeli, Avadhi, Bhojpuri, Magahi, Maetheli, and Angika sub-civilizations emerged.

The Brahmaputra civilization is a combination of the proto-Chinese and Indo-Tibetan civilizations. The civilization of Assam is a blending of the Tibetan-Chinese and Gauṋgá civilizations, due to the proximity of Assam with the Gauṋgá civilization. After this, the Brahmaputra turns to the left and enters Bengal, which is in its delta stage. The delta stage of the Brahmaputra civilization is its final stage. Bengal is the finality of the Brahmaputra civilization.

In Bengal there is another civilization as well, the civilization of Ráŕh. The hill stage, plain stage and delta stage of the Ráŕh civilization is in Bengal. So many rivers merge in the area of lower Bengal, which results in further blending. Thus in Bengal, there is a blending of three delta civilizations – the Gauṋgá, Brahmaputra and Ráŕh civilizations. This is the highest blended civilization of the world. Nature helps the people of Bengal in their intellectual progress, because no two great rivers like the Gauṋgá and the Brahmaputra merge together anywhere else in the world.

In original civilizations (maolik sabhyatá), people are physically strong. In blended civilizations, people are strong in the psychic stratum and the civilization is complicated as well as forceful. In the simple Gauṋgá civilization people are simple and physically strong; in the delta stage people are complicated, less physically strong and strong psychically.

The people of Bengal are intellectually developed because first, Bengal civilization is a blending of three deltaic civilizations and secondly, it is not a simple civilization but a great, complicated civilization – the blend and finality of three deltaic civilizations. Naturally, therefore, it is a powerful civilization, advanced in the intellectual and other spheres.
January 1986, Kolkata

While discussing destiny, or decree of fate, I still vividly remember an old story which is still vibrating my mind. I went to Allahabad to deliver a lecture on Indian philosophy in response to an invitation from the university. Usually I do not accept such invitations, but this particular case was a little different and more significant for me. First I knew many of the university administration and teaching staff, and secondly the University of Allahabad was highly reputed and influential.

My lecture was completed by evening and I left Allahabad city without delay for Muzaffarpur. My visit became urgent as I had some important work there. Suddenly, in the waiting room at Rambag Railway Station I happened to meet Sutanuka and her son Himavan. She was delighted to see me and exclaimed joyfully, “Elder brother, what a surprise! I would never have dreamed that I would meet you here.”

Sutanuka Mitra is my cousin. I had last seen her fifteen years before in Chandannagar at the marriage of her younger sister. Her husband, Arupratan Mitra, was a veteran military officer who earned a name for himself during British rule. I met him for the first time during that marriage at Chandannagar (Boŕo Káliitalá).
“Since we are meeting after such a long time,” I said to my cousin, “why donʼt you come with me to Muzaffarpur? From there youʼll be able to go directly to Burdwan.”

“Well, I was thinking to visit your place during the winter holidays,” she replied. “Himavan has to go to college, and Arupratan will be landing at Dumdum Airport the day after tomorrow after his trip to London. Heʼll be going straight to Burdwan from the airport. Our house is locked up, so if we get home late, heʼll be greatly inconvenienced.”

I realized that she was right. We decided to travel together in the same compartment from Rambag (Allahabad city) to Varanasi by narrow gauge railway and exchange stories. On reaching Varanasi I would take the narrow gauge on to Muzaffarpur and Sutanuka would take a train to Burdwan, arriving there either late at night or before dawn. It was expected that Arupratan would take a local train from Kolkata to Burdwan and reach home at about 10:00 a.m. the same day. That was finally decided. It had been a long time since Sutanuka and I had seen each other.

Though Sutanuka and her family were living in Burdwan they originally belonged to the Mitra family of Konnagar. Towards the end of Pathan rule, an intellectual society grew up in Hooghly District on the west bank of the river Bhagirathi. Konnagar was one of the intellectual centres. In those days the Ray-Mitras of Konnagar were the landlords. Konnagar was considered to be one of the most cultured and well-educated villages of Hooghly District of Ráŕh. Moreover it was one of the most famous places in the whole of Bengal. Its original name was Karnanagar. The name would be on the lips of every educated person of the locality. The people said that in Bengal if there was only one nagar or town it would be Karnanagar. If someone was asked, “Which town do you want to go?” They would reply, “There is only one town. Why should you ask ‘Which town’ [Kon nagar in Bengali]? – There is only one town: Konnagar.” And that is how the place became known as Konnagar.

I said to Sutanuka, “The name of the city weʼre about to leave is now known as Allahabad city, but its ancient name was Prayaga. Itʼs a fact that Prayaga is older than Konnagar. It was built towards the end of the Yajurvedic period [six thousand years ago]. But Burdwan is even more ancient than Prayaga. During Pathan rule Prayaga was renamed Álláha-ábád (Abode of Allah). Since then its popularity has been increasing. The Shia Moslems named the city Illahabad, but during the Mughal period, the fame and growth of the city came to a standstill. Thereafter, the city again began to flourish towards the end of the British rule when it became the capital of the United Provinces of then Agra and Oudh (UP for short).

“In the pre-Buddhist era Burdwan was the capital of Ráŕh. In the Buddhist and Jain era it remained the capital of Ráŕh. During the Mughal period (during the reign of Akbar) Burdwan was the capital of Subá-Báuṋgál [Suba Bangal]. ( 1 ) But Konnagar had no such royal glamour. It was just a cultured village of Burdwan District (the district of Hooghly was not created then). Iishan Chandra Ghosh, the renowned Bengali scholar of medieval Bengal; Rama Chandra Ghosh, the illustrious logician and author of scriptures; Pranatosh Biswas, the most erudite Sanskrit and scriptural scholar; and Dr. Krishnadhan Ghosh (Dr. K.D. Ghosh – Aurobindoʼs father), the first Bengalee District Medical Officer (DMO) and Civil Surgeon, were all born in Konnagar.” Then I turned towards Himavan and said, “Your father was born at Konnagar but you belong to Burdwan.”
He pointed out, “You told us a little while ago that Konnagar was within Burdwan District.”
I said, “Thatʼs a hundred per cent true.”

We were travelling from west to east – from ancient Brahmávartta, or Brahmarśidesh, to the ancient Kashi kingdom. That part of the Gangetic Valley is considered as the middle part of the Ganges river civilization. The Prayaga area is considered to be the upper part of the Ganges river civilization. The area stretching from Prayaga to the confluence of the rivers Shon and Ganges is the middle part of the Ganges river civilization. And the area from the Shon-Ganges confluence to Sahebganj is regarded as the pre-Gaoŕá part of the Ganges river civilization. The area from Sahebganj, where the Ganges starts flowing southward, to Gangasagar is known as the final part of the Ganges valley civilization, or Gaoŕiiya [Bengalee] civilization. The Gaoŕiiya civilization reaches the peak of its individuality where the rivers of Ráŕh, carrying with them the local cultural specialities of Ráŕh civilization, and the Brahmaputra River, coming from the northeast [and] carrying with it the flow of Mongolian civilization, merge into the Ganges. If judged properly, the part of the Gauṋgá valley civilization which was the homeland of the pre-Gaoŕiiya and Gaoŕiiya civilization cannot be called the Aryan civilization. Actually, it is the East India civilization or extended Gauṋgá delta civilization.

So the area from Allahabad to Kashi or Gandakii (here Gańd́akii means Náráyańii-Gańd́ak – not the Buŕi Gańd́ak of Muzaffarpur and Samastipur) is part of the Aryan civilization. Burdwan can be considered to be the nucleus of Ráŕhiiya civilization, and Konnagar can be regarded as the main source of the Gaoŕiiya civilization which is itself based on the Ráŕhiiya civilization. The current Bengalee civilization springs from this Ráŕhiya civilization. “So you see, Himavan, your Burdwan and your fatherʼs Konnagar are both bathed in the light of the same golden moon.”

Himavan was a B.Sc. student, but I was amazed by his ardent interest in river-valley civilizations. Even though he was a young boy he had an unusually keen interest in the origins of civilization! He asked me, “Uncle, different species of plants, trees and animals and a particular human civilization have followed the Ganges downstream from its source in Gangottari. Similarly, other species of plants, trees and animals as well as a different human civilization have followed the banks of the Yamuna downstream from its source at Yamunottari. What is the result of the merging of the Ganges and Yamuna at Prayaga?”

I answered, “Thatʼs a good question. Just as the Ganges has brought special types of flora (plants and trees) and fauna (animals) and its own alluvium along with saffron-coloured clay, the river Yamuna has also carried her own distinct characteristics down from her source. A little further downstream, another river, the Charmanvati or Chambal, carrying the distinctive features of the western Indian civilization of Málava [Malwa] and Bundelkhanda, merges into the Yamuna. In this area a new mixed civilization came into existence, which can be called the Baghelii civilization. The Yamuna carried this mixed civilization, and merged its black waters into the Ganges at Prayaga. So, the middle stage of the Gangetic Valley civilization starts from Prayaga.

“The Gangetic River Valley civilizations upriver and downriver from Prayaga are not the same. The middle stage lying to the south of the Ganges continues up to the Ganga-Shon confluence at Patna, and that lying to the north continues up to the Ganges-Náráyańii confluence near Hajipur. Thereafter the valley of pre-Gaoŕiiya civilization, on which the Austric influence is comparatively more than the Mongol-Tantric influence, begins,. This area has been known as Trihotriiya Bhúmi since ancient times. On the south of the Ganges, after the Ganga-Shon confluence, the pre-Gaoŕiiya civilization starts no doubt, but there the Mongol-Tantric influence is less than the Austric or Gondawana influence.

“From the ethnological point of view, there is a difference between Trihotriya Bhumi and Magadh Bhumi. In the physical structure of the people of Trihotriya Bhumi the Austric influence is less than the Mongolian influence. Dark people are few in number. From the complexion of the people in Magadh it is evident that the Mongolian influence is almost nil. Flat-nosed people are rarely to be seen. There are many dark-complexioned people but with aquiline noses.

“Although Trihotriya Bhumi (Videha, or Mithila) and Magadh belong to the same language group, the Mágadhii Prákrta group, the Maethili language belongs to the eastern Demi-Mágadhii group, and the Magahi language belongs to the western Demi-Mágadhii group. The difference in intonation of the languages is particularly discernible, yet both languages belong to the pre-Gaoŕiiya Gangetic civilization.

“The last part of the pre-Gaoŕiiya Gangetic civilization is noticed in Auṋga Bhúmi, where the Trihotriiya and Mágadhii cultural characteristics have blended into one. These characteristics came in contact with the Gaoŕiiya civilization. This Gangetic Valley civilization has been transformed into pure Gaoŕiiya civilization or deltaic civilization where the Ganges and the Vindhya Range have come closest to each other near Sahebganj in Angadesh, and from that point the Ganges flows southwards.”

Himavan said, “I want to do research on the subject when Iʼm grown up. But from my conversation with you I can clearly understand that this sort of research cannot be done sitting at our Borehat residence in Burdwan or at the Shyampur residence in Kolkata; rather we have to move a great deal in the fields and along the banks of the rivers.”

I said, “You are right. This type of work cannot be done theoretically or half-heartedly. One hundred per cent sincerity is required for this sort of task, and then one will achieve one hundred per cent success.”

Sutanuka said, “Well, brother, I think we have now almost reached Kashi. After a while weʼll reach Benares city by narrow gauge. Iʼd like to know how deep the Vedic influence was in this area which you describe as the middle part of the Gangetic Valley civilization.”

I replied, “Look, as far as I understand the matter from the linguistic point of view, the land of Ráŕh is the land where Sanskrit originated. But the ancient language which we describe as the Vedic language came to India from the northwest along with the Aryans. The Aryans first migrated to the Sindhu-Saoviira, and the land of Sapta-Sindhu, the Seven Rivers (Sutlej or Shatadru, Bias or Vipasha, Ravi or Iravati, Chenub or Candrabhaga, Jhelum or Vitasta, Kabul and Sind). These seven rivers together are known as the Sapta-Sindhu. Later on the land became known as the Punjab (paiṋj + áb), that is, the land of five waters [rivers]. The names of the Sindhu and the Kabul have been dropped, so there remain only five.

“This is the first phase of Vedic influence in India. In the second phase the Aryans moved further southeast: their influence extended to the northern part of the Yamuna Valley. That area they named Haritadhánya or the ‘Land of Green Vegetation’ (Haritadhánya → Hariahánna → Harihána → Hariyána).

“Then, in the next phase, the Aryans reached Prayaga around the Gauṋgá-Yamuna Valley. This we can describe as the third phase of Vedic influence. Then they moved further east, and their influence extended to the Gandakii River on the north and the Shon River on the south. This can be called the fourth phase of Vedic influence. In this area was situated the ancient Káshiirájya or Kingdom of Kashi. We are now journeying through the Káshiirájya. One thing to be noted here is that in the first phase, the Vedic language left two daughters behind: Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prákrta. In the languages born out of Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prakrta (for example, Pashto, Punjabi, etc.) there is a multitude of derived words from the Vedic language. In the second phase, that is, in the Hariyanavi language, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is somewhat less. In the third stage, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is still less, for instance in languages like Máŕoyári, Haŕaoti, Bundeli, Bagheli, Avadhi, Brajabháśa, etc. And in the languages of the fourth stage, like Bhojpuri, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is still less. But no one should misunderstand that in the fourth stage the Vedic influence was nil. No doubt the direct Vedic influence in the fourth stage was nil, but the indirect influence remained inextricably linked with pre-Gaoŕiiya and Gaoŕiiya civilizations, and that influence persists even today.”

Sutanuka said, “Iʼve noted with interest that in the fourth stage the external appearance of the people and the size of the cattle are quite different from those of the pre-Gaoŕiiya and Gaoŕiiya civilizations.”

Then I said, “Youʼre right in your observation. The structure of the human skull of people in this area is different from that of the people of the area of pre-Gaoŕiiya civilization. But the human skull of the people of Angadesh is almost the same as that of the people of the Gaoŕiiya area; the difference is hardly discernible.”

Kashi is not very far from Allahabad. After a short while we reached Benares city station by narrow gauge. Himavan said with a choked voice, “Uncle, now we must get off. I donʼt know when we shall meet again. It was a very lively and interesting discussion.”

Both Sutanuka and Himavan were repeatedly requesting me to visit them at Burdwan: they complained that I had forgotten Burdwan. I protested, saying “No, I havenʼt forgotten it – I have so many pleasant memories of Burdwan, so many songs of sweet love filled with joys and sorrows associated with Burdwan.”
They proceeded to the city centre. My private secretary approached me and said, “My in-law is sitting in the next compartment – heʼs going to Chapra.”

I said, “When your in-law is sitting nearby, why donʼt you go and have a chat with him for a while? I wonʼt mind. Tomorrow morning there is an auspicious occasion of holy bathing in the Ganges, so most of the passengers are bound for Benares. There will be relatively few passengers from Benares to Muzaffarpur. Perhaps I will be the only passenger in this compartment.”

My private secretary went to the next compartment to talk with his in-law. I supposed he was enjoying a hearty meal of lit́t́i [a type of fried or non-fried unleavened bread] soaked in ghee. The train left with a whistle, and the wheels started moving. Suddenly, a handsome gentleman dressed in military uniform came running up and, gasping for breath, entered the compartment. Immediately he approached me with rapid steps. After a while, when I looked closely at him, I was amazed to see that he was none other than my brother-in-law, Arupratan Mitra, Sutanukaʼs husband, whom I met about fifteen years ago at Boŕokáliitalá at Chandannagar! I requested him to take his seat beside me, and said to him, “How are things going – why are you running, gasping for breath? Why are you coming to meet me at 9:00 at night in this empty compartment? Iʼm on my way to Muzaffarpur; where are you going?”

Arup said, “About fifteen minutes ago, at a quarter to nine, my mind suddenly became restless and agitated with so many thoughts and feelings. I thought to myself, ‘However possible, and as fast as possible, I must come to you immediately.’ It is my firm conviction that this restlessness, this agitation, will be put to rest as soon as I come near you. I now desperately need peace… only peace. I donʼt want happiness or prosperity – I donʼt want the least amount of wealth or jewels of this vast world – I want only peace. ”
Arup sat down. He was still gasping for breath. I asked him, “When your mind became restless, where were you then?”
He replied, “I was far away from here… on the shore of a sea.”
I said, “If you were so far away from here, then how could you come here in fifteen minutes?”

With the glimmer of a sweet smile on his lips he replied, “I came very fast, so I am gasping for breath. Immediately after reaching you, my mind has become peaceful. Now I feel a deep tranquillity within.”
I said, “Unrest or peace are all in the mind. Well, let us talk for a while.”

Arup said, “Some time ago I heard from someone that you have already addressed a few symposia on river valley civilizations. I couldnʼt realize what it was, but I guessed that you might have said something about how at the different stages of rivers the patterns of civilizations vary.”
I asked him, “Were you then in Britain?”

He answered, “Yes, I was,” and continued, “Perhaps you know that Great Britain is a small country; the distance from any part of Britain to the ocean is not more than fifty miles. So naturally in that country there cannot be any large river: the distance between the source of a river and the ocean cannot be very great. Yet if we move along the banks of certain rivers, there is a difference between the civilization of the upper areas of the river and the lower ones, and there is also a variation in language.

“Take for example the case of the Thames: it is not a big river, either in length or in breadth. The part of the Thames where the ships sail is not really a river; it is only an estuary of the sea, just like the Matla near Canning. Many people think that the Matla is perhaps a wide and large river. They may think that in olden days that Vidyadharii, the southern branch of the Yamuna, emerging from the Ganges at Trivenii, moved southwards, and then it and the southeastern tributary Piyali of the Ganges both flowed separately for a certain distance and then joined together to form the Matla. Though this is a fact, yet the collective waters of these two combined rivers are quite small. In fact, the Matla is nothing but the backwater or kháŕi of the sea entering into the land. The proper English word for kháŕi is ‘estuary’.

“The deltaic portion of the Thames is somewhat similar. The more one proceeds down the river from the source of the Thames, the greater is the Anglo-Saxon and Norman influence. If one moves from the southern bank of the Thames along the coast of the Straits of Dover and the English Channel, there is still a tremendous Norman influence, like a subterranean flow. If one moves from the northern side of the river towards the port of Grimsby on the delta at the coast, there is a greater Anglo-Saxon influence than Norman influence. If one moves towards the coast, the Norman influence becomes negligible. Where there is Norman influence, there are large numbers of Latin derivations in the spoken language. Where the Anglo-Saxon influence is predominant, the number of Latin derivative words is comparatively little. The difference in intonation in the respective areas, too, is quite discernible.

“If one moves towards the opposite part of the Thames, or towards Wales in the west, the ancient Briton influence is not negligible, even in the spoken language. This is the reason why, though Welsh is a language of a small country, yet it has certain specialities of its own. Even the difference in peopleʼs external appearance, though not very prominent, is not negligible either.”
I said, “You are right, Arup, in your observation. I notice that both you and Himavan are equally interested in river valley civilizations. I was not aware of this before!”

Arup blushed and smiled faintly. He said, “Perhaps you once said that in our land of Ráŕh, on either bank of the Bakreshwar River in central Birbhum, there is a local civilization. Though small in area, it has its own speciality even in the style of its temples and also in its terracotta works. There is also a difference in the use of verbal forms in the spoken language of that area. Similarly, in southern Birbhum also, there is a small river called the Kopai (Kupitá, or "angry") in whose valleys there is also some sort of local civilization. As far as I remember, someone said that the water of the Bakreshwar Valley is one of the best for it is full of sulphur. But the water of Kopai Valley, though it is as good as that of many places in Bengal, is not as good as that of the Bakreshwar Valley. The two small rivers, with their own distinctive streams of water, flow from the west to the east in cadence with the soil of the most ancient human civilization, that of the land of Ráŕh. When the two rivers meet at Melanpur [meaning “meeting place”] at one end of the area under the jurisdiction of the Nanur Police Station, they are known as Kuye, and at that point both their local civilizations become blended. Melanpur really joins the two rivers in all respects. If one listens intently to the local dialect, one will hear a particular drawled intonation which is lacking in west Birbhum. Besides this, other local variations also came into being there.”

I said, “You are right, Arup. Really I am delighted by your description. The specialities of the river valley civilizations are very distinct in our Birbhum. In the upper reaches of Birbhum, the spoken language has no drawled intonation: it is one of the flawless branches of the Ráŕh language. But in the lower reaches of Birbhum, the same Ráŕh dialect has a local drawl – have you noticed it?”

Arup said, “Yes, I have. This subtle difference in intonation between the area of the Khayrasol Police Station and Labpur Police Station, and again between the Khayrasol Police Station and the Mayureshvar Police Station, can be easily discerned just by listening to it.”
Arup said, “Though it is not directly concerned with culture, still it is a funny story…”
Smiling a little, I looked at Arup and asked him, “What do you mean?”

Arup said, “At Khayrasol in the upper reaches of Birbhum, there is widespread use of poppy seeds, whereas in the lower reaches, the use of poppy seeds is less by five to seven per cent. That is to say, in the upper reaches there is an empire of poppies, and in the lower reaches there is merely a kingdom of poppies!”

Arup burst into laughter. I too joined in his laughter. To continue, I said, “The other symbols of Ráŕh culture – like d́iḿle [a type of pumpkin], kheŕo [another type of pumpkin], green gram, jhumur dance are equally popular in both the upper and lower reaches.”

Arupratan smiled, and said with a voice growing in excitement, “Yes, brother, Iʼve noticed that too. You see, although I live in Burdwan in central Ráŕh, I was actually born in Konnagar in the low-lying area of Ráŕh. In our place also, pumpkin and green gram are very popular, and people can hardly live without poppy seed.”
“By the way, Arup”, I said. “You rushed into this compartment at exactly nine oʼclock. How long were you able to speak with Sutanuka and Himavan on the platform?”
Arupratan exclaimed in wide-eyed amazement, “What! Did Sutanuka and Himavan come here?”

“Donʼt you know that?” I asked. “They accompanied me in this very compartment from Allahabad city and got off the train in Benares. They were in a hurry to get to Kashi where they were planning to catch an evening train which would get them to Burdwan by dawn on Wednesday morning. They told me that you were expected to land at Dumdum Airport at around the same time, and that you would take a local train from Howrah to Burdwan, reaching there at about ten the same day. They have the keys of the house, so if you were to arrive there before them you would be put to great trouble. They knew they had to reach Burdwan by dawn on Wednesday by any means.”

“No, I didnʼt see them,” said Arupratan. “I missed them at Benares railway station. But what you said was correct: I was expected to arrive at Burdwan at ten on Wednesday morning.” He paused for a while and then continued. “They shouldnʼt catch any train which will get them there late at night or at dawn – I apprehend some danger.”

“If you sense some impending danger, under no circumstances should they catch any Burdwan train at that particular time. You should get off the train at the next station and find some way to go to Kashi.” And I advised him, “Youʼd better go to Kashi and look for them in all the probable places. They have to be prevented from taking any of those Burdwan trains.” He said, “Thatʼs a good idea. Thatʼs a good idea.”

The train slowed down. We were approaching a station, no doubt. Arupratan jumped to his feet, rushed to the door, and, looking like a crow ruffled by a raging tempest, leapt onto the platform without waiting for the train to stop. He had reason enough to be worried.

As soon as the train stopped, my private secretary hurriedly entered my compartment. I guessed he had just finished his dinner of lit́t́i [a type of fried, unleavened bread] with his in-law. Perhaps his in-law had also served him kaŕiibaŕii [a type of dumpling made of chick-pea flour and served in yoghurt water] and mákhána kśiir [a type of sweet] for dessert. My private secretary sat beside me and asked me if I had been inconvenienced in any way. I said I hadnʼt. Our train was moving from west to east across the border of the ancient Kashi state.

I had told Himavan, that this was the last area to come under Aryan influence. In the fourth phase of the Aryan invasion of India, Kashi can be regarded as a border state of northern India [Áryávartta]. In those days the Sarayu was considered to be the eastern border of Áryávartta. The Sarayu not only carried the Aryan influence along its banks but also Mongol and to some extent Austric influence as well. That is why its eastern bank was considered to be non-Aryan land. Later on this boundary was further extended to the Gandakii (Náráyańii Gańd́ak) which was accepted as the eastern end of the land. The Kanyakubja Brahmans of those days did not like to cross the Sarayu. As the land on the other bank was non-Aryan, it was regarded as unholy. They were afraid they would lose their Aryan purity. Those Kanyakubja Brahmans who dared to cross the river, being lured by the fertile land of the trans-Sarayu area, were declared outcastes. They lost their identity as Kanyakubja Brahmans and became known as Sarayupari Brahmans.

During Pathan rule, the last boundary of Áryávartta was the present Ghazipur District. In those days North India consisted of three subas [administrative divisions]: Suba Bangal on the east, Suba Punjab on the northwest and Suba Hindustan between the two. Even today, the people of Bengal and the Punjab call the inhabitants of the middle part of northern India “Hindostani”. Some people are of the opinion that as Hindustan means the whole of India, why should the inhabitants of a small part of India be called Hindustani? However, this is wrong, because the term “Hindustani” is used for the people who were once the inhabitants of Suba Hindostan, and not in the sense of Hindustan as being the whole of India. During the Mughal period when Akbar divided his empire into fifteen subas, the northern part of Suba Hindostan and the southern part were named Oudh and Suba Agra respectively. Ghazipur District was the last boundary of Suba Agra. On the east of Ghazipur District lies Balia District (Bahliika). In those days Balia District was in existence. Previously it was only a subdivision of Ghazipur District. Similarly, there was no Deoria District in those days. It was only a subdivision of Gorakhpur District.

The British occupied both Agra and Oudh Subas and made one administrative unit out of them – the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (UP for short) with its capital at Allahabad. In the last part of British rule, the capital was moved to Lucknow. In any case, there was a marked influence of Mongol and Austric cultures on the Aryan society inhabiting the Sarayu River Valley. Later on many Aryans crossed the Sarayu and declared the banks of the Gandakii as the boundary line of Áryávartta. The area lying on the west of the Gandakii Valley was called Shákyárańya and the area on the east was called Videha or Mithila. This latter area was not considered as an Aryan colony. I personally consider it as part of the area covered by the pre-Gaoŕiiya Gangetic Valley civilization.

King Mithi occupied Videha. To sanctify the land he held a Trihotriiya Yajiṋa (a big sacrificial rite presided over by three priests). It was then declared sacred. The land sanctified by the performance of a Trihotriiya Yajiṋa was named Trihut. The land of Shákyárańya, although not widely valued by the Aryans, was respected by the Buddhists. Lord Buddha visited it several times. Later, it became known as Shárańa (Shákyárańya → Shákyárańa → Shárańa). In later years it was wrongly spelt as Sharan.

On the north of Shákyárańya was the ancient and famous place, Champakárańya. A reference is made to it in the Rámáyańa [one of the two great Sanskrit epics] (Campakárańya → Campárańya → Campárań). Shakyaranya and Campakaranya are situated on the western bank of the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka Valley. On the eastern bank is Videha or Mithila or Trihut, the land which was occupied by King Mithi. Mithi + lá [holder] + d́a [suffix] + á [feminine suffix] = Mithilá. In the Buddhist period one of the famous villages of Shákyárańya was Hatthiigrám (Hastiigráma in Sanskrit). Buddha visited this place a number of times. It is now known as Háthoyá. During British rule the Háthoyá estate was one of the biggest estates in India.

Then came the river Gandakii – Náráyańii Gańd́aka. The biggest cattle fair in India, known as the Hariharkśetra fair, is held once a year on the banks of this river. Nearby is the Shonpur railway station.

Immediately after crossing the Gandakii River bridge at Shońpur we reached Mithila. During the Mughal period and the early part of British rule, the Mithila division of Bengal Presidency consisted of three districts: Trihut, Champaran and Sharan. The district headquarters of Champaran was Motihari, that of Sharan was Chapra, and that of Trihut was Muzaffarpur. This latter district was named after Muzaffar Shah. It covered a wide area, and until the early part of the British period its fertile soils were thickly forested. The forests contained an abundance of numerous species of flora and fauna, notably tigers, antelopes, crocodiles, pythons and deer. The large lake (called ma-a-na in local dialect) on the ancient river course of the Lakhandei in the eastern part of Muzzaffarpur town covered a larger area in those days and was surrounded by extensive forests full of abundant flora and fauna. A major part of the forest was part of the king of Darbhangaʼs estate. Some of it was within the Shúraśańd́a kingdom, and some part belonged to the estate of the Bettiah king. People today, out of necessity, but also out of immense greed have destroyed most of the forest, particularly in Trihut District.

At Vaeshali ( 2 ) in Trihut District Vardhaman Mahavir was born into a Vaeshya family. His fatherʼs name was Siddhartha and his mother was called Trishala. Trihut District as well as Mithila were located partly in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka Valley and partly in the Burigandaka and Lakhandei Valleys. There was more Gaoŕiiya influence here than that of Áryávartta. The Bengali script was used here. It is to be noted that both Buddha and Mahaviira were born in a place where there was relatively less Aryan influence.

Trihut District was quite large in area. The British divided it into two parts: Muzaffarpur District in the west with its headquarters at Muzaffarpur, and Darbhanga District in the east with its headquarters at Laheriasarai village (which has since become a large city; it almost touches the city of Darbhanga). The old Muzaffarpur District is now divided into three districts: Sitamarhi, Muzaffarpur and Vaeshali (Hajipur). This is the same Muzaffarpur which was regarded as one of the most cultured places in the whole of the then Suba Bangal. The old Darbhanga District has since also been divided into three districts: Madhubani (a place where there is an abundance of forest honey); Darbhanga (named after the famous Dáŕibhangá Shah; in Maethili the town is called “Daiŕbhanga” but spelt “Daŕibhangá”); and Samastipur (named after Samasti Narayan Ray).

The Maethili branch of the pre-Gaoŕiiya Valley civilization was enriched by the Mongol-Tantric civilization that flourished in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka, Buri-Gandaka, Lakhandei, Bagmati, Kamalabalan and Koshii Valleys. King Prithvi Narayan Shah established the Gorkha empire in Nepal at this time. The Gorkhas occupied Tirhut District and advanced up to Hajipur. Thereafter they were defeated by the British (the British commander-in-chief was General Octorloney, in whose name the Englishmen living in Kolkata built a war memorial – in recent times, the leaders, ignorant of history, have changed the name of the Octorloney Memorial to Shahid Minar [Martyrsʼ Column]) and were forced to sign the Treaty of Sugaoli (Champaran District). According to the terms of the treaty, the British got possession of Garhwal and Kumayun regions from Nepal, which was included in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and they also reclaimed a major portion of Champaran and Trihut Districts. Part of the northern portion of Trihut was left in Nepal and is still part of Nepalese territory. The former capital of Mithila, Janakpur, is situated in that area. Many people of Bengal know the famous Janakpur catechu.”

I got off the train at Muzzafarpur and spent two days of intense activity there. I arrived home about a week later, my mind full of pleasant memories. Waiting for me on the table was a letter from Himavan, sent from Burdwan, in which he wrote: “Dear Uncle, We had a shocking experience on our return to Burdwan. We left Kashi late Tuesday evening and were sure that we would reach home either late Tuesday night or Wednesday morning at dawn. Late into the night, mother and I were discussing river valley civilizations when we suddenly heard a huge crash and felt a severe jolt. I donʼt remember ever having heard such a loud noise in all my life. In a fraction of a second the train seemed to be smashing into pieces. There was commotion all around – people were screaming – chaos reigned everywhere. The train smashed into smithereens. Mother and I were violently thrown out of the derailed compartment. Pieces of train and the passengersʼ baggage were scattered here and there. We realized we were the victims of a tragic accident and death was inevitable – who knows how many were lying dead. Both of us were violently thrown towards a huge part of the derailed train. We screamed in fear. Then an amazing thing happened. Suddenly both of us perceived my father, Shri Aruprathan Mitra, rushing towards us. Grabbing each of us by the hand and pulling us out of the wreckage, he flung us to some distance. Thus we were saved from the jaws of inevitable death. What happened next we cannot say, for we both became unconscious.

“When the rays of the rising sun fell onto our faces we regained consciousness and, looking around, discovered that we were lying on a hay-stack on the edge of a paddy field beside the railway line. As we had fallen onto hay, our injuries were not severe – just some pain in our bones. A crowd of villagers had gathered around us. We saw the wreckage of the train in the distance and heard the pitiful screams and lamentations of the seriously wounded.

“The local people were very kind, as the people of Burdwan usually are. On seeing the slightest hardship of others, tears come into their eyes. Those people standing around us desperately wanted to help and kept asking what they could do to make us feel more comfortable. They were prepared to do anything to help. We asked them, ‘Please look for my father and to bring him to where we are lying.’

They searched everywhere for him, but without success. ‘Thereʼs no one called Arupratan Mitra here,ʼ they said. They helped us get to our feet – which we could only do with great difficulty – so that we could also look for him. But our search was also unsuccessful. My father was not to be seen anywhere. By that time the railway auxiliary van had arrived from Burdwan. We approached the authorities and with their help returned to Burdwan. The site of the accident was near Burdwan so we didnʼt have much difficulty getting home.
“Well, uncle, how were we saved? Is it called ‘fate’ or is it perhaps the work of destiny?”

I was utterly shocked by what I read. Himavan wrote further: “Father has not yet arrived in Burdwan. We went to the airport to make some enquiries about him and learnt that the plane he was supposed to take still hadnʼt reached Dumdum Airport. The ground staff informed us that they had received no news as to the planeʼs whereabouts, nor was it possible for them to find out for reasons of military security. The plane was carrying a military cargo and the passengers were military personnel. As a result, the military department was trying to black out all news about the non-arrival of the plane.”

No sooner had I finished reading the letter than I heard an announcement on the radio news. The news bulletin disclosed that there was a serious plane crash somewhere along the Mediterranean coastline last Monday at 8.45 p.m. Due to certain military reasons, the exact details could not be disclosed earlier. All the passengers died in the crash. From the passenger list provided at the airport it appears there were twenty Indian passengers. Their names and addresses have been confirmed, but the dead bodies were so severely burned that identification is impossible. The names of the Indians are 1)… 2)… 3)… 4)… Among the passengers there was a man from Kolkata, a Shri Arupratan Mitra.

I was speechless. I pieced all the events together and concluded that it was indeed at 9 p.m. on Monday that Shri Arupratan, gasping for breath, rushed into my compartment at Benares railway station. He told me that he had been feeling considerable mental unease for the past fifteen minutes, since 8.45. His mind was terribly restless. He had come to me in quest of peace. He had travelled a long distance and that is why he was gasping for breath.
After hearing the news I was so bewildered that I was unable to decide what to do. How should I reply to Himavanʼs letter, I thought.
January 1986, Kolkata

Perhaps many of you are aware that Gaoŕa Desh is the old, traditional name of our Bengal. It was named Gaoŕa Desh because it earned worldwide recognition in the production of guŕ [raw sugar]. Not only raw sugar made from sugarcane, but she also produced, and still does, a range of raw sugar made out of date palms, palmyra, coconut trees (prepared from the sap), juice of gol trees [Nipa fruticans], etc. Raw sugar was also extracted in ancient Bengal from a class of potatoes known as sháṋkhálu [yam bean, Pachyrrhizus erosus], as also from the mahul (madhuka → madhula → mahuyá → mahul) flower [Madhuca indica] of Ráŕh. The mahul flower is boiled before raw sugar is produced from its decoction. Besides raw sugar itself, several varieties and several types of sugar were also produced from raw sugars with the help of pát́áshyáolá [a type of reagent]. This sugar was sold at premium rates to the Egyptian, European and Chinese markets. There was a large demand for cakes (pát́áli or navát) of raw sugar also. Nor did the sweetmeat guŕsandarbha, made by mixing sunned rice powder with raw sugar, enjoy any lesser acclaim.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: This land of ours had the distinguished name Paiṋca Gaoŕa because it was primarily divided into five parts. The first was Ráŕh, which was also the largest. The word ʼRáŕhʼ is a derivative of the Austric word ‘Ráŕho’, which signifies a land of undulating slopes with a red soil. This territory of ours called Ráŕh comprises the contemporary districts of Midnapur, Howrah, Hooghly, Burdwan, Birbhum, Bankura, West Murshidabad or Ráŕh-Murshidabad, Dumka, Sahibganj, Deoghar, Gadda, Dhanbad, Purulia, Singbhum, Bhanjabhum, the eastern part of Ranchi, and southeast Giridih. This land of Ráŕh – the cradle of human civilisation, the fountainhead of Bengalee civilisation – is over three hundred million years old.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Samatat, the second part of Gaoŕa Desh, is the area covered by the Gauṋgá-Brahmaputra delta. The commonly used Bengali term for Samatat is Bagri, which consists of contemporary East Murshidabad (Bagri Murshidabad), Nadia, North 24-Parganas, South 24-Parganas, Kolkata, Khulna, Jessore, Kushthia, Goalanda, Gopalaganj and Patuakhali Districts and parts thereof. Nor is the civilisation of Samatat a modern-day one; it is decidedly pre-Vedic. It is true that the men of Ráŕh, clearing the jungle, set up habitation in Samatat when it raised itself out of the depths of the seas, with the help of their axes and shovels. So, the predecessors of the present inhabitants of Samatat came from Ráŕh. That was a long time back. Till this day, the Brahmans of Samatat are Ráŕhii Brahmins, the Kayasthas and Vaidyas [castes] are Ráŕhii Kayasthas and Ráŕhii Vaidyas. King Sagara, who finds mention in the Rámáyańa, was a king of the same Samatat. The word ságara [“sea”] is obtained by the conjunction of sagara [“all”] with the suffix ań. Samatatʼs fame in the art of warfare has endured since prehistoric ages.

t: Even in modern ages, many a son of Samatat has displayed particular talent in the art of warfare. King Bhagirath of this same Samatat excavated a hundred canals (Bhagirathii, Jalangi, etc.) from the river Padma and connected them to the sea. This is why the Ganges is also known as “Shatamukhii” [“river with a hundred mouths”]. These branches of the Ganges have rendered the soil of Samatat even more green and fertile.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: The third part of Gaoŕa Desh – Barendra (Bariind) – was to the north of Samatat, that is, on the northern shores of the Ganges or Padma and the eastern shores of the river Koshii. Samatat has been named thus because it is a plain (samatal) region – the same applies to Bagri. In just the same manner, the northern part of Padma is named Barendra, as it is composed of a mixture of different types of soils. The word bar means “the best”; so does the word indra. The etymological meaning of barendra is, therefore, “the best among the best”. The land of Barendra is somewhat older than Samatat. Besides, there were a number of large islands in the ocean adjoining this region in those days. Subsequently, the areas surrounding these islands filled up and became one and the same with the main land. The topography of these ancient Bariind plains can be seen in present-day Maldah-Dinajpur.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: The part of Gaoŕa Desh that lies to the north of the banks of the Padma or the Ganges, however, to the west of River Koshii, is known as Videha or Mithilá (mithi + lá + d́a + t́á, meaning “the land that was conquered by King Mithi”) or Tirhuta. The land that was sanctified by King Mithi through Trihotriiya Yajiṋa [a ritual which is performed by three chief priests or hotá] is Tirhuta or Tirabhúmi.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: The portion of Gaoŕa to the east of Barendra and Samatat, which was watered by many rivers, had the name Vauṋga (D́abáka). Vauṋga was an extremely fertile land. Although young by geological considerations, the civilization of Vauṋga evolved much before the emergence of the Vedic civilization. If not in well-defined documentation, Vauṋga does find mention in the Shatapatha Bráhmańa. The word bauṋga means “a fine or thin metal”. As the superior craftsmen and goldsmiths of Bauṋga were capable of producing delicate ornaments, the land was named “Bauṋga” (whose original meaning is “tin” or “ráuṋ”) as a mark of appreciation for these artisans. In later years, many people started writing “Vauṋga” instead of “Bauṋga”. Therefore, both “Vauṋga” and “Bauṋga” are acceptable spellings in Sanskrit. The Dhaka region of the present day represents this ancient Vauṋga. There was a time when the craftsmanship, wisdom, and acute desire to fulfil the ultimate aims of humanity that distinguished Vauṋga won the praise of the whole world.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: It was the people of Ráŕh that settled in Vauṋga when it rose from the sea. Some of them call themselves “Bauṋgaja” while others retain their Ráŕhiiya identity. For instance, a new society established by the group of Kayasthas who moved from Haripal of Ráŕh to Vauṋga is known as the Bauṋgaja Kayastha society. The society formed by the Vaidyas who migrated to Bauṋga from Shriikhanda of Ráŕh was known as the Bauṋgaja Vaidya society. However, the Ráŕhiiya Brahmans from Burdwan, Birbhum, Bankura and Manbhum who settled in Bauṋga continue to call themselves Ráŕhiiya Brahmans instead of Bauṋgaja Brahmans. A large number of people from Samatat and Barendra had built their homes in Bauṋga, the new land that had just made its appearance arising from out of the water. Hosts of Brahmans belonging to Barendra who had moved to Dhaka and Mymensingh still call themselves Bárendra Brahmans and not Bauṋgaja Brahmans.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: By comparison, Ráŕh was the largest part and Mithila the smallest. Because of its huge area, the northern part of Ráŕh was known as Vardhaman ( 1 ) Bhukti (Burdwan is the oldest city in the world). The southern part (Midnapore District) was known as Dańd́a [Danda] Bhukti. Although Barendra was smaller than Ráŕh, it was not all that small. Barendra also had two divisions – the northern part was Kamtapur Bhukti and the southern part was Paondravardhana Bhukti. Being relatively small, Samatat, Vauṋga and Mithila had no divisions.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: In ancient times, people outside Bengal called that land Gaoŕa Desh or Paiṋca Gaoŕa. The word bauṋgál, whose etymological meaning is “a place adjacent to Bauṋga”, came into circulation after the Buddhist period. In the [Sanskrit story] Vetálapaiṋcaviḿshati, the Vetala [ghoul] is said to tell Emperor Vikramaditya, “Emperor, in the city of Burdwan of Gaoŕa Desh…” In the Caryácaryavinishcaya we find [the sentence] “Bhu-su-ku, today you have become a Bengalee” (Bhu-su-ku áj tu Bauṋgálii bhaelii). Some people think that the name “Bauṋgál” came into being after the Pathan rule. However, this is not quite true. Over the past five thousand years, this Gaoŕa Desh of ours has been referred to as “Baiṋjalá” in the Chinese language. In Latin, the land is called “Banjal” (a product of Bengal is banjalitis in Latin). In the Turkish language, it is “Báuṋgálá” and in Arabic it is “Báuṋgálá”. (In ancient Arabic, there was no distinction between ga and ja – as an example, both gawahar and jawahar were in use. This usage had its influence on other Middle Eastern languages as well.) It is “Bauṋgál” in Farsi, Urdu and Hindi, “Bengal” in English, “Gaoŕa Desh” in Sanskrit, and “Báuṋgládesh” [Bangladesh] in Bengali.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Respected Mujibur Rahman Marhum gave the name “Bangladesh” to East Pakistan, which had been formed out of portions of Bengal and Gaoŕa Desh. Present-day Bangladesh consists of a substantial portion of Vauṋga, the south-eastern part of Barendra (Rangpur, Bagura, Pabna and Rajshahi Districts) and the eastern part of Samatat (Kusthia, Jessore, Khulna, etc). However, it is not only Dhaka that represents Bangladesh; Burdwan, Dumka and Tatanagar also do. When Satyendranath wrote –
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Se amáder Báuṋgládesh, ámáderi Báuṋglá re.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: [It is our own Bangladesh, our own Bangla]
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: – he had in mind the entire Bangladesh or Gaoŕa Desh or Paiṋca Gaoŕa. His observation was not limited to the erstwhile East Pakistan alone. Our contemporary West Bengal contains almost half of Ráŕh, the northern and western parts of Barendra and the western part of Samatat. Not a speck of the land that was Vauṋga now belongs to West Bengal. However, Tripura, Cachar, Karimganj, etc., are parts of that glorious Vauṋga of olden days. If today, an extravagantly learned person refers to Burdwan-Purulia, Nadia-24 Parganas or Jalpaiguri-Balurghat as ”Vauṋga”, that would be tantamount to calling Burdwan-Purulia Gujarat, Nadia-24 Parganas Rajasthan, or Jalpaiguri-Balurghat the Punjab. How ridiculous it is!
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Our Gaoŕa Desh can be conveniently named a “Gaoŕa Desh”, “Paiṋca Gaoŕa” or “Bangladesh”. It can also be named “Báuṋálistán” (Bangalistan) following the logic adopted while naming Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Nagaland or Mizoram. ( 2 ) That would not mean something alarming or turn things upside down. On the contrary, the name would offer that identity to the land which confirms that it is the motherland of the Bengalees.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: from Discourse 81
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Shabda Cayaniká Part 12
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Before the division of India, most of the date-palm trees were in the undivided Nadia District (in Nadia District of the present West Bengal, Kusthia District of Bangladesh and in Jiivananagar Police Station of undivided Chuadanga). However, the main habitat (mokán ) of date-palm trees was in Kortchandpur in Jessore. In modern India, 24 Parganas is the biggest producer of date-palm raw sugar, followed by Bankura District.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Bengal has earned its reputation as a producer of guŕ [raw sugar] and ciinii [refined sugar] since ancient times. The produce was exported abroad. Remember that raftánii [export] and ámdánii [import] are also Farsi words. All three types of raw sugar – those made from sugarcane, from palm and from date-palm – were exported from Bengal. The sugar ( 3 ) that used to be exported was made from sugarcane and date palms. It is not known whether raw sugar in liquid juice formed an item of export. However, dry raw sugar cakes (pát́áli) were definitely exported.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Yes, the subject reminds me of the word guŕ [raw sugar]. Guŕ is an age-old Vedic word. Nevertheless, it has not evolved but has survived merrily in several Indian languages. Many are of the opinion that the ancient Vedic people were not familiar with sugarcane. It was only after their arrival in India that they were first introduced to sugarcane (ákh and kushiár – both are Bengali equivalents). Maybe that is true. However, if they were not familiar with sugarcane, how did they know about raw sugar? The word guŕ happens to be an old Vedic word. That they were aware of guŕ is evident from the fact that the following edict was applied to several Vedic ceremonies:
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Madhvabháve guŕaḿ dadyát.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: [Raw sugar will suffice in case you are unable to arrange honey]
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: This goes to prove that they did know about raw sugar. On the other hand, it is possible that one may know about raw sugar even without knowing about sugarcane when the raw sugar is imported. For instance, although England does not produce sugarcane, it is neither impossible that they are familiar with raw sugar produced in India, nor impossible that they have their own name for it. Again, it is also possible that they [i.e., the Vedic people] were familiar with both raw sugar and sugarcane, but because they did not have script, we have come to know the part of their oral literature that contains references to gúr, but not the part that contains references to sugarcane. Due to the fact that different kinds of raw sugar and sugarcane were available in our homeland, the territory was named ”Gaoŕa” by adding the suffix śiṋa to guŕ in olden times.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: When the Portuguese arrived here, they were engaged chiefly in the business of exporting various types of raw sugar and refined sugar. For this purpose, they put to use two ports of Bengal – one of them was Satgaon (Saptagram) and the other Chát́igáon (Chattagram). The Portuguese used to refer to these ports as Porte-de-Grandis and Porte-de-Báuṋgálá. In Europe, this is how the ports were known. While on the subject, let me mention that the word “port” is of Latin origin. Even though it has extensive use in Bengali today, the word bandar [“port”] is Arabic.
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: 20 November 1983, Kolkata
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: from “Anthastha Lra to Ádi La”
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: Varńa Vicitrá Part 1
chapterTitle: “This Is the Same Gaoŕa Where We Were Born and Are Destined to Die”

t: The Historical Origin of Kaevarttas Involves All the Bengalees
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: Ka means “water”, ke means “in water”. Ke + vrtt (vartt) = kevartta. Kevartta + ań = kaevartta. The words kevartta and kaevartta can be used in the same sense. The etymological meaning of the word kaevartta is “one who lives in water”, that is, “one who makes a living based on water”. In common usage kaevartta means 1) “one who makes a living based on fish”, one who is called in Bengali, Jálik Kaevartta... Jele Kaevartta (kaevartta → kaevat́t́a → kevat́t́a → keot́a). ( 1 ) 2) The second meaning of the word kaevartta is “boatman” – meaning either the helmsman or the oars man. The word májhi refers to the person who does the steering of the boat (karńa in Sanskrit), and dáṋŕi refers to the person who plies the oar or who makes the boat move on with the help of the oar. The steering is called karńa. That is why a boatman is called karńadhár in formal Bengali. We hear in an ancient Bengali song:
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: Yamunáy tuphán dekhe bhay peoná brajáuṋganá,
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: Yadio mor bhagna tarii karńadhárer guń jánaná.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: [O milkmaids of Vraja, donʼt be frightened by the sight of the high waves in the Yamuna. Though my boat is a broken one you donʼt know the calibre of the helmsman.]
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: In North India even now a boatman is called keot́. Theoretically and also as a matter of fact all the people of Bengal were Kaevarttas at one time. The entire Bengalee race earned its livelihood based on water. That is why people took pride in those days to introduce themselves as Kaevarttas or Keot́. Then came from the western part of the world [from the Aryans] the nightmare of the ruinous system of the division of castes. ( 2 ) Those who were intelligent enough started forming small castes and sub-castes in imitation of western India. Even then in the beginning the bond of caste was not very strong in Bengal. Social relations and marriages between different castes still prevailed. The notion of untouchability was not so pronounced as it was in North India. Notwithstanding the facts that newer and newer castes were formed, Bengalees remained, by and large, Kaevarttas. It was a matter of common sense that the mushroom growth of these new castes cannot outnumber the Ját Báuṋálii [original Bengalee] Kaevarttas. The saddest thing is that Bengalees who were primarily and originally Kaevarttas formed small castes and sub-castes based on different groups and sub-groups, and began to consider the original kaevarttas as lower caste. A great misfortune came down in the social life of Bengal… there came down the curse of fatal fragmentation.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: In the Buddhist period fishing began to be considered as a mean job. If fishing is a mean job, then how is eating fish not also a mean job! Catching fish and slaughtering fish is certainly not good, but why do the fishermen catch fish at all? Is it not because there are people who eat fish? Theoretically speaking, if catching fish is a mean job then eating fish is not only an equally mean job, it is, in fact, a meaner job. But in the Buddhist period while catching fish was considered a mean job, eating fish was not considered so. During the time of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu catching fish was considered a mean job, but Mahaprabhu did not oppose the act of eating fish. He never opposed the eating of fish in Bengal and in the entire area stretching between Bengal and Kashi [Varanasi]. He opposed fish-eating in the lands to the west of Kashi. So, in those days many people used to ridicule the Vaeśńavas by saying:
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: Bol haribol, kháo mágur mácher jhol.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: [Shout the name of Lord Hari, and eat the fish curry.]
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: Even now in Bengal some of the orthodox Vaeśńavas who consider not only the shield and the sword but also the spade, axe, knife, scissors, sickle, and naruń [nail-cutter] as weapons, and recoil in fear, and jump away from those things, eat rice and fish publicly or in the corner of the house. Possibly it did not occur to them that the fish-cutting baṋt́i is also a weapon.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: During the reign of the second Devapal, in the last phase of the Buddhist period, a great Kaevartta rebellion took place in North Bengal. The Kaevarttas declared that the vitality of the Bengalee race does not lie in a few artificially- constructed new castes and sub-castes… It lies in the Kaevarttas who are original Bengalees. It is unfortunate that soon afterwards the Kaevarttas became divided under the pressure of a few so-called high-caste people. Those who gave up fishing as a livelihood became known as Hálik Kaevarttas [“Kaevarttas using the plough”] or Cáśii Kaevarttas [“Kaevarttas who are farmers”] or Máhiśyas [“those who tend buffaloes”]. They were recognized as high- caste people. And those (the fishermen) who continued to make a living based on fish became known as Jálik or Jele Kaevarttas [“Kaevarttas using the fishing net”]. However, anthropologically it is difficult to find any difference between a Brahman or a Kayastha of Bengal and a Jele Kaevartta. The same sweet, graceful facial structure, the same well-built physique with tender appearance, the same emotional disposition, the same lively humanitarian qualities and temperament, manifested in joys and sorrows of life.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: Anyway, now you understand the actual meaning of the word “Kaevartta”, and remember that the historical origin of Kaevarttas involves all the Bengalees.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 1

t: Kamtapur / Land of Koch – Pride of Bengal
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: Yáke niye moder garva ei sei Báuṋálii,
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: Púrvákáshe nútan kare jválábe diipálii.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: [One in whom we take pride is the Bengalee,
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: Who will ignite bountiful new lights in the eastern sky.]
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: Kuc + ghaiṋ = koc [Koch]. The meaning of the root kuc is “to attract”, “to give shelter”, “to attract so as to give shelter”. For example, “the vicinity of hills”, “sandy ocean shore”, “long wavy stretch of forests”, “a girdle of green fields”. This story comes from a long time back, though long after the creation of Ráŕh, when the rest of Bengal came into existence – several lakh [hundreds of thousands of] years ago – perhaps some time after the appearance of man – but certainly not too much later. It must be in between the Oligocene and the Mesozoic age. Eastern Ráŕh first emerged from the sand and silt, carried by the rivers of western Ráŕh. Then, just as the rivers of western and eastern Ráŕh in a similar process created the Samatat in the south, in the same way the formation of the land of Barendra began out of alluvium and sand, carried by the rivers Gauṋgá and Brahmaputra. (The literal meaning of the word barendra is “unparalleled” or “the best of all”.)
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: (Bar + indra = Barendra.) The last [region of Bengal] to be created was the entire Vauṋga (D́abák) or East Bengal, including Shriibhúmi (Sylhet), Chat́t́al and Upavauṋga. The soil of Samatat, Barendra and Vauṋga is extremely fertile. Within a short period, there sprung up verdant forests. The people of Ráŕh headed eastwards with spades and axes to Samatat and across Samatat to Vauṋga.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: When Aryan civilization reached Samatat and Vauṋga (as far as their cultural uniqueness and their blood, Bengalees are not Aryans), eventually Bengalees were impacted by Aryan culture. Not only Bengalees, the same applies to the rest of India east of Kashi. It was the people of Ráŕh who, crossing the Ganges, went to Barendra. Thus, when Ráŕh accepted the Brahmanic religion, this cult spread primarily from Ráŕh to Samatat and Vauṋga. After a few preliminary inquiries, you will come to know that Samatat has no shárasvat samáj (intellectual society) of its own. It was simply the transplanted culture of Ráŕh. The original Kayasthas and Vaidyas of Bengal are the people who migrated there from Haripal in Hooghly District and Shriikhanda in Burdwan District. The Brahmans of Vauṋga migrated from so many places in Ráŕh that no specific names can be mentioned. That is why in East Bengal there is no so-called Brahman born in Vauṋga. Even today, those who have been living there for generations introduce themselves as Brahmans of Ráŕh. In sociological language this is called cultural transplantation. Even with regard to Barendra, largely similar events transpired.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: When, after crossing the Ganges and Padma Rivers, the people of Ráŕh migrated northward instead of eastward, with spades and axes in their hands, accompanied by cows of the zebu subspecies, and with ploughs and yokes on their shoulders, there came from the north a substream of Mongolian culture. Through a sweet blending of these Ráŕhii and Mongolian cultures evolved the Bengalee society of Barendra. While a little paler in complexion than the Bengalees of Ráŕh, with somewhat flatter noses, they were very cultured, gracious and simple human beings. At that very point in time, we obtained the original Bengalee Kaevarttas of Barendrabhumi as vital resources for the Bengalee race. I have mentioned elsewhere that originally every Bengalee was a Kaevartta. Just as the Kaevarttas moved from Ráŕh to Samatat, they also migrated northwards from Ráŕh to Barendra. The Namashudras, who are the essence of the Bengalees of central Bengal, were merely an ornament of the Kaevarttas. The people of Barendra have likewise descended from the Kaevarttas. The subterranean flow of Kaevartta culture mingled together with the Máhiśya culture of South Bengal or Midnapore, meaning that their bloodstream reverberates with the tender and adamantine traits of the original Bengalees. In the last phase of the Buddhist era, the Kaevarttas of Barendra became vocal against the tyranny of King Devapal II. In the history of the world, such a well-organized peopleʼs resistance movement is rare – it may be that there has not been any comparable movement in history. The Kaevartta Rebellion [11th century] ushered in a unique renaissance of the Bengalee race – it infused in them an intense consciousness to discover new horizons of ideas.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: These very Kaevarttas moved to the north, northwest [and northeast]. Those who moved northwest settled down in Mithila and initiated a new way of life. Even today, thousands of original Bengalee Kaevarttas live in the Purnea – Saharsa region. Those who went northeast advanced throughout the entirety of the region of Bengal. In Kaevartta society, men slightly outnumbered women. Those who went towards the northeast corner were compelled to marry Mongolian women in order to preserve their society, thus creating a new branch of Bengalee ethnicity. These very people, moving gradually northwards, advanced near the peaks of the Himalayas. They settled down on both sides of the River Sankoch, which originated from Bhutan. This new generation of Bengalees came to be named Koch after the river Sankoch. In their days of woe, when Bengalee life was battered by the impact of the descent and explosion of gigantic meteors [socially], the Kaevarttas were the greatest refuge and asset of Bengal. That is why they were named Koch ( 1 ), not only after the River Sankoch, but also due to their characteristic of providing shelter to the shelterless.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: When an idealistic youth of the Koch race saw that the social life of Bengal was heading towards disaster, and had degenerated in its cultural life, he came forward as the living symbol of Bengalʼs resurrection. This Bengalee youth of the Mech dynasty established Kámtápur [Kamtapur] State in the Sankoch Valley with the help of only two hundred dedicated young men. (According to another opinion, the Mech people had not yet been recognized as a branch of the Koch society; they were treated as an undifferentiated part of the Koch race.) The name of that youth was Haridas Mondal (There is, of course, some difference of opinion on this question.)
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: Since the pre-Buddhist era, Bengal had remained divided into five parts for reasons of geographical diversity and administrative convenience: 1) Ráŕh, to the west of the Bhagirathi River, 2) the central region, comprising the Bhagirathi and Madhumati Rivers (Bagri), 3) Barendra, to the north of the Padma River, 4) Vauṋga, on the eastern side of the river Madhumati, and 5) Mithila, to the north of the Padma and west of the River Koshii (Kaoshikii). Compared to other regions, Ráŕh and Barendra were slightly larger in area. The other parts each had a bhukti [administrative district]; that is, Bagri Bhukti consisted of the entire Samatat. The entire Vauṋga area constituted Vauṋga Bhukti, and the entire Mithila constituted Tirhut Bhukti. Yet Ráŕh and Barendra, being larger in size, each had two bhuktis. The northern part of Ráŕh (north of where the Damodar River used to flow but no longer does today), meaning the present Dhanbad, Burdwan, Birbhum, Deoghar, Dumka, Gadda, Sahebganj, and Ráŕh-Murshidabad, comprised Burdwan Bhukti. (In those days Hooghly and Howrah were included in Burdwan.) Midnapore, Bankura, Manbhum, East Ranchi, Singbhum and Bhanjabhum comprised Dańd́a Bhukti (Midnapore). Similarly, in the southern part of Barendrabhumi was Paondrabardhan Bhukti, and its northern part formed Kamtapur Bhukti. The Bengalee Kaevarttas of those days, infused with vitality, selected Haridas Mondal as their leader and at the same time made him the king of Kamtapur. From the time of Haridas Mondal, the Kaevarttas of this region came to be called Koch. In the course of time the Koch people came to be divided into four characteristic branches: 1) Mech, 2) Rajbangshi, 3) Rajgun, and 4) Kolia (Kolliká – Koliá). Needless to say, all four branches were the original Bengalees, and they accepted as the quintessence of their existence the task of upholding, conveying and nourishing the original Bengalee culture, and continued to provide evidence of their worthiness as “the shelter or koch of Bengalee culture”.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: Later, Kamtapur split into two fragments – its eastern part was called Bijni and the western part was named Coochbehar. The Koch people had been Shaivites since ancient times. Though Jainism and Buddhism had some influence upon them, it was not extensive. However, in the southern part of Barendrabhumi, that is, in Paondrabardhan Bhukti, the impact of Buddhism was widespread. Later, the people of Paondrabardhan Bhukti, who had been influenced by Buddhism, accepted Islam as their religion. The same thing happened in Kamtapur Bhukti; but compared to Kamtapur Bhukti, the number of Muslims was far greater in the Paondrabardhan Bhukti. The names of Baneshwar, Bangarh, Jateshwar and Jalpeshwar remind us of the Shaivite influence in these areas even today.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2

t: The Ahoms who came from Burma occupied the upper part of the Brahmaputra Valley, but they were not able to set their foot in the lower part, that is, Barendrabhumi. So though the impact of the Ahoms on Assamese culture was vast and pervasive, there was not one iota of influence by them on Kamtapur or Barendra. In the pronunciation of vowels and consonants in the Assamese language, the influence of the Ahoms is universally acknowledged. However, there is not the slightest Ahom influence on Barendra. A look at the spoken language of Kamrup and Goalpara makes this as clear as daylight.
chapterTitle: The Original Bengalee Community of Earlier Times – 2
