But in Bengal the situation is different: the winter is over on the fourteenth day of the previous bright fortnight of the moon, and the spring season begins from the fifth day of the next fortnight, or Shrii paiṋcamii, the day when the Goddess of Learning is worshipped. In Bengal, today is not the starting of spring; in fact it starts from the day of the worship of Sarasvatii. I do not know whether you are aware of the fact that in those days in Bengal the small children used to wear deep yellow clothes (vásanti) on the fifth day. So you see, the spring season starts in Bengal long before it starts in other parts of India, in the Bengali month of Mágha and not in Phálguna. Thus in the dhyána mantra of the mythological goddess of learning Sarasvatii, it is mentioned that winter is over from the date of her worship. The Buddhist Sarasvatii, or Niila Sarasvatii, is called Tárá. She is also worshipped in Tibet.

The Buddhist Sarasvatii is blue and four-armed, but the Sarasvatii of Bengal is all white, not blue. Saras+vatii = Sarasvatii. One meaning of Saras is “white colour”; another meaning is “lake” or “large pond.” In the dhyána mantra of the goddess Sarasvatii the word jád́yá has been mentioned

Yá puŕnendutuśáraháradhavalá Yá shubhravastrávrtá Yá viińdbaradadańd́ashobhitá kalá Yá shvetapadmásaná Yá Brahmáeyutamaheshaprabhrti devae sádávandita. Sá máḿ pátu Bhagavatii Sarasvatii nisheśajádyapahá.

Jád́yápahá means that which kills or removes dullness. The old date for the spring festival in Bengal is Shriipaiṋcamii, the fifth day of the fortnight. Now the question may arise, why was the spring festival in Bengal not observed in a grand way? Because the winter in Bengal is not very severe, so spring also is not very conspicuous. In Bengal there are three seasons: summer, rainy season, and autumn. Autumn is very conspicuous, but spring is not. In autumn, the kash and shiulii (lower) blossom, the rains are over, and the land is all green. In this season the planetary position is as follows. If the full moon comes during the presence of the stars Púrva Phalgunii or Uttar Phalgunii in the northern hemisphere (north of the equator), the lunar month is called Phálguna, and the name of the solar month is also Phalguna. On the night before the full moon, people burn the effigy of an old woman which represents winter. This is the astrological as well as the astronomical interpretation of the spring festival.

In Indo-Aryan mythology there is mention of a king named Hirańyakashipu. His sister, Holika, was a woman of violent nature. She was a cannibal. (You should note that she was a cannibal, not homivorous. A human eating another human is called a cannibal, whereas an animal eating human flesh is called homivorous. Holika was a cannibal, whereas a tiger is homivorous). The people out of anger burnt Holika alive the night before the full moon, and to celebrate this occasion, they arranged a festival of joy which was called Holikadahana (the burning of Holika). That is why even today in northern India particularly in the Punjab and Uttar Pradesh, this Holi festival is celebrated. And since the moon enters the zodiac sign of the Uttar Phálgunii star, the festival is popularly called Pháguyá in Bihar and in the eastern regions of Uttar Pradesh. But as neither winter nor spring is conspicuous in Bengal, so neither festival, Holi nor Pháguyá, is celebrated. The festival that is celebrated on that day in Bengal is the Dolyátrá of Shriikrśńa, and thus that day is also observed as a holiday in Bengal.

The history behind the festival is this. About 500 years ago Mahaprabhu Shrii Caetanya once went to visit Brindaban, where he observed the Holi festival. Brindaban is situated in the western part of India, where the Holi festival is celebrated, not the Pháguá, which is popular as far as Allahabad. To the west of Allahabad, i.e.in the non-Bhojpurii-speaking areas, there Holi is celebrated.

After his return to Bengal, Mahaprabhu pondered deeply and decided to introduce the festival but, of course, in a different form. He said to his followers, “Go to the Krśńa temple on that day, and apply red powder and red colour to Krśńa. Then you should play with the red powder and colour amongst yourselves,” And those who gave red powder and colour to others would also feed them with malpoa [delectable sweet]. In Bihar there are both poa and malpoa sweets. The difference between the two is that if flour is mixed with sugar and spices, and dipped in sugar-water, it is called poa. And if flour without sugar is first fried in ghee and then dipped in sugar-water, it is called malpoa. What is known as poa in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh is known as malpoa in Bengal. And what is known as malpoa is known as dhákái malpoa. Mahaprabhu was very fond of malpoa. In his biography it has been written, Malpoa sarbhájá ár, luchi purii, ananda bhojan karen nadiiya biharii. (“Malpoa, sarbhaja, luchi and puri are relished by Mahaprabhu”). In my boyhood days when I first heard these lines, I said, “Well, it's all right that Mahaprabhu relished malpoa, sarbhaja, luci, puri, etc. – but is there anyone who does not relish these delicacies? Personally as far as I know, all people like them!”

As I said, Mahaprabhu saw the festival in Brindavan and then introduced it in Bengal. It has never become a social festival in Bengal, as Pháguyá has become a social festival in Bihar and in the eastern part of Uttar Pradesh. Rather, it has become a kind of religious festival in Bengal. So it is neither Holi festival nor Pháguyá – it is the Dolyátrá of Shriikrśńa, and the government of West Bengal has declared that day as a holiday.

Now, what is the significance of Dolyátrá? The winter is over, and the people are active again. Various colourful ideas and plans are appearing in their minds, and they plan to do so many things for the benefit of society. Similarly when they think of Lord Krśńa, their minds are filled with joy. The very thought of Krśńa produces ripples of joy in people's minds, and these vibrations of joy in the devotees' minds also produce a corresponding vibration in Krśńa's mind. They think, “Oh Krśńa, I love you – but you also love me, that I know.” In this way the ripples of joy in their own minds also create vibrations of joy in His mind. This is the inner significance of the Dolyátrá of Shrii Krśńa. In our Ananda Márga Caryácarya, this festival is celebrated as a spring festival.

In the days of Mahaprabhu, the prevailing rule was to seek the prior permission of the person to whom you were going to give the red powder. If that person gave permission, then only could you smear him or her with coloured powder, and then treat them to malpoa. These days all these customs have degenerated.

Let us discuss the science of colour. In Saḿskrta language there are two similar words: varńa and rága. Though the meanings are approximately the same, they are not completely synonymous. Varńa means colour (what is termed in Bengali as rauṋg). But this word varńa does not indicate the colour which will colour other objects as well; an object has its own colour but its colour may not necessarily dye other objects. But the word rága means that particular colour which can dye other objects also. So the inner spirit of the science of colour in Vaeshnavii Tantra is this – that each and every expression of this universe has its own rhythm, its own vibration, its own sound, and its own colour, and thus it has its own form as well. And as it has its own sound, it has a particular sweetness of its own. Suppose there is a person who is dumb but very good; and there is another person who is equally good, but speaks well also. Obviously you will prefer the second man, because he possesses the power of expression. Dumb people can give expression to their inner thoughts only with their gestures and postures, whereas those who can speak can express themselves with gesture, posture, and also language. A dumb person can only look at you and express through gesture to come to him, but a person who can speak can say, “Come little child, come to me.” This vocal expression of the second person conveys more sweetness.

When Tantra was first invented, there was only one science of Tantra; but later various cults emerged according to their respective philosophical viewpoints. Each had a different name although their inner spirit was the same: for instance, Baoddha Tantra, Jaina Tantra, and in later times Shaeva Tantra, Shákta Tantra, Saora Tantra, Gáńapatya Tantra, Vaeśńviiya Tantra, etc. The inner idea of the Vaeśńaviiya Tantra is that there is form and colour (both rága and varńa) in the rhythmic expressions of Parama Puruśa, and those cosmic rhythms also have a sweet sonic vibration. This sonic vibration is instrumental in giving expression to various other forms in this universe as well. The resonance of the collective vibrations of the universe is called the flute sound of Krśńa, another name for oṋḿkára, the cosmic sound which reaches the ears of spiritual aspirants in various ways. When human beings attain spiritual progress step by step, they will also hear this sound with their own ears.

In this expressed world full of various emanations there are so many varieties of colours – not only seven colours, but numerous colours made through permutations and combinations. And all these colours which people know, as well as all those which they do not know – all are included in that divine sound, that oṋḿkára. It the Upaniśads it is said,
Yá eko'varńo bahudháshaktihyogád Varńananekán nihitártho dadháti Vicaeti cánte vishvamádhao sa devah Sa no-buddhyá shubhayá saḿyunaktu.
“That one Parama Puruśa has been creating this unique colourful world with His various powers. Why He is doing so is known to Him alone; no one else knows it.”

The scriptures on devotion emphatically insist that only He knows the answer, no one else. It is a fact that human beings with their limited intellect can never understand the secrets of why and how Parama Puruśa has been creating this universe; their wisdom can never fathom this mystery. That is why the scriptures say, “Be a good person, but do not be foolish. Be intelligent and clever.” Now what is the clever approach? Just as on the one hand you are moving towards Parama Puruśa to attain Him by concentrating your mind through mudrá, práńáyáma and kiirtana, at the same time you should constantly remember why He is creating all these things, and what is your relation with Him. You should think, “My little intellect cannot fathom all this – rather let me do one thing, let me establish a relation of sweet love with Him. When this relation of love is established, He will be my own, and I will know His inner secret; I will certainly find the answers to all the questions 'why'.”

To find the answer to those questions of “why”, just as the devotees run towards His sonic expression which the Vaeśńavas call His flute sound, they also run towards the expressions of His colour. They think, I will colour my mind with the same colour in which He manifests Himself before me, and move towards Him. If I can colour my mind in His colour, I will be very close to Him. This attempt to colour oneself with the colour of Parama Puruśa is called anurága (anu means “afterwards,” and rága means “colour”). Those who want all their actions to be crowned with success should love Parama Puruśa with all their hearts, and understand what He likes and what He dislikes, what He wants and what He does not want. They should not even go near those things which Parama Puruśa dislikes. And when they guide all their desires and ambitions according to His wishes, their success will be inevitable, because whatever He wants will surely be fulfilled.
Kii habe iccháy, iccháte kii nay Krśńa icchá viná phal phalená.
[Even if one wishes, the wish may not be fulfilled; without the wish of Krśńa, no wish can bear fruit.]

So all must work according to the wishes of Parama Puruśa. [[To dye oneself in the colour of Parama Puruśa I call anurága. In the cult of devotion, it is said that the best sádhaná is the sádhaná of kevalá bhakti. “I do not ask anything – I do not ask anything from You. Do whatever You think proper]], and do not do what You think improper. I will not apply my little intellect to You, because Your intellect is infinitely superior to mine.”

In the cult of devotion, a higher [[form of sádhaná is]] rágánuga bhakti. The word rágá is derived from the word rańj + ghaiṋ suffix. The verb rańj means “to colour”. Rágánuga bhakti means that type of devotion which gives expression to one's inner devotion. The psychology behind this type of bhakti is, “Because of my rágánuga bhakti, because I have dyed my mind with His colour, He will be pleased. And when He is pleased, I will also get pleasure.” Some people may think, “Parama Puruśa likes to eat malpoa, so let me prepare a few pieces of malpoa for Him. When He will eat malpoa He will feel pleasure, and when He feels pleasure, I will derive joy from His joy.”

But there is a still higher type of devotion than rágánuga, in which devotee thinks, “I will do exactly as He wants, I will colour my mind with His colour, and I will not think whether that will bring joy to me or not. Let Him be pleased… that is my only wish.” This is the highest stage of devotion.

According to Vaeśńava Tantra, a person in a certain circumstance is coloured with a particular vibrational colour. Thus unit beings must offer that particular colour to Parama Puruśa saying, “Oh Parama Puruśa, please accept my colour, and colour my mind with your colour.” To offer the colour of one's mind to Parama Puruśa, is a kind of ragasádhaná.

When Mahaprabhu first introduced the Dolyátrá festival, the psychology behind this festival was to give one's mental colour to Parama Puruśa. The inner idea was, “Let my mind vibrate in the same way as Krśńa's mind is vibrating” This Dolyátrá has no relation to the Holi festival of north India or the Pháguá of central and east India, for it is something purely psychic. The word Dolyátrá is popular in the almanacs of Orissa, Bengal, Assam, Manipur, and Mithila. The inner significance of Dolyátrá is, in the swinging vibration in which the entire universe is vibrating, I will also be vibrated.

During the Vedic age, the post-Vedic age, the Mahábhárata era, the Buddhist and post-Buddhist eras, during the reign of the kings of the Sen dynasty in Bengal, and in the southern part of East Bengal during the rule of the kings of the Chandra dynasty, the language of the legal courts was Sanskrit. However, [during the later of these periods] Bengali became prevalent for matters related to the general public. From the Pathan period onwards, the language of the court became Persian; but Bengali remained the peopleʼs language. During British rule, English became the language of the court, yet Bengali continued to be used as language for matters relating to the common people, and this is still the practice today. Since the proceedings of the court continued to be conducted for a long time in Sanskrit, many legal terms are still in Sanskrit. Neglecting those words and attempting to create new terminologies are simply a waste of time and energy.

The use of Bengali in official work was first introduced by the maharajas [kings] of Tripura (who were designated by the people as “Maharaj Manikyabahadur”). The king of Ráŕh (according to some, he was a feudal king), Ichai Ghosh, was possibly the first in the pre-Pathan era to use Bengali in conducting royal affairs. Yet he also retained Sanskrit words in the language of the court. In matters relating to the common people, however, he began using Bengali instead of Sanskrit.
The mention of Ichai Ghosh reminds me of several kingdoms of ancient Ráŕh. Ráŕh was the cradle of civilization. It was not only the cradle, it was also a hub whose influence spread everywhere.

The northernmost is Birbhum (Kandi and Jangipur Subdivisions of the present Murshidabad District, Rampurhat Subdivision of the present Birbhum District, and Sahebganj of Bihar [Rajmahal Subdivision]). The farthest border of Birbhum extended up to Mirzachouki, the outermost boundary of Sahebganj. These kings of Birbhum were Kayasthas with “Singh” as their surname.

To the south of Birbhum was Gopabhum. By Gopabhum is meant the Shiuri Subdivision of present Birbhum District, the newly-created Bolpur Subdivision, Pakur Subdivision of the present Sahebganj District of Jharkhand (in Sanskrit Parkat́ipur, from which has come the “Pákŕáshii” surname of present Bengalee society), Dumka Subdivision and Deoghar Subdivision. The kings there were Sadgopes with the surname Ghosh. Hence the state came to be called Gopabhum.

To the south of Gopabhum was Samantabhum, and to the west of Samantabhum was Shikharbhum. Samantabhum referred to Durgapur Subdivision in Burdwan District, Asansol Subdivision and Jamtura (the word “Jámtáŕá” ( 1 ) is the derived form of “Jámtuŕá”) Subdivision of Dumka District. The kingdom of Samantabhum was known during British rule as Raniganj Subdivision. When, in 1856, the district of Santal Pargana was constituted, Jamtura in Samantabhum was included in it. When Asansol became a bigger town than Raniganj, the headquarters of the Subdivision was shifted from Raniganj to Asansol (Cheridanga). Still later, in independent India, when Durgapur turned into a very big town, this subdivision split in two. Its eastern part formed a separate subdivision called Durgapur. The kings of Samantabhum were Ugrakśatriyas having the surname “Sámanta”.

Just west of Samantabhum was the kingdom of Shikharbhum, to the north of which lay part of Birbhum and Samantabhum, to the south of which lay Panchakot or Manbhum, and to the west of which lay Jharkhand or the Chut́iá-Nagpur kingdom. (The British pronounced the name “Chotanagpur” or “Chot́ánagpur”.) The Pareshnath Hills, situated in the Tundi Police Precinct in the present Dhanbad District and Pirtar of Giridih District, are on its western border. In ancient times, the hills were known as Sametshikhar. That is why the kingdom was named Shikharbhum. The present-day Dhanbad District used to be known as Shikharbhum.

To the south of Samantabhum and Shikharbhum, three kingdoms existed side by side. One was Mallabhum. (The Vishnupur Subdivision of present Bankura District; the kings bore the surname “Malla”, which is why the kingdom was called “Mallabhum”.) Exactly to its west was Senbhum, consisting of Bankura Subdivisional headquarters and parts of Purulia and Midnapur Districts. The kings were Vaidyas with “Sen” as their surname. That is why the name of the kingdom was “Senbhum”. Its ancient capital was Senpahari. Later, King Banku Roy set up a new capital at the confluence of the Darakeshwar and Gandheshwari Rivers, and the new capital was called Bankura after the king, Banku Roy.

To the west of Senbhum was Manbhum or Paiṋcakot́, [also known as] Páchet́i Kingdom or Páiṋcet Kingdom. Later, the kingdom was named Manbhum after King Mansinghadev, and its capital was Manbazar. To the north of the kingdom was the river Damodar, to the south Barahabhum, to the east the Sushunia Hills, and to the west Jharkhand or Chut́iá-Nagpur. The western boundary of Manbhum was near Angara where the hills ended and the plains of Ranchi began.

To the south of Mallabhum, Senbhum and Manbhum was Shabarbhum (Midnapur). Shabars, that is, Kheriá Muńd́á kings, ruled the kingdom. To the west of Shabarbhum was Dhabalbhum, which consisted of Jhargram Subdivision of the present Midnapur District, part of the present Bankura District, and Dhabalbhum Subdivision (Tatanagar) of the present Jharkhand State. The surname of the kings was “Dhabaldev”. For this reason, the kingdom was named “Dhabalbhum”.

Adjacent to the north and northwestern extremities of Dhabalbhum was Barahabhum (Barabhum). Its capital was Barahabazar (Barabazar). Two Muńd́á brothers, Adibaraha and Keshbaraha, founded the kingdom. Barahabhum Kingdom consisted of the southern part of the present-day Purulia District, Chandil of Singbhum District and Patamda, and the Ichagar and Nimdih Police Stations of Singhbhum District. The kingdom is surrounded by the Dalma Hills range. Very ancient relics of the Bengali language and script have been found and are still being found, largely in Barahabhum. On the western side of Dhabalbhum was Singbhum. The kings of that kingdom belonged to the Kole sub-tribe. Singbhum was bifurcated some time before the Pathan era. The western part retained the name of Singbhum, and the eastern part was named Porahat. (The Keraikela kingdom, situated southeast of Ranchi District, was included.) Later, the Porahat kingdom split in two parts – the western part was called Kharsoan and the eastern part Seraikela. To the south of the Dhabalbhum and Porahat kingdoms was Bhanjabhum (the current name is Mayurbhanja). Since the kings of that kingdom used the surname Bhanjadeo, it was named “Bhanjabhúm”. They used the peacock symbol in their thrones and crowns and in the ornaments of their queens, so the kingdom later came to be called “Mayurbhanj”. ( 2 )
The collection of these bhúms constituted the ancient Ráŕh Bhúmi or land of Ráŕh.

The eastern part of Howrah, Hooghly and Burdwan Districts and the northern portion of Ghatal Subdivision of Midnapur District in eastern Ráŕh were not included in any bhúm. This portion was once called the kingdom of Bhurisreśt́ha [Bhurishreshtha]. Today we colloquially call it Bhurshut. The capital, Gar Mandaran, was located where the Amodar River, which originates from Sumudrabandh [Lake], converges with the Damodar.

From very ancient days to the time of the Sen dynasty, the kings of Ráŕh were practically independent. Of course, they used to pay a nominal tribute (nazráńá) to the king of Gaoŕa (Bengal) or, if not paying so, would accept in writing the sovereignty of the king. I came across the ruins of an ancient Jain Shiva temple at Mardu village in the Silli Police Station on the banks of the Suvarnarekha River, in the ancient kingdom of Manbhum or Panchakot. I also found near the house of a Muńd́á villager, a stone statue of Dákśáyańii. Dákśáyańii was the state goddess of Bengal during the Sur dynasty, which means that Manbhum Kingdom acknowledged the sovereignty of the Sur kings of Gaoŕa. During the Pathan rule, most of the kingdoms of Ráŕh were independent principalities. Only under the Mughals did these principalities accept the suzerainty of the nawab of Bengal. They paid only a nominal tribute to him. In Bhurshut, the Mughal rulers had tremendous influence. Burdwan, in Bhurshut, was the capital of Bengal a number of times. [Some say] the word “Burdwan” came from [the Persian] bár-e-diiván. The British spelled it “Burdwan”. Previously the name of this administrative division was Sharifabad.

In those days, the bhúmyadhikáriis or bhaomiks (bhaomik → bhouaṋa → bhuṋiá) [landlords] of Bengal struggled hard to maintain their independence. King Pratapaditya of Jessore, King Kandarpanarayana of Chandradvip, King Lakshmanmanikya of Bhulua, and also Isha Khan, Kedar Roy and Sitaram Roy were amongst them. It is difficult to say what the outcome would have been had all these kings cooperated with each other. However, as each of them fought alone, they were defeated.

The king of Jaipur, Raja Man Singh, entered into an agreement with Akbar, the emperor in Delhi, and became commander-in-chief of the Mughal army. There were twelve [kings] who were particularly prominent. Raja Man Singh took upon himself the onerous responsibility of subduing these twelve. He defeated Pratapaditya of Jessore and carried off the statue of Yashoreshvarii, the guardian deity of Jessore. He installed her in the Ambar Fort of Jaipur, bringing the Bengalee priest of the temple along with her. It was Raja Man Singh who built the Ramnakali, or Dhakeshvari, temple in Dacca.

When King Jagatnarayan of Bhurshut saw other rulers of Bengal in rebellion against Mughal rule, he too became encouraged to revolt. The nawab of Bengal used to stay sometimes in Burdwan and sometimes in Dhaka. One commander [under the nawab] was posted in Dhaka, one in Gaoŕa [Samatat], one in Burdwan and another in Azimabad (the present Patna city). Emperor Akbar separated Suba Bihar from Suba Bengal, so Azimabad was no longer part of Bengal. A new nawab was posted in Azimabad. Many soldiers were transferred to this newly-established capital from the Burdwan Commissionary [in Bhurshut].

King Jagatnarayan decided to declare independence, taking advantage of the circumstances. This decision was welcomed by his ministers, as well as his own queen, Bhavasundari. Everyone agreed that when Bhurishrestha was superior to many other principalities and had a glorious heritage of its own – in art and architecture, in wisdom, in literature and in all spheres of life – then surely it should declare its independence to uphold its dignity. Bhurishrestha was the best not only in name, it had then reached the pinnacle of glory in agriculture and industry, trade and commerce, education and knowledge, etc. Why should such a kingdom remain under the bondage of the far-off Delhi emperor? Why should it not launch a struggle to assert its own sovereignty and dignity?

This royal declaration was loudly acclaimed by the strongly-built, hard-working Játbáuṋáliis ( 3 ) [sons of the soil of Bengal]. The Ugra Kśatriyas, Sadgopes, Máhiśyas and Bágdis of Bengal volunteered for the army. They shouted the slogan, “Outsiders stay out! Bhurishreshtha has never submitted and never will.”

Akbar sensed danger. Bhurshut was the most fertile and prosperous territory within his empire. Bhurshut produced the largest crops of sugar cane, the most raw sugar, the largest crops of cotton, the most cloth, the largest crops of rice paddy, the largest mining output and the most silk, all of which the merchants used to export abroad, making huge profits. Akbar would collect a huge fortune for the royal treasury by levying taxes on those merchants. As such, the important Bhurshut could not be allowed to secede from the empire.

The emperor sent his commander-in-chief, Man Singh, to suppress the rebellion. Even at that time the journey to Burdwan from Delhi or Agra was not difficult. During the middle part of the Mughal era there had suddenly emerged a mighty Pathan emperor, Shershah Suri. He was an intelligent ruler and a prominent mass leader. He introduced radical agrarian reforms by popularizing the system of leasing land. He built a long, broad highway from Suvarna Gram in Dacca via Kalighat, Sutanuti and Govindapur, and from there through Howrah and Burdwan to Delhi and up to Attak, Punjab. In those days people used to call this royal highway variously such names as the Benares Road, the Kashi Road, or the Kingʼs Road. The British called it the Grand Trunk Road [in short G.T. Road]. Man Singh with his large army marched to Burdwan along this highway.

It is Burdwan which emerged and developed in prehistoric times. The Rgveda does not mention it. Astiknagar, referred to in the Yajurveda, is the ancient name of this Burdwan. Astiknagar and Kanchannagar – both these names were prevalent side by side. Astiknagar and Kanchannagar now lie buried under the earth. One can still hear groans from the graves of this city. It is this very Burdwan where King Chandraketu ruled during the Mahábhárata era. Bithur (Briśt́ipur) or Prayag (Allahabad), the oldest town in North India, had not yet been built. Of course, Mathura existed, but it emerged in the post-Vedic era. It is the same Burdwan that was resplendent with pride and glory during the rule of Ashoka and Chandragupta. And it is in this very Burdwan, then the capital of Gaoŕa, where the great king Vikramaditya used to hear [stories] from the lips of Betal [a legendary figure].

During the Buddhist era, when Sanskrit was transmuted into Mágadhii Prákrta, the name of Astiknagar became Atthinagar. When the Buddhist era began, Vardhaman Mahavir visited Astiknagar. He was the son of the famous tradesman, Siddhartha, of Vaishali town in the land of Videha. His motherʼs name was Trishala. For several years in Magadh, Vardhaman Mahavir preached his ideals, his religious doctrines, his precept that “non-violence is the supreme dharma,” and his doctrine of nirgrantha [nudism]. The people of Magadh could not accept his excessive non-violence or his doctrine of nirgrantha.

In those days, the residents of Magadh used to follow the path of argument [and debate.] The reasons for which Magadh could not accept the Vedas were the same as for its rejection of Vardhaman Mahavirʼs nirgrantha doctrine (the Digambar doctrine) and its obsession with non-violence. Vardhaman Mahavir came to Atthinagar, and preached his religious ideas there for seven long years. For the same purpose, he went from Atthinagar to even as far as Swamisthan. Swamisthan later became a sacred religious place for the Jains. The present name of Swamisthan is Sáiṋthiyá (Sainthia). The well-to-do vaeshyas [merchants] of Atthinagar, who were extremely fascinated by him, changed the name of their town to Vardhaman (Burdwan). At that time, for a brief period Pandua was the capital of Ráŕh, and later on Mahanad [of Hooghly District].

Since then, the name “Vardhaman” has remained. During Akbarʼs time, the name “Vardhaman” became “Bar-e-diwan” (from which has come the English name “Burdwan”), which is a slightly distorted form of “Vardhaman”.

Man Singh pitched his tents at Shákt́igar ( 4 ) [Shaktigarh]. The news of the arrival of the Mughal army reached Mandaran. Mandaran is not very far from Shaktigarh. If one proceeds a little farther east along the bank of the Damodar, one soon reaches Mandaran. It was just at the confluence of the Damodar and the Amodar. King Jagatnarayanʼs courage was deflated when he heard the news of Raja Man Singhʼs arrival. His bravery waned; he stopped bragging and boasting about his military strength. He called his ministers and said, “I am just a small castor-oil plant. How can I dare to fight against the huge banyan tree? I want you to send a messenger with a white flag to Man Singh at Shaktigarh. I want to unconditionally surrender. The sun of Bhurishresthaʼs days of glory are over. It will never again see the glorious dawn.”
The ministersʼ faces fell. But the kingʼs subjects and soldiers had not yet heard of the kingʼs mental setback. It is easily imaginable what they would have done had they learned of it.

Queen Bhavasundari received the news through the prime minister. She immediately rushed to Jagatnarayan. She said, “It is not a question of your personal honour, neither is it a question of the honour of the kingdom. It is a question of the dignity of the whole country of Bengal. Moreover, it is not merely a matter of prestige; it is for the survival of the entire Bengalee race. I beg you to summon all your courage and rise to the occasion. We are all with you. Whether you win or lose, the honour of Bengal will be enhanced.”

King Jagatnarayan took no heed of his queenʼs advice. Rather he remonstrated, saying, “You are just a woman who should keep to [your] inner apartments. How little you know and understand about warfare – donʼt meddle in these delicate issues. Itʼs better to go back to the royal apartments and attend to the petty household duties.” Bhavasundari turned away with a heavy heart. A violent storm was raging in her mind. She could not bear to sit silent, so she called the council of ministers to the royal apartments.

The queen told the ministers that the king had developed a mental derangement. “He wants to throw the prestige of Bengal on the ground. I am a daughter of and you are sons of Ráŕh. The honour and prestige of all Bengal depends on you and me. Under these circumstances, are you willing to go to Man Singh at Shákt́igaŕ carrying a white flag in hand?”
The army generals cried out with one voice, “No! We will go to welcome Man Singh with naked swords.”
Bhavasundari said, “Will you support me in the struggle for the freedom of Bhurshut?”

They responded, “Yes, Your Majesty, and without the least hesitation.” Bhavasundari took upon herself the entire administration of Bhurshut. She immediately arrested the king with the help of the security forces. At her command, they put the king in prison. She organized her combat forces within three days.

The emperorʼs forces had already reached Shákt́igaŕ, a village just beside the Grand Trunk Road. I have said before that the Grand Trunk Road was a cobblestone road. There were no metalled roads in those days to be found either in India or anywhere else in the world. Some time after the death of Akbar, Emperor Jahangir surfaced the road with stones and gravel. That gravel was collected from the quarries of Birbhum. However, when the battle was fought with the forces of Mansingh, there was no imperial highway cobbled with gravel.

Speaking of Jahangir brings to mind a few more stories. Jahangir was a man of extremes, both in merits and demerits. He had many positive qualities, along with a cornucopia of defects. This son of Akbarʼs Rajput wife, as a prince, was known as Selim. An alcoholic with an impetuous nature, Selim cared little for any rules. Several times Emperor Akbar received complaints that Prince Selim was not offering prayers [namáz in Islamic parlance] and not observing rozá [holy fasting from sunrise to sundown during the month of Ramadan] and was an extreme alcoholic. Emperor Akbar usually did not interfere in anyoneʼs religious affairs. Thus Selimʼs waywardness was on the rise.

At that time Burdwan was the capital of Bengal, and Sher Afghan was the governor. His wife, Meher-Un-Nisa, was a Persian lady. This exquisitely beautiful woman fell into many hands before coming to India and was at last married to Sher Afghan. Although Sher Afghanʼs name included “Afghan”, the family had come from Persia. Hence though they spoke Bengali in public, they spoke Persian at home. Urdu had not yet become the state language of India; it became the state language starting from the time of Shahjahan.

Prince Selim had his eyes on Meher-Un-Nisa. He tried several times to snatch her by force from Sher Afghan. Emperor Akbar expressed his extreme displeasure and severely rebuked Selim for this. After Akbarʼs death, there was no one to keep Selim in check. He took the name of Emperor Jahangir and occupied the throne of Delhi. After becoming the emperor, his first act was to lead an army to Burdwan. With his army, he reached Burdwan by the royal highway. He asked Sher Afghan to hand over Meher-Un-Nisa. Sher Afghan refused and a fierce battle followed. It was fought in the northeastern part of the then Burdwan. From Baje Pratappur to Kanai Natshal – this extensive area turned into a battle field. Plenty of blood was shed in this fierce battle. Thousands of innocent soldiers, who had nothing whatsoever to do with either Selimʼs appetites or Sher Afghanʼs honour, died. In those days, Báṋká was a lively river. In addition, it was the rainy season. It is said that thousands of bodies of slaughtered soldiers, without being buried, were set afloat in the river Báṋká. Sher Afghan died where the present Burdwan railway station stands. Since thousands of people died at that spot, the residents of Burdwan deserted the place. No one would go anywhere near it after dark. The place came alive only after the railway station came into existence. After the construction of the Curzon gate, the town gradually extended towards the east. Prehistoric Burdwan and Burdwan of the Jain era receded into the west, and subsequently vanished into the abyss of time. The Burdwan of those days, built with thin, large-sized bricks, today lies deep under the earth. King Banbehari Kapur made some attempts to recover the memory of the [former] Burdwan from under the earth. I have not heard of any further serious efforts. The recently discovered Bardhamaneshvar Shiva is a very ancient Jain Shiva.

Be that as it may, Prince Selim, alias Emperor Jahangir, returned to the capital with Meher-Un-Nisa. Sher Afghanʼs dead body was buried in Burdwan. His tomb remains there still. For a fickle-minded man like Jahangir, it was quite impossible to run the administrative machinery of a huge state like India. Therefore, as regards official matters and royal duties, he slipped into the grip of Meher-Un-Nisa. After their marriage, her new married name became Nur-Jahan (“the light of the world”). Nur-Jahan was a very sharp-witted woman – a lady of developed tastes, as well as highly fashionable and luxury-loving. She used to bathe in rose water, and after her bath, she would spray rose attar (iitr) on her body and clothes. She did not invent attar; it existed in India long before her time. Yet it was she who first produced rose attar. Though white roses were Indiaʼs indigenous flowers, roses of diverse colours came there from Persia. The word gul is essentially a Persian word. Nur-Jahan was also a poetess of high quality. She had compared the eyebrows of dear ones with the moon. The Bengali rendering of one of her famous poems is as follows:
Gariiv gore keu dviip jvelo ná
Sájáio ná keu gule,
Shyámá pokár ná poŕe pákhá,
Dágá ná páya bulbule.
[Do not light lamps on the grave of a poor soul, Do not decorate it with roses, Let not the flies burn their wings here, Let not the bulbul ever feel sad.]

Poet Nur-Jahan says: “I am poor and my grave is poor and simple. Let no one light lamps on it, for if lamps are lit, the flies would get their wings burnt and die, which I will not be able to tolerate. Let no one place wreaths on my grave, for then roses would have to be brought from the rose garden and my bulbul will feel hurt, which I will not be able to bear.”
In any case, the events of Jahangir and Nur-Jahan took place much later than the era of Bhavasundari.

As soon as news of the arrival of the Mughal army reached Mandaran, the people sounded the war drums. However small Bhavasundariʼs army might be, it was large in morale and conviction. Although her army chiefly consisted of recruits from the Tuntule Bágdis of Ráŕh, there was also a large number of young, brown-skinned soldiers from the Ugra Kśatriyas, Sadgopes and Máhiśyas, the original inhabitants of Ráŕh. Their eyes glowed with joy at the coming victory, with the valour and eagerness to uphold the dignity and prestige of Bhurishrestha and Bengal.

King Jagatnarayan, restless within the prison walls, shouted repeated warnings to Bhavasundari to desist from the path of inevitable disaster. “Bhavi,” he said, “you are treading a dangerous path. I request you to give up this path. You are simply a noblewoman. It doesnʼt behoove you to take to the warpath.”

Queen Bhavasundari went to meet the imprisoned king and spoke to him from outside the cell. She reprimanded him: “When the question of collective interest is involved, some people will have to sacrifice themselves, O king. You should understand that. I didnʼt have much formal education; I was schooled only a little. You may say that ”a little learning is a dangerous thing,“ but I cannot agree with that. I am convinced that there are times when one has to sacrifice self-interest to protect the interest of many others. The one who readily sacrifices his self-interest is the best among all. He is acclaimed and crowned king of the people. Yah rájate sah rájáh [”He who rules is king“]. You were the king. This was your first duty. According to the scriptures, the king should take care of his subjects. You failed in your duty, so I had to decide what my responsibility should be.”

“Bhavi,” the king pleaded, “I implore you, I entreat you, to shun this path of war. If Emperor Akbar is like the Himalayas, then our army is just the small Shushunia Hill of Bankura. Who and what is your source of strength in treading such a risky path?”
“Ideology is my source of strength,” she replied; “the honour of Bengal is my pride. The blood of the fighters for Bengal, and my own, too, is the offering.”

“You can continue to indulge in your dreams of doom, Iʼm off to the battlefield. I am not fighting merely for my prestige; I am waging war so that the future generations of my motherland can dream of a glorious future. I am going to war. This isnʼt the time to decorate my feet with red ochre and draw a veil over my head. ( 5 ) I leave those things to you.”

The king, while trying desperately to dissuade her, wanted to say something. But she was adamant (Tel dáo siṋdur dáo Bhavii bholbár nay [“Give good-quality oil or vermilion. ( 6 ) But Bhavi is not going to be cajoled”]).

Bhavasundari advanced towards Burdwan along the southern bank of the Damodar. She and her forces were challenged by the Mughal army on the way. The Mughals had arrayed themselves where Amirpur and Manikahati now stand on the left bank of the Damodar and Natugram stands on the right. It was an unequal battle. The fighting went on for two days. Amar Ghosh, the leader of the Sadgopes, led the troops along the right bank, and Nityananda Singh, the leader of the Bágdis, came down the left bank at a place near Shuṋŕe-Kalna. The Ráŕh fighters were routed. Amar Ghosh and Nityananda Singh died on the battlefield.

Queen Bhavasundari found herself alone. There was no one either to her left flank or her right, in front or behind. Her sword was already unsheathed; she would not retreat to Mandaran. Akbar and Raja Man Singh had given orders that Bhavasundari should not be physically harmed, and she was taken captive untouched.
Man Singh said to her, “You were born and brought up in a noble family, you married royalty, so why did you take such grave risks in bloody battle?”
“Yes, I was born into nobility,” Bhavasundari replied, “and I married royalty. Because of that, I took to battle.”

“Now there is no one to help you,” Man Singh taunted. “What of that? I myself am here!” she said. Man Singh found himself in a very awkward position. He sent a detailed report to the emperor explaining the situation.

Akbar wrote back. “I accept the independence of Bhurishrestha, but let Bhurishrestha accept the supremacy of the Delhi emperor. Bhurishrestha need not pay any tax or tribute to Delhi. It shall be independent as regards internal matters. I have never known any woman as great as Bhavasundari. She is not only the pride of Bengal, she is the pride of the whole of India. I order her release and confer [on her] the royal title ”Ráybághinii“. (The title ”Ráybághinii“ has three meanings. One meaning is ”a lady of the Ray family having the prowess of a bághinii [tigress]“, the second is ”the queen of tigers“, and the third is ”a queen who is as powerful as a tigress”.)

For a long time afterwards, the story of Queen Bhavasundari and her title “Ráybághinii” continued to be popular among the people. The word ráybághinii came to denote a high-spirited lady. It gained a permanent place in the popular rhymes of Ráŕh.
Nanadinii ráybághinii
Nanadinii kuler káṋt́á
Ut́hte baste dey go khoṋt́á.
[The sister-in-law ( 7 ), that ráybághinii,
Is a thorn in the family,
She is constantly taking digs.]

After her release, she triumphantly returned to her capital Mandaran. The subjects gave her a tremendous welcome, with conches blowing and women ululating and throwing parched rice. Bhavasundari released her husband from prison and said to him, “Bhurishrestha is your kingdom; you should rule it as the king. But remember that women are not to take care of the kitchen twenty-four hours a day. They must come out whenever the needs of the nation call them. They must face the clashes of life with or without the men.”

The king said, “You are right, Bhavi, I now realize my mistake.” King Jagatnarayan lived for seven more years. He consulted Queen Bhavasundari on every important matter, particularly in correspondence with the Delhi emperor or the nawab of Bengal. He would not make any decisions alone.
It is related that before her death she said, “The tree which I planted for the future women of Bengal should not be allowed to wither or be cut down by anyone. ( 8 )

“As has been said in the scriptures, putrádicched parájayam or shiśyádicched parájayam [‘accepting being outdone by oneʼs son or disciplesʼ], I am also praying to God before death that women of Bengal in the future move ahead, leaving me far behind; let the speed of their movement take them closer and still closer to the sun.”

After Emperor Akbar, Emperor Jahangir had Bhurishrestha included in the Mughal Empire. There was no longer any Bhavasundari or Ráybághinii to resist this annexation. Bhurishrestha became lost somewhere in time.

Emperor Jahangir divided the land into several parganas [administrative divisions]. Among them, Sharifabad Pargana (Burdwan) and Arambag Pargana (Jahanabad) deserve special mention. Bhurishrestha or Bhurshut was now to be found written on the torn pages of history.

Why should I say “written on the torn pages of history”? Even the ink with which its name was written was also very indistinct. Bhurishrestha, surging with vitality in those days, was lost in the whirlpool of darkness.

The Gorkhas came to the hilly areas of Bengal in 1787, that is, exactly 30 years after the British conquered Bengal in the battle of Plassey. Prior to that, the Lepchas and Bhutias lived in the hills of Darjeeling. When the Gorkhas came from Nepal, the Sherpas came from Tibet almost at the same time. During the reign of the Chou Dynasty in China, some Tibetans migrated from Tibet and settled in the hilly regions of Darjeeling. They still live there, but in a very poor minority.

At that time I used to go for a walk nearly every day in the mountains east of Jamalpur. I used to sit on the second mountain. One after another, several small and large mountains run parallel to each other. The summit of the second mountain was the highest place among them. I used to arrive there in the middle of the afternoon and stay there until about eight at night. Then I would climb through the gáb (a large variety of kendu or mangosteen) forest that lay in the valley between two mountains. In this valley there was also a small lake. First I would cross the mountain, passing by the right side of the lake, and then I would take a shortcut back home.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: One day I was sitting on the peak. It was the bright lunar fortnight and I knew the path through the forest well so there was no need of a torch. Behind me, that is, to the east, there was a high plateau that was completely covered with woods. Most of the trees were sal [Shorea robusta], piyál (piyáshál) [Mimosa odoratassima], and palásh [Butea monosperma]. In front of me, that is, to the west, on the slope of the mountain, was a dense gáb forest. After that, in the valley in front, was an old tamarind tree. Other than this, there was very little vegetation. The mountain in front was completely barren.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: It was the lunar fortnight, beautiful moonlight. I was probably the only person for several miles, completely alone. To my right was a dried-up spring. The spring would have water for three or four months during the rainy season when the water would rush down quickly from above into the valley below. From that mass of water the lake was formed and the overflow from the lake would flow through many small streams into the little Dakra River which emptied into the Ganges west of Monghyr, below the Monghyr-Patna Road.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: Behind me, the jungle-covered plateau, though not plentiful with wildlife, still had some tigers, bears, hyenas, and the shambar and bársiuṋgá varieties of deer. That evening, however, I had not heard any sounds from them. Most likely they would not begin making sounds until after 10:00 or so at night. Beside the peak that I was seated on was a path that led down the mountain; they would take this path down to the lake to drink.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: That day a strong, sweet breeze coming from the forest was caressing my back and blowing out towards the mountain in front. I started feeling a little drowsy, having worked more than normal that day.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: I was about to get up when I heard what sounded like someone approaching me from behind. I turned around to look and saw a fair-skinned person wearing western clothes. I was somewhat surprised, for three reasons. First of all, it was extremely unlikely that anyone would be in that area after the sun went down. Secondly, though there was a lot of forest, even thieves would not dare come to cut wood for fear of wild animals. Thirdly, in those days western clothes were completely out of place there.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: Though this was the time of British rule, everyone knew that Westerners never came anywhere near such places. I asked him in English: “Who are you?” Looking at him, I could see that he was a real gentleman but he approached me without replying. He started looking around in all directions until his eyes came to rest on the valley in front of us. This time I asked him in Angika who he was and what he was doing there so late at night in such a deserted place. In those days such places were not completely safe. Then he answered me in a very soft and sweet, but unnatural, Bengali. “As long as you are here Iʼm not at all afraid.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: I was speechless. At any rate, his face bore the stamp of a gentle, courteous soul. As best as I could see in the moonlight he looked to be about twenty-three or twenty-four years old and from a good family. I invited him to sit down on the rock next to me. He thanked me politely and sat down. As he sat, I felt a change in the environment around me, as if someone had fashioned a dream world out of the power of Máyá.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “I am very near and dear to you,” he said. “You know me but perhaps nowadays youʼve forgotten me.” I gazed at him and noticed his unblinking eyes. It was as if all the wonder in the world, a fathomless, magical collyrium, was contained in those eyes. My ears pricked up to hear what he had to say and I looked at him carefully. His body did not seem to be of this world. Somehow it seemed to be made of light and shadow… as if I were watching a talking picture.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: Seating my guest near me, I asked him in Angika: “Are you one of our Angadesh boys?”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “No,” he replied, “but I have been here so long that I have become one with the soil. I love Angadesh with all my heart.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Why have you come to this solitary wilderness so late at night? By looking at you it seems to me that youʼve been here before.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “You are quite right. I often come here; rather, you can say I come here daily.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “What do you mean?”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “If youʼll give me a few moments of your time,” he replied, “there are a few things Iʼd like to say. If I start bothering you, please let me know and Iʼll stop.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: Then my visitor continued speaking. “This happened a long time ago, at the end of the Mughal period when the kingdom was in disarray. At that time the capital of the Province of Bengal (Bengal, Bihar and Orissa) was Murshidabad, and there was a zamindar [landlord] in Singur (Hooghly District – at that time Burdwan District) by the name of Viirendravijaya Vasumálika. Although he was a small landlord, he was a man of strong and independent thought. While the other landlords were indulging in addictions and luxuries, he was not. He was directing all sorts of efforts to preserve the freedom of Bengali culture, civilization, and way of life.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “He was quite dissatisfied with the character and conduct of weaker-minded men like Nawab Alivardi Khan. The nawab should have made the governmental machinery strong by making sure the commander-in-chief and the subedárs ( 1 ) performed their respective duties properly; on the one hand to develop Bengalʼs military prowess and on the other hand to solidify its economic structure, but he failed to do this. While it is true that he was a man having both merits and demerits and his character was somewhat unblemished, still, in matters of behaviour and comportment he was prone to weakness at every step – something which his wife, Lady Sharf-Un-Nisa, was unable to check or hold together despite much effort. He used to hide many things from his wife.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “At that time the Marathas of the Bhonsale family used to attack quite often. Those attacks, which were under the leadership of Bhaskar Pandit, were extremely bloody. The nawab was unable to make any provisions to resist them. This conduct of his was completely unpardonable. Rather, in order to avoid war, he was somehow able to strike a truce with the Marathas by giving them one fourth of the collected state revenue. When the Marathas arrived in Katoya, throwing Ráŕh into complete disorder, Alivardi Khan became aware of the danger but the nawab was not able to mount any resistance from Poŕahát (Seraikela-Kharsoan) to any part of Katowa. This weak conduct of the nawab continued to afflict the mind of the Bengalee people.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Many of those who were wealthy took shelter in Kolkata and in Angadesh out of fear of the attacks of the Marathas. While the Marathas were skilled in land battle they were not known for their naval skills. Thus, to save Calcutta from Maratha attack, a ditch was dug northeast of Calcutta – today it is known by the name "Maratha Ditch". Seeing that he was being routed by the Marathas, the nawab committed yet another blunder. He took four large districts, Burdwan (what is today Burdwan, Hooghly, Howrah, and Jamtara), Midnapore, Chittagong, and 24 Parganas, formed from the eastern portion of Nadia-Chakla, and delivered them into the hands of the East India Company with the condition that the East India Company would help the nawab turn back the Marathas. The people of Bengal did not like this behaviour of the nawab – the freedom-loving Viirendravijaya Vasumálika was completely against it.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Seeing the bad condition that Bengal was in at that time, Shobha Singh, the king of Midnaporeʼs Cheriyaberia, came forward. Shobha Singh was as brave in character as he was firm. Most of the people of Bengal wanted him to be king of the entire Bengal. The British also secretly wanted this and thus supported him from behind the scenes. Shobha Singh saw that the British had come to his country to do business and realized that if they were afforded convenient business opportunities their friendship could be won, but two people were thorns in Shobha Singhʼs path. One was Maharaja Bahadur of Burdwan. He was not a man of strong character but he was Bengalʼs biggest zamindar. ( 2 ) In a secret corner of his mind he felt that he had the greatest right to be Bengalʼs king. The second thorn in Shobha Singhʼs principled, strong-charactered path was the king of Mallabhum (Bishnupur of Bankura District) – Raghunath the Second (there is some difference of opinion in this matter).
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Raghunath was a man of vacillating character, a symbol of poor conduct. Forgetting his familyʼs illustrious tradition, he became infatuated with a certain Persian dancer by the name of Lalbai ( 3 ) and made up his mind to marry her. This fueled a dispute with the queen and with his ministers. Finally he met his death at the hands of the queen (Shobha Singhʼs daughter). Lalbai was probably also killed at this time. Anyhow, as a result of his own conduct Shobha Singh came into conflict with Raghunath the Second.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “The king of Singur, Viirendravijaya, helped Shobha Singh in many ways. He was not afraid of incurring the nawabʼs displeasure for this but Shobha Singh was stabbed and killed unexpectedly by the Princess of Burdwan. ( 4 ) After the death of Shobha Singh, Viirendravijaya was wondering what path should be taken to save Bengal. After the death of Alivardii Khan, his immature grandson became the nawab of Bengal, taking the name Mirza Mohammed Siraj-Ud-Daola. ( 5 ) In addition to his young age, he had many kinds of defect in his character and conduct. Virendravijay did not like this at all.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “At the time the East India Company was encroaching like a cat extending its claws, trying to gain control of the throne of Bengal by any means possible. On the other side, the public was divided into three camps. One group was vocally against the conduct and character of Siraj. Directly and indirectly, they supplied help to the East India Company.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: A second group supported the nawab regardless of his faults, following the policy of Nun khái yár guń gái tár [“If you eat someoneʼs salt then you have to praise their virtues”]. Mir Jafar, Jagat Seth and Umichand ( 6 ) fell into this category. Among them were also a few men who recognized the faults of the nawab but who did not want to allow the administration of Bengal to pass into the hands of the East India Company. For this reason alone they supported the nawab.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “The third group consisted of those who could not support the bad behaviour of the nawab but who also did not want to allow the East India Company to gain political control over Bengal. They supported neither side. Queen Bhavani was of this mind. Her relationship with the nawab was extremely bitter. Yet when she was asked to help the East India Company against the nawab, she said: ‘I do not want to dig a canal to bring the river crocodiles into my backyard pond.’ Because of this the East India Company was quite displeased with Queen Bhavani. Viirendravijaya was of the same opinion as the queen. Thus it was impossible for him to do anything either for or against the nawab.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “There was one more thing worth mentioning about these last days of Mughal political dominance. The Bengalee people were unable to consider the family of the nawab of Murshidabad as their own. No matter how much fuss and bother the writers and historians of today make over Siraj, the family of Murshidabadʼs nawab was very distant from the common people of Bengal. It was not only that they were Urdu-speaking immigrant Shias; ( 7 ) though they had settled in Bengal and were Bengalees in the eyes of the law, they did not think of themselves as Bengalees. They called the Bengalees ”rustics“ or ”Muslim rustics” (cáśá Musalmán). ( 8 ) Of course, they learned to speak Bengali, more or less, so that they could communicate with these Muslim rustics, but at home they spoke Urdu or a corrupted form of Urdu that was mixed with Bengali, and put on airs that they were not out-of-fashion Bengalees. This mental attitude kept them quite removed from the common people.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “If a person is great, if their mental arena is very large, then people lose sight of their worldly identity. Because Sirajʼs character was not very expanded there was no scope for people to forget his worldly defects. It is true that most people accepted that he was broad-hearted and generous, but this was not enough for him to gain a seat in the heart of the Bengalee people. And he was the nawab for how long!
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Most of the people who supported the nawab were senior Hindu officers. The East India Company put forth their best efforts to try to please the Hindus so that they would withdraw their support from Siraj.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Viirendravijaya died shortly after the battle of Plassey. At the time of his death he told his only son, Viireshavijaya, that he should dedicate himself wholeheartedly to the task of strengthening Bengalʼs culture, unity and economic situation, and asked him to use both his intellect and his courage properly in this matter. At the time Viireshavijaya was a boy of eighteen or nineteen. Viireshavijaya carried out the instructions of his father and became well-versed in the martial treatises.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Neither Viirendravijaya nor Viireshavijaya could support Mir Jafar. Mir Jafar was an undisciplined, power-hungry, spineless drunkard. His main preoccupation was to keep his nawabship intact by whatever means possible. For some time after his death the throne of Bengal was thrown into confusion. Thereafter Mir Qasim became the nawab. His conduct was spirited, his behaviour showed individuality, and he was a man of strong character. Viireshavijaya came into contact with him and Mir Qasim, touched by his sincerity, befriended him. ”In those days the throne was the nawabʼs in name only. The power was in the hands of the East India Company; the administration was in the hands of the nawab but the economic power was not. Moreover, if one was to repel the East India Company, it would not be possible to accumulate power by sitting in Murshidabad because Murshidabad was right next to the East India Companyʼs chief outpost. Viireshavijaya advised Mir Qasim to shift his capital from Murshidabad to Monghyr. He did not advise him to move his capital to Azimabad (Patna) because Azimabad was, to some extent, a centre for the East India Company.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “There were one or two other reasons for making Monghyr the capital of Bengal. During the time of the Mahábhárata, when Angadesh was first accepted as an independent kingdom, Duryodhana made Karna the king of Angadesh, and rather than consider him a vassal, he allowed him to wear the crown of a sovereign king. Since ancient times the Anga region was not considered part of northern India. Neither Anga, Vauṋga nor Kalinga were considered part of northern India. Starting from this time, Anga was declared an appendix, or auṋga, of northern India and hence its name became ”Auṋgadesha”. Vauṋga remained outside of northern India. Kalinga gained acceptance as a part of southern India. Thus even today, Oriya Brahmins are sometimes known as Dakśińátya Vedic Brahmins in Bengal. At the time of Karna the capital of Angadesh was Champakanagar. ( 9 ) Karna also founded an auxiliary capital in Mudgagiri (mudgagiri → muuṋgagiri → muuṋgir → muuṋger), on the western border of the kingdom of Anga. Hence Monghyr has a tradition as a capital. ( 10 )
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “When Gujaratʼs Rastrakuts [a royal dynasty] defeated eastern India, then Angadesh came under their jurisdiction. The Khirkhiriya Hills that we are sitting on were the eastern boundary of the Rastrakut kingdom. Thus they established a capital in their border city of Muṋgagiri. So we see that Monghyr became a capital more than once. At that time the road system of Bengal, as well as India, was not at all developed. The long highway Shershah built that extended from Suvarnagram in Dhaka District to the city of At́ak [Attak] in western Punjab via Teota (Manikganj Subdivision) and Howrah-Burdwan, and passing by Kolkata, did not afford much convenience to Murshidabad, Monghyr or Patna, but Monghyrʼs water-route transport system was good. The waterway worked well all the way from Dhaka to Benares-Allahabad passing via Narayanganj, Teota, Rampur, Boyaliya (Rajsahi), Lalagola Ghat, Godagarii Ghat, Chapaghati, Rajmahal (at one time Rajmahal was the capital of Bengal), Bhagalpur, Monghyr and Azimabad. Benares and Allahabad used to be aided by the Shershah-built Badshahii Road. Thus, since Monghyr was marked as an important centre of water transport, the capital could be established there without any communication problems as such.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Mir Qasim accepted Viireshavijayaʼs reasoning and moved the capital to Monghyr. On Viireshavijayaʼs advice, the nawab set about preparing the capital in Monghyr with great speed and began constructing his armoury. A great fortress was built in Monghyr as well as a munitions factory, heavy-weapons arsenal, huge parade grounds (Karheya Maidan or Kora Maidan), and a new cultural centre, Kasimbazar. The East India Company recognized the danger. Seizing on various small pretexts they declared war against Mir Qasim. They had economic power and were prepared for war – the nawab had nothing. He had just begun organizing. On the other side, the East India Company had concentrated their power at Fort William in Kolkata and in Alinagar (present-day Alipur, now a part of Kolkata).
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “The first battle was a trifling affair; it took place in Katwa and the nawab was defeated. The second battle took place in Gheriya and there also the nawab was defeated. The third took place in Udhuya or in the Udhuyanala. The East India Company advanced along the Ganges in the direction of Monghyr. A great battle took place in the Dakra Canal. With his finger, my visitor pointed out to me the Dakra Canal which originated on the western border of the Khirkhiriya Hills and joined the Ganges a little to the west of Monghyr. In reality, the Dakra was not a canal but a river. In the East India Company records it is mistakenly called a canal. At the time of the monsoon deluge, the water of the Ganges goes upstream through the Dakra River and floods a wide area in Monghyr District. At the time my visitor pointed out the Dakra Canal there was heavy flooding.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “When the nawab was defeated in the battle of Dakra Canal he started heading by water for Azimabad. The map and plans of the next battle site remained in the hands of Viireshavijaya. The planning of how the next battle in Buxar and on the banks of the nearby Karmanasha River could be fought was not in the hands of the nawab. All he knew was that there would be a battle fought in those places. Viireshavijaya became separated during the fighting and fell back a little to the south. He was not able to reach the banks of the Ganges and go upriver to Azimabad. But the warplans and maps were in his hands so he took shelter in the jungle of the Khirkhiriya Hills.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Another of the nawabʼs chief difficulties was his severe lack of economic resources. Viireshavijaya knew that King Karnaʼs huge treasury was secretly preserved in a cave in the Khirkhiriya Hills. He set about searching for that treasure, thinking that if it came into his hands he would much better be able to help the nawab.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “At this point I should say something about the history of Angadeshʼs terrain. In Karnaʼs time the north of Angadesh bordered on the Himalayas. ( 11 ) The southern border was the source of the Chandan River, a little to the north of Deoghar. On the western border was Ramdiri and Shamhodira (Samidhá) near Beguserai, and the eastern border was the Rajmahal Hills near Sahebganj where they approach the Ganges. The Rajmahal Hill Range occupies a large area in eastern Angadesh. Their eastern branch stops abruptly near Sahebganj and the Ganges; its western branch ends near Monghyr by the side of the Ganges. The western branchʼs Sanskrit name is the Kśirakśiriká Hills. In Auṋgiká [Angika] they are called Khirkhiriya Hills and in English the Kharagpur Hills. The Kharagpur Hills are a branch of the Rajmahal Hills.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Southern Angaʼs chief river is the Chandan which has two companions, the Baruya and the Chiir. In this Chandan-Baruya-Chiir River Basin ( 12 ) one finds the Kalhan Hills (near Kahalgaon, named after Maharshi Kalhan), Ajagavii Hills (near Sulatanganj), Mandar Hills ( 13 ) (a little north of the railway station), and the Khirkhiriya Hills on the western border where one can find, scattered here and there, innumerable examples of the culture of ancient Angadesh. Like the Angika culture, the language also belongs to this place.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Those who think that the Khirkhiriya Hills are the western border of Angadesh, however, are mistaken. To the west of the Khirkhiriya Hills lies the Dakra River Basin. This Dakra River Basin is Angaʼs final western border. Beyond the Dakra River Basin lies the Kiul River Basin where one can find many examples of Magadh culture, that is, it belongs to the land of Magadh.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “The Angika language has three chief dialects: Dharamapuriyá, Champánagarii or Chekáchekii, and Muṋgeriá. The Dharamapuriya dialect is spoken on the north bank of the Ganges. The Chekáchekii dialect is spoken in the far eastern region where the Rajmahal Hills approach the Ganges near Sahebganj, and in the western border area where the Khirkhiriya Hills stop near the Ganges. Miirzachauki, near Sahebganj, was at the border of the provinces of Bengal and Bihar during the time of Akbar. Miirzachauki was a busy checkpost. It occupied a narrow strip of land between the Ganges and the mountains and thus was an ideal spot for a checkpost. The Muṋgeriyá dialect is prevalent west of the Khirkhiriya Hills in the Dakra River Basin.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Besides these, there are also two mixed sub-dialects of Angika: The first is the Shriipuriyá sub-dialect, which is used in the region lying between Purnea and Kisanganj. Purneaʼs language is Angika, and Bengali is the language of Kisanganj. The Shriipuriyá language that is spoken in the interlying areas is a mixture of Angika and Rauṋapurii Bengali (Suryapurii). The second sub-dialect is the Northern Khot́t́á dialect, which is used in the region between Katihar and Maldah. The language of Katihar is Angika, and in Maldah, Bengali. In certain places between the two one can find this Northern Khot́t́á sub-dialect. It is a mixture of Angika and Shershahabad Bengali. In Muṋgeriyá Angika one can find some influence of Magahi. Similarly, in the Magahi of the Kiul River Basin there is some influence of Angika.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “As I was saying,” my visitor continued, “I hope I am not annoying you by talking for so long. Earlier I told you that I loved Angadesh with all my heart. So when the topic of Anga comes up, I start going on without any hesitation. Then afterwards, I think to myself that I hope I havenʼt annoyed whoever Iʼve been talking to.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Why should I be annoyed?” I replied. “Rather, Iʼm quite astonished; I wonder how you came to know so much at such an early age.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: The light and shadow body of my visitor trembled as he spoke. “These are all your own thoughts. Earlier I said that I am in your mind. So your thoughts are coming out from my mouth.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Yes,” he continued. “Viireshavijaya started searching the forest of the Khirkhiriya Hills for Karnaʼs ”treasury“ in order to save it from the hands of the East India Company. Do you know,” he added, “when I visit these hills I feel as if my entire being is overwhelmed by that Viireshavijaya. It feels as if I am also searching for someone in these hills and in this forest. Shall I say one more thing?… Please donʼt mind. Please say you wonʼt mind.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “No, I wonʼt mind,” I replied. “Go ahead.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Now,” he continued, “it seems to me as if I have come searching for you.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: I stared at him, speechless. There was the whisper of a smile on his guileless face.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “After a few daysʼ search, Viireshavijaya came across one of his faithful followers. He entrusted him with the secret plans and maps as well as various urgent matters and sent him to the nawab in Buxar. It was impossible for him to go himself. It would not have been so bad if he himself were to be caught, but it was essential that the war documents not fall into the hands of the Company. But to the good fortune of the East India Company and the misfortune of Bengal, his follower was caught by the Company near Surajgara. He was killed and the Company learned of the movements of both Viireshavijaya and the nawab.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “The Company dispatched a large advance army to Buxar and the bank of the Karmanasha River where they laid in ambush waiting to draw up battle formation. Needless to say, Mir Qasim lost the battle of Buxar and was completely routed in the battle of the Karmanasha. He had neither manpower nor economic resources. Disheartened, he went first to Zamaniya, then later to Gazipur. At the time Gazipur was under the control of Agra Province. The East India Companyʼs direct rule had not yet been established there. In poor health and with a broken spirit, Mir Qasim breathed his last in Gazipur. The nawab of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, Mir Qasim, died like an ordinary man, or not even, since no one dared to give him a proper burial for fear of the East India Company. Simply a hole was dug and he was thrown in. Even this was washed away and vanished when the Ganges flooded.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “When he received news of the nawabʼs death,” my visitor went on, “Viireshavijaya became very sad but he didnʼt lose heart. He decided to leave the Khirkhiriya Valley and head for Ráŕh. There he thought to build a new army with the help of the Bágdiis [a fighting community belonging to the ”lower” strata of society].
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “In fact,” he went on, “Viireshavijaya was sitting and thinking in the very spot where you are sitting now, thinking and thinking.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “I was telling you about Gazipur City. Lord Cornwallis introduced a permanent land settlement for the landed property of Bengal Presidency. Before introducing the land settlement in Bengal, he went first to Gazipur District to make the same arrangements for the province of Agra. ( 14 ) Gazipur was at that time a huge district. Later, the eastern portion of this district was separated and a new district was formed called Baliya (Bahlik). When Cornwallis arrived in Gazipur City he fell ill and died there. His tomb is still there today.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Yes, since Mughal times, the city of Gazipur has been famous for rosewater and attar. This fame still continues to some extent. Rabindranath Tagoreʼs elder brother, Satyendranath Tagore, was the district magistrate of Gazipur city. It was in his government residence that Rabindranath wrote his book Naokád́ubi [The Wreck].
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Talking about Gazipur reminds me again of Monghyr. Shahjahanʼs son, Suja, had the same kind of relationship with Monghyr that Mir Qasim had with Gazipur. He fled the country from Monghyr for fear of his life during the Aurangzebʼs invasion. People today still call the wharf that his barge left from Sujiighat (Sujá-i-ghát́). Of course, Suja stopped for one night while passing through the city of Bhagalpur in order to draw up his next plans. Thereafter he went to Akiyab, the capital of Arakan [Burma], to take shelter with its king. But he disappeared into oblivion there – whatever happened there is still a mystery today.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “After Viireshavijayaʼs messenger fell into the hands of the East India Company in Surajgarha, they knew that he was holed up in the Khirkhiriya Hills. The Khirkhiriya Hills were then part of the zamindary kingdom of Dwarabhanga. Badshah Akbar had given them to Mahesh Thakur as a feudal estate. During Mir Qasimʼs time the Khirkhiriya region was controlled by the king of Dwarabhanga from his residential offices in Kharagpur. ( 15 )
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “At the time that Viireshavijaya was wandering in the Khirkhiriya Hills, the director of the Kharagpur Zamindary offices was his maternal uncle, Mohankrisna Mitra. The East India Company didnʼt know that Viireshavijaya was Mohan Mitraʼs nephew. Mohan Mitra was well-aware of the steely character and fiery behaviour of his sisterʼs son. He also understood that his nephew was carrying out the instructions of his father. So despite the fact that Viireshavijaya was the same age as his own son, he showed him the greatest respect and helped him in every way possible.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “The East India Company surrounded the Khirkhiriya Hills with their troops in an effort to trap Viireshavijaya, who got word of this through his uncle. Through similar means, Viireshavijaya discovered the cave where King Karnaʼs treasure-store was hidden; however, the treasure was no longer there. Someone, it seemed, had emptied the cave of all its wealth after King Karna had left. Viireshavijaya was only able to get hold of three siinakas [gold coins].” Then my visitor pointed out the cave to me with his finger. It was very close to where I was sitting.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “It is a very small cave,” he continued. “A few miles to the southwest of this hill is a cave with paintings from the Buddhist era, and to the east is Risikunda. Nowadays people have forgotten its history, so they say that it is the áshram [hermitage] of the Risyashrnga Muni mentioned in the Rámáyańa.
