Actually there was a Buddhist monastery here during the Buddhist era. On the western edge of these mountains you will find the grave of Jamal Miya. Jamal Miya came here from Rajnagar in Birbhum and was the first to propagate Islam in this area. This place was named Jamalpur after him.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Yes, I was talking about Rajnagar. Rajnagar is now a very small city but at one time it was the district headquarters. During the Mughal era, certain districts in the Province of Bengal were extremely large (Monghyr, Sylhet, Birbhum, Mymensingh, Purnea, etc.). In many districts the district administrator was called the Zila Hakim but in Birbhum and Purnea he was called the Bara Hakim or governor. The governor of Birbhum used to live in Rajnagar. The last governor, Alinakhii Khan II, only ruled Birbhum for a short time, and Purneaʼs last governor, Shaokatjang, ( 16 ) after being defeated in the Katihar war by Siraj-Ud-Daola, was removed from the post of Purneaʼs Bara Hakim.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Anyhow, Jamal Miya came from Rajnagar. Later the area of Birbhum District was reduced and the district headquarters was shifted from Rajnagar to Suri. Various cultural artifacts are scattered throughout our Angadesh, but who is there to point them out? Angadeshʼs condition is like that of an orphaned child. What to speak of Angadesh, a great part of India is in the same condition today. Where will the historical materials come from if we continue to neglect these cultural artifacts? Nearby, for example, near Kahalgaon (Áńt́icak) was the Vikramshila university from the Buddhist Age, but how much research has been done on it? Yet, nowadays thousands of universities are springing up like mushrooms.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: My visitor paused for a moment, then said softly: “I am talking a lot, quite a lot. But you donʼt seem to be annoyed at all. Of course, these are all your thoughts. They are only coming out of my mouth.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: Then he continued. “Viireshavijaya began to worry that the Company had picked up his trail and might capture him at any time and persecute him. There was also the danger that they would learn about the work he had just begun with the help of his followers among the Bágdiis in Ráŕh and make them suffer greatly for it. One cannot bear to think about it. What kind of a future would Bengal have? Would Mother Bengal pass her days crying? Would the time he had spent on earth go in vain? This is what Viireshavijaya was thinking that night, seated in this very spot around 8:30 in the evening. Perhaps the next morning the Company would catch up with him. Viireshavijaya slowly made his way down to the rain-swollen falls and plunged into its waters. Within moments his body was swept up in the current and carried down into a deep cavern, from there to a lake, then to the Dakra River and finally to the Ganges. There was no one to attend the funeral services for this twenty-three year old, ideologically-dedicated young man. No one even knew his history.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “This is what I thought, and exactly what I wanted. Now your watch is showing 8:27. Please sit here for another three minutes, that is, until 8:30. I know youʼll be late returning home, but I beg you to please stay another three minutes. I am going down to the falls.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “Donʼt go too close to the waterfall,” I requested. “These falls have a very strong current, as you can see; it will be dangerous for you to go too close.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: My visitor slowly made his way down to the falls and stood there. He looked once at the sky, once at the ground, once at the forest before him and once at me. One leg was very close to the falls. I called out to him: “Take your left foot away from the falls. If you step back you may fall in.” A soft smile appeared on his bright face and he brought his foot forward. I said: “You were telling me such a long story, but you see, I have committed a great mistake by not asking your name.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “No, no. You havenʼt made any mistake. I am the one who has made a mistake. My offence is that I am a gentleman, from a good family, but still I havenʼt introduced myself. I should have given you my name as soon as we first met. Please forgive me.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: I did not know what to say. Again he repeated: “Please tell me that you forgive me.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “There is no question of forgiveness,” I said. “If you want to tell me your name then you can.”
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: “I am that Viireshavijaya Vasumálika,” he replied. Saying this, he threw himself into the water. The rapids flung his body around violently and carried him off towards a deep cavern. After that his body sank and disappeared from sight. A sudden strong gust of wind blew at my back from the direction of the forest. Then the gust of wind started blowing towards the mountain in front of me. All around me I could hear the sound soṋ, soṋ, soṋ [sound of the wind]. If someone else had been there they would not have heard anything else, but in the middle of this soṋ-soṋ sound I could hear Viireshavijayaʼs last words “má-má-má go” [mother, mother, oh my dear mother]. With steadfast eyes I looked at the rapids. Unknowingly, my eyes lit upon a few drops of water. In all directions one could hear the hills reverberating with the sound – má-má-má go.
chapterTitle: Will Bengalees Forget the Valour of Viireshavijaya?

t: Iitr was first discovered by Empress Nurjahan. Jáhán means vishvabrahmáńd́a ( 1 ). Núr means “light”. Koh-i-núr means “mountain of light”.

I think it is important to mention here that the diamond which is known as Kohinúr [Koh-i-Noor] was the locket [pendant] on Shrii Krśńaʼs jewelled necklace. After many battles and campaigns it came into the hands of Nadir Shah, and thereafter Punjabkesharii Ranjit Singh. After him, Jhindan acquired it, and finally it came into the hands of the East India Company. They had it cut and polished in Holland and then had it set in the British Royal Crown, although some people are of the opinion that it was not set in the crown but was preserved in a different location. Whatever the case may be, Krśńaʼs kaostúbhamańi and the kohinúr are one and the same.

Now let us come back to the actual subject. By mixing rose essence with water, Nurjahan invented the process of preparing rosewater. It is said that she used to bathe daily in rosewater. By mixing rose essence with sandalwood oil she invented rose iitr [attar]. Later she started to prepare other types of iitr by using flowers other than rose.

Nurjahan was a Persian lady. This uncommonly beautiful woman was sold by her father in India. Her real name was Meher-Un-Nisa. During Akbarʼs time, Burdwan ( 2 ) was the capital of Bengal. It was during this time that she was married to Sher Afgan, the governor (or subedar) of Bengal. Selim, the son of Akbarʼs Rajput wife (later known as Jahangiir ( 3 ) after ascending the throne), put pressure on Sher Afgan to surrender Meher-Un-Nisa to him, but Sher Afgan did not agree. There followed a fierce battle in Burdwan between Sher Afgan and the Mughal army. ( 4 ) Sher Afgan was slain in the battle (his grave is still in Burdwan city) and Jahangiir forcibly abducted Meher-Un-Nisa. At first Meher-Un-Nisa refused to marry her husbandʼs killer, Jahangiir, but later, under pressure of circumstances, she agreed.

After her marriage to Jahangiir her new name became Nurjahan. Jahangiir was an unstable drunkard; India was actually ruled by Nurjahan. Both Rajiya Begum during Pathan rule and Nurjahan during Mughal rule became famous as especially skilled female administrators. But the name of Nurjahan is more famous for iitr. Nurjahan was also a highly skilled kavii [poet] ( 5 ) in the Farsi language.

Speaking about iitr reminds me of an experience from the old days. I was staying in an ordinary hotel in the city of Gaya doing research on the culture and civilization of Magadh. At the time I was working in the hilly wilds around Gaya searching for the deep, hidden similarities between the pre-Buddhist Magadh civilization and the ancient civilization of Ráŕh. I had found a striking similarity between the two and had never before felt such excitement and enthusiasm in my research. In terms of my river valley research I was concentrating then on the Naeranjana-Mohaniya-Phalgu River Basin.

The hotel was small but neat, clean and orderly, as if someoneʼs house had been turned into a hotel. I arrived there about six in the evening, took a good look at the bedroom and the bathroom, and then, after finishing some important work, I retired early, tired after the dayʼs labours. Sleep came on quickly. Ah yes, before sleeping I noticed a white stone iitr-pot in one corner of the dressing table, a Gayan artifact of ancient Mágadhii culture. I could tell that the iitr-pot had not been used in a long time because it did not smell at all of iitr.

Sometime later, Iʼm not sure exactly what time it was, I was awakened by a strange sensation just above the ankle. There was a dim light in the room – the rest of the lights I had turned off before going to bed. What did I see in that dim light when I looked down but what looked like a pair of hands catching me just above the ankles! I freed my legs with a jerk and called out in Magahi: “Who are you? Why have you come into my room like this? This is not good.”

The two hands drew back. Then I saw a shadowy figure slowly move back into the dark part of the room and lose itself behind the dressing table. I quickly got up, turned on the lights and thoroughly searched the bedroom and the bathroom as well as the closet but no one was there. The door was still locked from the inside as I had left it, which meant that nobody had come in from outside. Then what was it? Whose hands was it with their indistinct touch? And those hands had left the scent of jasmine essence!

Keeping the light on I lay down and called out mentally: “Hey, bodiless one, have courage, come out once again. I never do anyone any harm, so there is no possibility of your being harmed by me. Come and tell me your untold story.” But nothing or no one came out.

Then suddenly I see… what is this? Astonishing! Smoke is rising out of that abandoned iitr-pot. But how? And that smoke was filled with the scent of jasmine. I was dumbfounded. Gradually the smoke began to twist into coils. They became denser and denser, but what was behind those coils of smoke could not be seen or understood.

After a short time the smoke began to thin and what did I see behind the coils but a young man of good breeding, perhaps twenty-four or twenty-five years old. He looked at me and greeted me politely with folded hands, stood silently for a while, then softly made his way towards the door. He opened the locked door and quietly went outside. I found this all very mysterious.

He went down the stairs from the first floor to the ground floor, but his footsteps were completely silent. He was walking, but no sound was coming. I also followed silently behind him, determined not to leave him until I found out who he was… for what reason he had entered my room at one in the morning… what it was he wanted to say.

The main entry door to the hotel was locked, but he opened it and went straight out into the street. I was following right behind him, but he never turned back to look. The city was dead quiet. Not even a dog was awake and about. He walked on and so did I. Not far from the hotel was the Phalgu River, and after a short time he reached the river and stopped. He stood there silently for a short time, then turned around to look at me and said in Magahi: “I have given you trouble… quite a lot of trouble… please donʼt mind.”
“What trouble have you given me?” I replied. “I followed you of my own accord. I wanted to see what your destination would be.”
“I entered and left your room abruptly and came here for no other reason than that you would follow behind me.”
“I have come to hear what you have to say,” I said. “Tell me briefly whatever it is you want to say.”
He looked around once carefully in all directions and then began. “At the moment there is no one here besides the two of us; in these surroundings my words will make a stronger impression.

“I am a child of Magadh. History has never done full justice to this land of Magadh. Every dust particle of its villages and markets is mixed with the gold-dust of its heritage, but no one has properly recognized it or recorded it. The little that has been written about it has been written by foreign historians – some out of sport, some out of merriment. The shrivelled Phalgu that you see today was not always in this condition. The hills of southern Magadh were once covered with dense forests. Beyond the mountains, from the north to the south, the Mágadhii River valley was also covered with thick forests. Even a portion of the plains and the banks of the river were also forested. This heavily-forested Magadh used to enjoy an abundance of rainfall and thus the rivers were full of water twelve months out of the year. Because of the abundance of forests there was no problem of soil erosion, and because the forests contained the water there was very little severe flooding. Seeing the Magadh of today, it is difficult to imagine the lush green Magadh that once was.

“You are certainly aware of the fact that Magadh was once a vast empire. At the time of Ashoka and Samudragupta it was probably the largest empire in the world – but nothing lasts forever. Those glorious days came to an end and a cimmerian darkness descended over Magadh. The most difficult days in Magadhʼs history drew nigh during the reign of Skandagupta.”
“Tell me a little more, in brief.”

He went on. “Skandagupta was one in a string of unworthy sovereigns to occupy the throne of Magadh. At that time the empire had disintegrated and the kingdom was on the point of collapse, confined to its ancient borders. To the north was the Ganges and north of that Mithila, which was at one time part of the empire of Magadh and which Ráŕhʼs King Shashanka had wrested from the hands of Magadh. To the east were the Grdhrakút́a and Cakravarttii Mountains. In the eastern region of the Grdhrakút́a Mountains was Angadesh and the Magadh Empire. King Shashanka of Ráŕh also took possession of these areas. In the eastern regions of the Cakravarttii Mountains was the land of Ráŕh, which came under Shashankaʼs direct rule. The southeast cornerʼs border was Sametashikhar. Next came ancient Ráŕh, which the king of Ráŕh had conquered. The southern portion of the Ramgarh Mountains to the south, and the western portion of the Shon River to the west were first controlled by the king of Kashi, Citrasena. After his fall, this entire area was controlled by the royal house of Thaniishvar. Magadh did not have a direct struggle with Prabhakaravardhana but rather with Rajyavardhana and Harsavardhana.
“Iʼve gone on quite a bit about the borders of Magadh at that time. I hope you didnʼt mind. Without it the picture would not be complete.”
“Go on,” I said. “I am enjoying listening.”

“Magadh had lost all its previous power and glory,” he continued. “King Skandagupta was a weak-minded, vacillating drunkard. He did very little of what we normally consider great deeds; rather he led Magadh to the brink of destruction.

“Of course, nothing in this world is completely one-sided. No matter how much historians blame him, Skandagupta did some good also. This city of Gaya, which we are standing in the heart of, was designed by him. He founded Sanskrit schools and training centres in various parts of Magadh, such as Dvádashavardhaká (Barbigha), Brhadhiká (Barahiya), Madhukamadhá (Mokama), Urubilva (Arawal), Grdhrakút́a (Gidhaor), and so forth, which endured for quite some time. He was the first to introduce the use of the Mágadhii language of that time (Western Demi-Mágadhii) in government service alongside Sanskrit. Still, he watched the Magadh Empire crumble in front of his eyes. He died watching an entire empire fall apart due to his own incompetence.

“At that time there was a fierce struggle going on for the capture of Magadh between King Rajyavardhana of the royal house of Thaniisvar and Ráŕhʼs King Shashanka. Thanisvaraʼs kings used to repeatedly move their capital from place to place, but Shashanka did not. Rather, he would enlarge his capital according to necessity and befitting the times. He founded Paiṋca Gaoŕa [the five ancient parts of Bengal] after capturing Anga and Mithila and then North Bengal (Barendra), Central Bengal (Samatat) and East Bengal (Vauṋga). That is, during his time Bengal was divided into five political divisions: 1) Ráŕh, 2) Mithila, 3) Samatat, 4) Barendra, and 5) Vauṋga-D́abák (East Bengal or Shriibhúmi or Cat́t́al was then included in Bengal) – but he kept his capital at Karnasuvarna. ( 6 )

“There were several reasons for the war between Rajyavardhana and Shashanka. Rajyavardhanaʼs aims were to plunder Magadhʼs wealth and to take possession of Angabhumi. Shashankaʼs main aims were to take possession of Angabhumi and to root out the Buddhist religion and culture from Magadh. Although Rajyavardhana put on a show of liberality he was really narrow-minded. In actual fact, he never treated the Shaivite religion as equal to the Buddhist religion. Shashanka was a staunch follower of Shaivism and completely against Buddhism. He openly declared that as long as one drop of blood remained in his body, he would not allow Buddhism the right to enter either Ráŕh or Paiṋca Gaoŕa ( 7 ) (Bengal).

“I am sure you are familiar with Ambabhumi, ( 8 ) which is situated in the western part of our Magadh. Ambabhumi was the ancient name of that fertile region (modern name Mokámá T́ál) composed of the western areas of what is now Monghyr District – Surajagara, Laksmiisarai, Baravigha, Barhiya, and so on; the eastern portion of Patna District, especially Mokama and surrounding areas; the eastern part of present-day Nalanda District; and the northeast areas of present-day Nawada District. There was no other region in all of India which was as fertile and as affluent at that time. Thus everyone had their greedy eyes set on Ambabhumi. Rajyavardhana and Shashanka were no exceptions.

“Their style of attack, however, differed. Rajyavardhana wanted to plunder wealth, so he would set fire to peopleʼs houses and ransack them. Shashankaʼs aim was to destroy Buddhist monasteries (what are now called gaŕa in modern Magahi) and Maháyána Buddhist images and idols. You are certainly aware of the fact that, according to social and religious regulations, idols can no longer be used for worship once there is any defect or deformation in them. So Shashanka had the different statues of Buddhist gods and goddesses deformed with a chisel. Today you will find that most of the ancient Buddhist religious statues still in existence have had their noses broken off.

“Foreign historians claim that they were damaged during the time of Baktiar Khiljii, or Kálápáháŕ. ( 9 ) Although there is a grain or two of truth in this, it is, for the most part, a false assertion. They were actively fostering conflict between the Hindus and Muslims of our country, because they followed the policy of ‘divide and rule’. Actually Shashanka was responsible. He was not interested in looting. In this way, with Rajyavardhana burning his way from the west and Shashanka applying pressure from the east, the two of them brought Magadh to its last gasp.

“Now the sacred banyan tree that you were sitting under yesterday was not the real Bodhi Tree where Siddhartha attained enlightenment. Ashokaʼs son, Mahendra, took a branch from the original tree and brought it to Sri Lanka. That branch grew into a second Bodhi Tree in Sri Lanka and a branch was taken from that second tree and brought here and planted. This Bodhi Tree was produced from that branch. Shashanka not only extirpated that ancient Bodhi Tree, he also dug a deep ditch around it afterwards and filled it with honey so that the ants would come and eat whatever remained of the roots while they devoured the honey; as a result that Bodhi Tree could not grow back again.
“This is the history of my Magadh of those times.”

“You canʼt be very old,” I said. “One could say that you are still a lad, so how is it you know so much? There was no clear or formulated system of studying or teaching history in those days. The study and teaching of history in India was first provided for by Emperor Nasiruddiin during Pathan rule and by several foreign travelers during the Mughal era. Thus there were no history books in either Sanskrit or any of the Prákrta languages. The real beginning of the teaching and study of history came during the time of British rule. So the things you have been talking about have never been properly recorded.”
“I am not saying all this myself,” he replied. “I am thinking about you and whatever you are thinking about is coming out through my mouth.”
“I appreciate your competence and erudition very much,” I said.

“As a result of the clash between Shashanka and Rajyavardhana,” he continued, “the amount of harm that Magadh suffered was doubled. It would be a mistake to say that neither one wanted to see the other; neither one of them could even stand hearing the otherʼs name. Shashanka, in an unexpected development, captured Kanyakubja, slew its king, Cakrayudha (in some peopleʼs opinion, Inrayudha), the husband of Rajyavardhanaʼs sister, Rajyashrii, and installed his own nephew from Ráŕh, Keshariivijaya, on the throne, giving him the name Indrayudha (some say Cakrayudha). Rajyashrii returned to her fatherʼs house and instigated her brothers, Rajyavardhana and Harśavardhana, to turn against Ráŕh. As a result, Magadh, which lay between those two lands, had to suffer many outrages. This is our Magadh.

“Mag means ‘he who moves about independently’, that is, one who does not follow the Vedic injunctions. Dha means ‘follower’. The land which follows the anti-Vedic, Buddhist doctrine is Magadh. The Sanskrit dha is transformed into ha in Prákrta. Thus magadha becomes magaha – the name of the language is Magahi. Following the Buddhist era, the language of all of eastern India was this Magahii Prákrta. Lord Buddha, The Enlightened, made his appearance in this land.

“Our Magadh is situated in the northeast corner of the prehistoric Gondwanaland. Since Gondwanaland is the oldest land on earth, it is also the original home of human beings, the birthplace of human civilization. Ráŕh is in eastern Gondwanaland. In the prehistoric era, human beings came from Ráŕh to make their home in Magadh and they brought with them the current of their civilization and culture. Just as the geography of Magadh slopes downwards from north to south and the rivers flow from north to south, similarly the culture and civilization flowed from south to north. Thus the people of Ráŕh and Magadh are fundamentally one. Like the people of Ráŕh, the common people of Magadh are dark-skinned. Magadh borders Ráŕh along its southeast border. The skin and bodily structure of the people of Ráŕh and Magadh are identical. There is also a noticeable similarity between their languages.

“Earlier I told you that in those days Magadh was full of forests and had abundant rainfall so there was no need of irrigation. The pre-Aryan people of Magadh used to believe that their land received rainfall due to the grace of the sun-god. Thus they used to worship the sun-god according to their ancient local customs, once during the autumn paddy harvest and again during the spring sun harvest (chaetii harvest). This sun-worship of pre-Aryan Magadh is known today as chat́ pújá. This worship was not performed according to Aryan rules. It was a completely local Magadh practice. The people of Magadh did not bow their heads and submissively accept any of the Aryan practices. For that reason the Aryans called the land Magadh. They were afraid of Magadh and used to pay it respect. Thus, to satisfy their grudge and vent their spite, they declared Magadh an unholy land. They said that if a man died there he would not go to heaven and they made efforts to forcibly impose their language, culture and civilization on Magadh. It is up to the historians and social scientists to consider just how successful they were in their efforts.

“Magadh did not accept the Aryan civilization. In ancient Magadh there was no custom of racial or caste divisions. The caste system in Magadh came much later due to the influence of the Aryans. Even after the advent of the caste system, the Kraoiṋcadviipii and Magadhʼs Shrotriya Brahmins did not like the severity of caste divisions. For this reason the Kraoiṋcadviipii and Magadhʼs Shrotriya Brahmins were not recognized by the Brahmins of northern India.”
The boy looked at me and said with a choked voice, “You know, today Magadh is torn apart by caste differences. I want to hear from your lips if Magadh has a future or not.”

“Why are you weeping?” I asked. “Why are you thinking in this way? I tell you, Magadh has a bright future. Magadh will once again break down the walls of narrow-mindedness and hold its head high in the world community. Magadhʼs past was bright and its future will be radiant.”
He was consoled and happy.

“It was an unbelievable and unforgettable happening. Nearly two and a half thousand years ago two great spiritual leaders appeared on the earth at about the same time on the soil of Magadh to sow there the seeds of their spiritual teachings. One was Vardhaman Mahavir and the other was Gaotama Buddha. Gaotama Buddha was the son of the feudal king of the central terái, Shuddhodana (Malla dynasty, Shákya branch of the Kśatriyas), and his wife Mayadevii. He practised austerities for a long time in Magadh in the areas of the Barábar, Brahmayoni and Grdhrakút́ mountains. His guru in Sáḿkhya philosophy, Acarya Sanjaya (Nawada District), was also from Magadh. Although what is called avidyá in his philosophy is not the same as pradhána or prakrti in Sáḿkhya, there is some similarity between the Buddhaʼs concept of avidyá and the Sáḿkhya concept of pradhána.

“The Buddha attained enlightenment in the village of Urubilva, located on the bank of the river Naeranjana (Urubilva is called Bodhgaya today). That Sujata who fed him kśiira [rice pudding] and saved his life at that moment when the period of his radiant austerities had brought him to the point of death, was Buddhaʼs cousin and the wife of a certain feudal king of Magadh. One should remember here that at that time the Naeraiṋjana River coming from the south joined the Mohaniká (Mohaniya) River near Urubilva and flowed together from there as the Phalgu River, later joining the Ganges near Modhukamadhá [Mokama]. About 2000 years ago the two rivers underwent some physical changes due to a huge earthquake and for that reason the Phalgu River of today is much smaller than it was.

“At any rate, the prince of the Shakyas, Gaotama, attained enlightenment on Magadh soil. Many say that Buddha first introduced the Buddhist dharmacakra [wheel of dharma] and initiated his first disciple near Benares in the Isipattana Migadaba (Rśipattana deer grove, alias Sárauṋganáth or Saranath). Although this is partially correct, it is not the complete truth. It is certainly true that he introduced the dharmacakra in the Isipattana deer grove and that his five disciples, Kaondinya (Kaońdilya), Bappá (Vapra), Bhaddiiya (Bhadreya), Mahánáma, and Ashsháji (Ashvajit), were present there. But he gave his first initiations on Magadh soil – to Sáriputta, the son of Rúpasári, and Mahamoggallan Arhan, the son of Mahamoggalii.

“In those days Magadhʼs matriarchal system still retained some influence alongside the patriarchal system. So Buddhaʼs first two disciples in Magadh were known by their mothersʼ names. The merchant that the city of Pataliputra was named after due to his philanthropy also carried his motherʼs name in accordance with the matriarchal system. The name of the merchantʼs mother was Pát́alii.

“Vardhaman Mahavir was born in Vaeshálii in a Vaeshya family. His fatherʼs name was Siddhartha and his motherʼs name was Trishala. Like the Buddha, however, he did not propagate his teachings first in his native land but came to Magadh to do so.

“One does not have to go far to find the reason why both of them selected Magadh as the proper place for their work. Magadh was not bound hand and foot with the bonds of the Vedic religion. Their natural liberal mentality gushed forth in all aspects of their lives. Buddha was successful in spreading his teachings (dharmadeshaná) there because they were based more on logic than on superstition and belief. Of course, the spirit of revolt against conventionality was present in Vardhaman Mahavirʼs teachings also, but in the opinion of the Magahi people his doctrine of ahiḿsá [non-violence] did not accord well with reality so they were not able to accept it easily. Of course, some people did accept it, but others considered him an unrealistic theoretician and tried to bring him down to earth by using occult powers. Thus he felt the need to go elsewhere to propagate his new religion.

“At that time the most famous city for progressive thinking, education and culture was Ástikanagar (Atthinagar), the capital of Ráŕh. Vardhaman Mahavir went there and stayed nearly eight years. There he managed to fit his doctrine of ahiḿsá into a somewhat realistic framework. Some prominent merchants of Ástikanagar accepted his doctrine and they renamed the city Vardhaman [Burdwan] after him. Thus it is said that the Jain religion was first established in Ráŕh.

“Thereafter he took the road back to Magadh from Burdwan and stopped for a short time in a small village named Svámiisthána (Svámiisthána → Sáiṋitthán → Sáiṋithiiṋá → Saṋithiyá) on the banks of the Mayurakshi River to preach his gospels. By then he was an elderly man, while Gaotama Buddha was still a young man. He breathed his last in Pavapurii on Magadh soil.

“There were many in North India who did not appreciate this free mentality of Magadh. They did not spare any efforts to belittle Magadh in the eyes of the people, but Magadh was not discouraged by this.
“The seven Prákrta languages that arose after the demise of Sanskrit were as follows:
1. Maháráśt́rii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Konkanii, Marathi, Vaedarbhii (Váŕárii), etc.
2. Málavii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Gujarati, Saorastrii, Kacchii, Málavii, Mewari, Haraotii and Marwari.
3. Saendhavii or Saobiirii Prákrta which gave rise to Sindhi and Mulatani.
4. Páshcáttya Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Pashtu, Káshmiirii, Uzbeki, Tazaki, etc.
5. Paeshácii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Dogri, Pahari, and Punjabi.
6. Shaorasenii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Hindi, Abadhi, Bundeli, Bagheli, and Vraja.
7. Mágadhii Prákrta, which was the forerunner of Magahi, Bengali, Oriya, Angika, Assamese, Nagpuri, Maethili, Chatrishgarhi and Bhojpuri.

“This Mágadhii Prákrta had two daughters – Eastern Demi-Mágadhii and Western Demi-Mágadhii. Western Demi-Mágadhii later gave birth to the Magahii language. At one time Mágadhii Prákrta was used not only in eastern India, but in central India as well among the educated community for the exchange of thoughts. Educated people used to show the same zeal for learning Mágadhii Prákrta as they showed for learning Sanskrit. The structure of the Mágadhii Prákrta language is both straighforward and easy. The grammar is also not complex. Both Mahavir and Buddha gave their teachings in the Mágadhii Prákrta of that time, which many people today call Pali. A great deal of literature was composed in the Pali language and its successor, Occidental Demi-Mágadhii. Magadh also had its own script. Inscriptions in that ancient Mágadhii script can still be found in certain places in Bodhgaya. It is the younger sister of the Shriiharśa script and closely related to modern Maethili (Tirhuti) script and Bengali script.”

The young man looked at me and smiled. “You know what the sad thing is? Today many educated people in Magadh are ashamed of speaking their mother tongue. They think that it is perhaps a rustic language, unsuitable for respectable society. Yet this Mágadhii – Occidental Demi-Mágadhii – was once the language of the state administration. Who else can I tell this sad tale to?

“Just as Magadhʼs language has its own style of pronunciation and syntax, its popular culture also shines with originality. Today this popular culture is being swept away, but do you know what is even sadder? At one time Magadh had a sound economic infrastructure, but since the time of Skandagupta that infrastructure has crumbled. Today, wherever you look, you see a stark picture of poverty and distress. There is no plan for economic development. The young people of Magadh do not have any economic legs to stand on. Magadh has not been built up; rather, for 1500 years it has been hammered into the dust.”

The young man looked at me again and said in a tearful voice: “You know, it maddens me to think about Magadh. Anyhow, as I was saying, the war was going on between Ráŕh and Thanishvara, and Magadh, lying between the two, was being destroyed. Shashanka was an intelligent and courageous man. He built a large army through whatever means he had at his disposal and took Rajyavardhana by surprise when his adversary was temporarily absent from his capital, taking possession of the city. After this he waged a fierce war against Rajyavardhana in which Rajyavardhana was defeated and slain. Some people claim that under the pretence of a truce, Shashanka extended an invitation to Rajyavardhana, and then either stabbed or poisoned him when he came. One can say what one wants in this matter, but there is no sound historical evidence that Shashanka killed Rajyavardhana unfairly.

“After Shashanka returned to Ráŕh, Rajyavardhanaʼs brother, Harsavardhana, liberated his kingdom once again and continued the struggle with Shashanka. As long as Shashanka was alive, the war against Thanishvara continued without pause. And so there was no end to Magadhʼs distress.

“After Shashankaʼs death his widow, Jayashankari (in some peopleʼs opinion, Trigunashankari), ruled Ráŕh along with Paiṋca Gaoŕa or Bengal after installing his under-age son, Mrigankashekhara, as the crown prince. Harsavardhana did not let this opportunity go by and struck a powerful blow against Ráŕh. War ensued and after two sanguinary battles at Nalhati and Parkat́iipur (Pakur), Ráŕh fell under Harsavardhanaʼs control. The same Harsavardhana who has achieved everlasting fame in India, who, as legend has it, was known for his generosity and who, in some peopleʼs opinion, was the founder of the Kumbhamela and the Mághamelá, also killed Ráŕhʼs Queen Jayashankari and her under-age son, Mrigankashekhara, with his own hand, and utterly exploited Magadh, tossing it aside like a worn-out banana peel. According to the scriptures, the elderly, the women, the sick, the disabled, conscientious dissenters, under-age men and emissaries must not be killed. Harsavardhana blatantly violated this scriptural injunction. Both the people of Bengal and the people of Magadh condemned and censured him for this.

“As long as Shashanka was alive, he did not allow the Buddhist religion into Ráŕh. After the defeat of Bengal by Harsavardhana, Buddhism, despite not enjoying his open support, became predominant, due to the tremendous indirect support he gave it. In their hearts the people remained Shaivites but on the outside they became Buddhists. Later on, during the time of Shankaracharya, a small number of Ráŕhʼs Jains and large numbers of Buddhists throughout Bengal accepted the Puranic religion. This may have been because in Ráŕh there was some similarity between the traditions of the Puranic religion and the Digambar Jain doctrine of that time. So Harsavardhana dealt a strong blow to the religious thought of Ráŕh, as well as Bengal, and by exploiting Magadh brought it to its lowest point.”
The boy looked at me again and said in a choked voice: “Now tell me, who can I express this to? Today Iʼve poured my heart out to you.”
“Go on, go on,” I said. “Donʼt hold anything back.”

“Magadhʼs misery is not a recent thing. It dates back to the time of Harsavardhana. The people of Magadh have tried to pull themselves up from time to time, but after so many blows theyʼve had their back broken. Now they can no longer stand up straight at all.”
“I am really moved by your sincerity, overwhelmed. There should be more boys like you all over Magadh.”

He continued. “While returning back after defeating Bengal, Harsavardhana tried to pulverize Magadh into submission even more. He knew about Magadhʼs tradition and was afraid that Magadh might overthrow his throne. At that time Magadhʼs last general, Agnimitra, and his younger brother, Chandraketu, were directing its final efforts to resist Harsavardhana and a great war ensued. In the battle of Barabar Hill, near the city of Gaya, Magadhʼs army was utterly routed and destroyed. Even then Agnimitra did not accept defeat. His final confrontation with Harsavardhana Ráŕh and Its Neighbour Magadh – 1 399 400 Bengal And Bengalees was at Brahmayoni Mountain in Gaya; in this battle Agnimitra was killed.”

The young man stopped again, then continued falteringly. “You know, people say that Agnimitraʼs relatives, friends and neighbours offered sesame, water and so forth to the gods so that his soul would go to heaven, but Agnimitra did not attain salvation. As long as Magadh does not regain its lost glory, Agnimitra will not get salvation. Even if he attains it he will not accept it.”

He went on in a halting voice. “You know, it was in this very spot that the funeral pyre burned for Agnimitraʼs cremation. The boy stopped speaking. I looked at him but somehow he had vanished and a funeral pyre was burning in his place. The flames of the pyre were rising from the soil of Magadh and scattering these words on the winds: ʼI will never let Magadh die.ʼ

I looked around but there was no one there. Seeing no reason to remain there I started back for the hotel. I met no one on the way; not even the animals were awake. The main entry door of the hotel was open. I went inside and closed it, then went up to the second floor and headed for my room. I went inside, locked it and lay down unperturbed. I lay there thinking for a while and began feeling sleepy. Then I seemed to hear a voice coming from the direction of the incense burner on the dressing table. “Do you know, I forgot to tell you. I am Agnimitra. I canʼt tell you how happy I am that you are doing research on my Magadh. I took hold of your leg so that I would have a chance to talk to you. Please forgive my audacity. I would like to request you to come back to Magadh as often as you can. Try to awaken the consciousness of its people. Talk about it, write about it, and promise me” – his voice surged with emotion – “that my Magadh will survive.”
“That Magadh which has given birth to noble persons such as yourself,” I replied, “will never perish. There is no power on earth that can destroy it.”

I had gone at the time to a village in Nawada Subdivision of Gaya District in search of archaeological artifacts from Magadh. This place was more or less in the Kśuri River Basin. On the southwest it bordered the historically renowned Grdhrakút́ Mountain where Buddha performed spiritual austerities and later gave his spiritual teaching.

I was somewhat late returning. Though it was night there was no harm done because the night train from Gaya would pass through Nawada station quite late. Most of the time the train would be running late and dawn would break in when I would arrive home in Jamalpur.

It was the full moon night in the middle of Hemanta ( 1 ) and a cool breeze was blowing; I had no trouble seeing even without a torch. I was feeling quite happy after having verified several important facts. The issue under consideration was whether or not the Buddhist Mantrayána was dominant in Magadh during the middle of the Buddhist era or the Kálacakrayána. In the Buddhist Mantrayána they recognized the goddess (which also happened later in Tantra and the Puranic religion) and she was also honoured in the Buddhist Kálacakrayána, but the two were divided along doctrinal lines – one accepted Vajratárá and the other Niiltárá or Niil Sarasvatii. ( 2 ) With the passage of time Niil Sarasvatii took the form of Prajiṋápáramitá in Tibet and later Prajiṋápáramitá was accepted in India by the followers of Maháyána. At the outset, Prajiṋápáramitá and Niil Sarasvatii were considered to be one and the same, but later they became separate goddesses. In the beginning, their dhyána mantra was also the same, but it also became different afterwards.

In Magadh I found the whole or broken statues or remainders of destroyed statues of Niil Tárá, Ugratárá, Bhrámariitárá, and Prajiṋápáramitá. From this I arrived at the firm conclusion that they were accepted in Magadh despite the divisions that took place on or outside of Magadh soil.

I was walking in the direction of Nawada station, the station still about six miles away, when I saw a pond on the left side of the road. In Magadh there are very few ponds, but during the Buddhist era ponds were often dug next to Buddhist monasteries because many mendicants and students used to stay there and a great deal of water was needed for them for which a well would not be sufficient.

When I saw the pond I stopped. I thought that perhaps there might be a gaŕ ( 3 ) nearby. There was no gaŕ to be seen, but I did see a tall mound next to the pond. If one sat on one side of the mound, then the other side was not visible, but if one stood one could see all the way around it. I sat on one side of the mound and started pondering – I had never heard of the existence of a Buddhist monastery in such a place. But then whose mound was this?

Suddenly I saw an ekká coming down the same path by which I had come. It came to halt in front of me and, lo and behold!, there was no driver, no one at the reins. The horse knew the path and brought the vehicle there. Just as it pulled up, a young gentleman appeared from the other side of the mound. I asked him in Magahi: “Who are you?” He greeted me with folded hands and said with a slight smile: “Look, it seems perhaps that the ekká has come for you. Otherwise wherefrom would it come in such an unlikely moment and place? Quite astonishing, in fact!”
“It certainly is.” I replied. “You are quite correct.”
“Please, get in the ekká,” he said.
“But there is no driver,” I replied. “How will the horse go to where I want to go?”
“Donʼt worry about it. I can drive the ekká.” Saying this, he helped me get in the ekká and then jumped into the driverʼs seat himself and started to drive.

“Look here,” I said. “This is quite astounding. An ekká has come for me – how, I donʼt know how – and you as well it seems. And another astounding thing is that you know how to drive it. It amazes me to see so many astounding things at one time.”

“I am not any the less surprised to see you here,” he said softly. “If you had gone a little further you would have come to Kaoyakol Village. ( 4 ) You used to be able to find statues of Vajrabáráhii and Vajrayoginii from the Chinese Buddhist Tantra there; in other words, they were recognized goddesses in Ciinácára [Chinese Tantra]. Their main place was Vikrammanipurʼs (Vikrampur) Vajrayoginii Village in Bengal (the village name is Badarajoinii). Statues of Vajrayoginii and Vajrabáráhii were also found in old Tripuraʼs Mayanamati (subsequently British Tripura or Comilla District) and Dattapara Village of Bhuluya.”
“You are so knowledgeable,” I said. “What do you do?”

He replied in a very polite and gentlemanly way. “I drive the ekká and I also do one or two other things. I was very happy to see that you are doing research on Magadhʼs archaeological wealth. Actually, I didnʼt just come here; Iʼve been with you secretly all along. When you sat down on one side of the mound, I sat down on the other side.”
“I see. But how is it that you know so much about the Buddhist era?”
“I live in this land and I wonʼt know it? I love every particle of Magadh.”
I was very pleased to hear this from him.

Finally we arrived at Nawada Station. I gave him my thank-you, but when I offered him some remuneration he folded his hands and said: “I am so happy to have had the opportunity to drive you. If I accept a fee then I will not be so happy, so please, donʼt give me any money.”

What could I do? I sat down in the waiting room and a short while later the train to Jamalpur arrived. The train was nearly empty and I was able to find a small compartment that was unoccupied. I fell asleep, but at one point the rattling of the train woke me up and when I looked up I saw the same young man who had brought me to Nawada station in the ekká sitting in front of me.
“When did you get in?” I asked.
This time he answered in Bengali. “I also got in at Nawada, just after you did.”
“What happened to the carriage?” I asked.

“After you got down I could no longer see it, almost as if it was magic. As if you had conjured it up with your magic wand. Do you know what I am thinking now? I am thinking that this body of mine is also yours; as if you created it with a magic incantation.”
“What are you saying!” I interjected.
He smiled. Now he was speaking completely in Bengali.
“I can see that you are also very enthusiastic about archaeological research,” I said. “Now tell me, what was this mound for?”

“That mound is not a relic of the Buddhist era; rather, it dates from the British era. As far as I know – but of course you are well aware of this – in the year 1905, Indiaʼs Viceroy, Lord Curzon, divided the homeland of the Bengalees, that is, Bangalistan, into two parts, East Bengal and Assam Province with Dhaka as its capital, and Bengal with Kolkata as its capital.
Included within East Bengal and Assam Province were:
North Bengal: Rajsahi, Pabna, Bagura, Dinajpur, Rangpur, Jalpaiguri, and Northeast Raungpur (Dhubri).
East Bengal: Mymensingh, Dhaka, Faridpur, Bakharganj, British Tripura (Comilla), Noyakhali, Cat́t́agrám, Párvatya Cat́t́agrám, Sylhet and Cachar.

The mountainous areas of eastern India: Garo Hills (previously part of the landholdings of Mymensinghʼs Susanga kings – these kings were Barendra Brahmins from Bengal), Khasi Hills (formed from many very small native kingdoms, one of which was the kingdom of Miliyem – the city of Shillong was in this kingdom), Jayantiya Hills, Mikir Hills, Naga Hills (Nagaland) and the Lusai Hills (Mizoram).
Assam: Kamarup, Darang, Shivasagar, Nagaon, North Lakhimpur, and the Baliapara border district (later NEFA, and even later, Arunacala).
Included within Bengal were:
West Bengal: Burdwan, Birbhum, Bankura, Hooghly, Howrah, Midnapore, Murshidabad, Nadia, Jessore, Khulna, 24 Pargana, Kolkata, Manbhum, Singhbhum, Santhal Pargana, Maldah, Darjeeling, and Purnia.
Bihar: Bhagalpur, Monghyr, Tirhut (Dwarbhanga and Muzaffarpur), Champaran (Motihari), Sharan (Chapra), Sahabad, Patna and Gaya.
Cut́iyá-Nagpur: Cut́iyá Nagpur (Ranchi), Palamu (Daltanganj), and Hazaribag.
Orissa: Cuttack, Puri, Baleshwar, Angul-Khandmahal and Sambalpur.
“The people of Bengal did not accept this partition. They started agitating strongly for the reunification of Bengal. One can say that the struggle for Indian independence began with this movement.

“One may ask why the Sepoy Mutiny was not part of the struggle for independence. [It is] because it was not inspired with the goal of liberating the country. That struggle began out of fear that the East India Company would destroy [Indian] religion. It was supported by some dispossessed local kings and nawabs. When the Sepoy Mutiny first started in Barrackpore and Berhampore, the thought of liberating the country was not in the smallest corner of their minds.

“When the movement began against the partition of Bengal, the desire to liberate the country had not yet arisen in their minds either. Their primary objective was to make the two Bengals one again. But after the agitation to unite Bengal had been going on for some time, the desire to liberate the country from the grip of foreign enemies arose in their minds. Thus we can say that this period saw the sprouting of the seed of desire for independence. The rulers of East Bengal and Assam Province at the time completely lost their senses, like a mad dog, in the effort to suppress the movement. As a result, "terrorism as an effect of helplessness complex" arose among the oppressed and persecuted Bengalee population. Such tyranny was not seen in [west] Bengal, so terrorism also did not flourish there.

“How does it strike us today to think that in those days it was forbidden to publicly utter the words Vande mátaram. ( 5 ) For the offence of saying Vande mátaram in public the youth of Bengal had their skulls cracked open in Barishal by the police, and those who did not die filled up the jails.

“When people are not given an opportunity for civilized and orderly agitation, they take to the path of terrorism… they accept the path of guerrilla warfare. Such was the case in this situation. Two youths of that time, Manotos Basu from Malakha Nagar in Dhaka District, and Shubhendu Narayana Guha from Banaripara in Bakharganj District, plunged bravely into terrorism under the inspiration of the itinerant poet, Mukunda Das. The police chief of East Bengal and Assam Province, Mr. Tegartt, scoured the region in a furious effort to capture them. Thereafter they quit East Bengal and Assam and came to Bengal where they continued to conduct their terrorist activities from Nawada in Gaya District. Along with their terrorist work, Shubhendra Narayana ran a betel shop in Nawada (on the way to Rajauli) and Manotosa Basu used to drive an ekká.

“The two friends used to meet each other in their spare time. As their terrorist activities in Gaya District grew, a lot of eavesdropping started. Informants were recruited in different neighbourhoods to help catch the terrorists. After a long search they were able to track the two of them down. There was a great battle between the police and these friends near the mound where you were seated, next to the pond. Both of them were killed. A grave was dug and Manotosa was buried on the spot. A mound was built up over it so that the site could be identified.

“Many local villagers arrived before a grave could be dug for Shubhendu Narayana so the body was sent to Kolkata Medical College to be used there. That is why I told you that the mound dates from the British era, not the Buddhist era.”

“What excellent research youʼve done!” I said. “Youʼve done better than any famous archaeologist could have done. Iʼm really amazed to see what excellent research work youʼve done at such a young age.”
“I have lived on Magadh soil for a long time,” he replied, “so I have a responsibility to know these things. You know, I love everything about Magadh.”
“That I can see,” I said. “When you were driving the t́omt́om you were speaking fluent Magahi.”

He laughed softly. “Those same Bengalees who had once fought with all their might to unify Bengal presented a petition to the British in 1947 to once again divide Bengal in two. When the two Bengals were united in 1912 ( 6 ) the Bengalees thought that they had won the fight. And when Bengal was again divided in two in 1947, again the Bengalees thought they had won the fight. What a tragedy of history!

“When the two Bengals became one in 1912, many parts of Bangalistan [homeland of Bengalees] were left outside it. History tells why. Nowadays I have realized that liberty means not only escaping the clutches of an external enemy; liberty means gaining oneʼs freedom from all kinds of bondages – economic, dialectical, intellectual, educational, linguistic and cultural. Geo-sentiment and racial sentiment alone are not all there is to freedom. External forces ruled this country because they were able to extract its essence, its vital juices. When they saw that they had to expend a lot of money to maintain the sugar cane production, when they saw that it was no longer profitable after having sucked the industry dry, then they left. They did not go due to any other pressure; economic difficulties forced them to leave. It is important to remember, both then and now, that it cannot be called freedom when black exploiters take the place of white exploiters. Even though the foreign powers have left, their exploitative machinery is still in place. That machinery will have to go. Then the threefold freedom will be possible – physical, mental and spiritual.
“Now go to sleep and donʼt worry,” he continued. “Iʼll return after I see that youʼve reached Jamalpur.”
“Why should you go to so much trouble on my behalf?” I said.
“I love you very much,” he replied, “and Iʼm concerned about you. Do you know what I am thinking?”
“Tell me,” I insisted.
He smiled and said: “I feel as if I am inside your mind.”
I laughed and he went on. “I wonʼt keep you awake any longer by going on talking. You go to sleep. Iʼll be sitting here.
“I am always anxious to be able to do some good for other people but I donʼt have the means to do so.”
I covered my face with my shawl and then said: “How so? You are so young. Youʼll have plenty of opportunities to do good work.”
He replied with a choked voice. “I am that Manotos Basu. You were sitting beside my grave.”
I pulled the shawl away from my face to look at him but there was no one there.

The city of Howrah is high in some places, low in others, replete with factories and neighborhoods of gentle, civilized folk. Howrah has been an industrial town since its very inception. There was a time when there was a factory here at every turn. It is difficult to find another such industrial town anywhere in the world, although at present Ludhiana and Batala of the Punjab can boast of a similar glory. This is quite good, no doubt, but Howrah should not lose its distinction.

Both government and private agencies derive a very good income from this industrial town, although in general we can say that the city is neglected. Only a very small fraction of what is spent for the improvement of Kolkata is spent on Howrah. Moreover, the sacrifices that Howrah has made for the improvement of Kolkata are indisputable. Kolkata is like a golden lamp with a slender wick made of fine cotton and clarified butter for fuel, while Howrah is like the lamp-stand that bears it on its head. It seems to bear the black stain from the lampʼs burnt oil.

Will no one pay any attention to Howrah? The British did not neglect the town in this way when they founded it in an area of marshy wetlands (háoŕ) after draining the water and filling in the holes and ditches. A botanical garden was developed here as well as one of Indiaʼs oldest engineering colleges. The Shalimar Gardens were fashioned in imitation of the Shalimar Gardens of Kashmir. The place is still commonly known today as Shalimar.

Howrah District was second to none in the area of scholarship. There was a time when a large number of Sanskrit scholars used to live at Maju, Shyampur, Andul, Peṋŕo-Vasantapur and Santragachi. They were quite erudite. The British selected Howrah, as a developing area of Bengal, to be the residence of the representative from Bhutan. Later on that particular place became known as Bhot́bágán.
It is this Howrah that we are passing through, neglected by history just as Urmila, the wife of Laksman, was neglected in the Rámáyańa.

I was traveling from Maju to Makarda. On the way I suddenly ran into Manimohan Manna. Many of you know our Manimohan. We say about people who are artful talkers that puffed rice bursts open from their mouths, but in the case of Manimohan I would say that puffed rice coated with raw sugar bursts open from his mouth. He is an expert talker but his every word is so sugarcoated that it seems to be puffed rice dipped in the famous palm raw sugar of Kolaghat.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Anyhow, I was travelling from Maju to Makarda. This part of Howrah District is very fertile. It has been densely populated since ancient times. When Howrah fell within the jurisdiction of Burdwan, it was the pride of Bengal. Afterwards, when it came within Hooghly District, it was regarded as one of the prosperous areas of Hooghly District. Later on, when Hooghly District was divided and Howrah District was formed, this area remained within Howrah District. Partially without industry, partially industrialized, it was the jewel of the region, shedding its lustre on the whole of Bengal through its scholarship, industriousness and erudition. There was a time when the vast Sarasvati River used to flow through this area. The Sarasvati River came out of the main branch of the Bhagirathi River at Triveni in Hooghly Districtʼs Mogra Police Station. It came out from the right side of the Bhagirathi. The Yamuna [Jamuna, not the river of Uttar Pradesh] River came from the exact opposite direction, that is, from the left side of the Bhagirathi through the Chakda and Haringhata Police Stations of what was then Nadia District, the adjoining region. This confluence of the Ganges, Yamuna and Sarasvati Rivers is renowned as the Triveńitiirtha [holy confluence of three rivers] or the Mukta [liberated] Triveńii.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Muktaveńiir Gauṋgá jetháya mukti vitare rauṋge.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: [The liberated stream of the Ganges joyously bestows liberation.]
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: From there the Sarasvati flowed through the fertile, verdant grasslands and grain fields of Hooghly District until it reached Howrah District. There it used to flow past the meadows of kenduá on its right side. What we call nowadays the kenduá meadows was a vast lake in prehistoric times. The lake gradually filled up and turned into the kenduá marshlands or Kendua meadows. Up until a hundred years ago the rice and paddy crops never failed in the kenduá marshlands. Rice and rice paddy used to be exported from the port of Amta by ship to foreign lands along the Damodar River. Those days are gone. Nowadays the Damodar is almost dried up. Its water is not even knee-deep now, so the plying of ships is out of the question.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: After moving a little to the south it joined the Bhagirathi near Andul. The Sarasvati River Basin was at one time one of the wonders of the world for its people and wealth. The wealth and scholarship used to humble even the most arrogant. Though that glory no longer exists, its memory remains, and that is precious enough. It is a matter of regret that Howrah District, like the city of Howrah, lies neglected and uncared for, though its prospects and possibilities are enormous.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Makarda was situated close to the Sarasvati River in those days. Although a large part of the external trade of Bengal at that time was carried out from the Port de Bauṋgálá (Cat́t́agram) and the Port de Grandi (Saptagram), Makarda also was a busy port. Merchants belonging to the Saha, Tambuli, Gandhabanika and Suvaranabanika communities were the principle contributors to the growth of its wealth. Brahmins and Kayasthas brought the glow of scholarship, and the skilful peasants of the Máhiśya and Sadgope communities produced golden harvests. The heroism of the Kaevartta fishing community became famous far and wide. They were respected in the society as “Bara” [a surname], the best, and were primarily responsible for the formation of the navy of independent Bengal. This area was also home at that time to a shipbuilding factory where indigenous methods were used. That industry perished during British rule. The expert carpenters and Kaevartta fishermen of this place built those ships. The merchants of this area also set out to sea after loading their goods on those ships.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Today things have changed. Makarda or Sarasvati has moved on, the Sarasvati has dried up, and the wealth of Makarda has been transferred to other places. There are three chief reasons for this. The first reason is the changing of course and subsequent drying-up of the Sarasvatii. The second reason is the decline of rural industries. The third reason is the loss of economic balance and equilibrium owing to defects in education and the social system.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: In general, in order to build a strong economy in a certain area thirty to forty percent of the population of that area – neither more nor less – should be dependent directly on agriculture. If it is less then agriculture is neglected; conversely, if it is more, then there will be a heavy strain on agriculture. That is exactly what has happened in the Maju-Makarda region. What to speak of Maju-Makarda, the same thing has happened throughout Ráŕh, throughout Bengal, throughout India, and even in China and the whole of Southeast Asia. To combat this problem a new social and economic evaluation is necessary.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Just as agriculture should be built up on an advanced scientific foundation, industry should also be organized in perfect adjustment with agriculture. The percentage of the population depending directly on agriculture should not exceed forty percent. Where rural industries have been destroyed, a major part of the population once engaged in that sector is now moving towards agriculture. Just as the percentage of people depending directly on agriculture should be thirty to forty percent for balanced economic development, about twenty percent of the people should depend on agro-industries, twenty percent on agrico-industries, ten percent on general trade and commerce, and ten percent on intellectual or white collar jobs.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Because village industries have been ruined, those who depended on those industries have turned to agriculture. The percentage of merchants has not increased much; rather, the opportunities for further growth have decreased. However, the number of people looking for white-collar jobs has increased, resulting in soaring unemployment.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: The sons of farmers, after receiving a little education, are no longer willing to labour in the fields. They want to become babus [title of a Hindu gentleman]; they consider farm work to be menial labour. As a consequence there is a dearth of educated youths in agriculture on the one hand, and on the other an increasing number of people from other vocations turning towards agriculture. In the rural areas the percentage of the population depending primarily on agriculture has gone up to seventy or eighty percent. What an unbearable situation! So just as social and economic life in other parts of Bengal have been turned upside down, Maju-Makarda is no exception. The Maju-Makarda region was Howrah Districtʼs greatest potential for economic development, but that hope has been shattered. Today the city of Howrah is neglected, so it is not capable of supplying vital energy to rural Bengal.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Non-agricultural industry (such as steel plants, brass industry, metal industry, oil refineries, salt industry and non-plant-based pharmaceuticals) refers to those industries that are neither direct agrico-industries (such as production of pick-axes, spades and tractors) nor industries that are directly dependent on agriculture, that is, agro-industries (such as jute mills, cloth factories, flour mills, paper mills and plant-based medicines). The percentage of people engaged in non-agricultural industry should be formed by reducing the percentage of people depending directly on agriculture, reducing the percentage of people depending on agrico-industries and reducing the percentage of people engaged in agro-industries. The percentage of people engaged in non-agricultural industries should be kept within twenty to thirty percent of the total population. If the percentage is less than twenty percent, the country is said to be industrially undeveloped and the per capita income of the people cannot be very high. The standard of living also cannot be very high because the purchasing capacity of the people remains very limited. Due to the reduced capacity for purchasing consumer goods, the import index remains lower than the export index, meaning the area has to remain the satellite of a developed country. As a consequence, the balance of power in the world is jeopardized and the possibility of war is always around the corner.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: If the percentage of people engaged in non-agricultural industry is kept between twenty and thirty percent of the population, then it creates a state of balance, a balanced socio-economic system. If the percentage goes beyond thirty percent it becomes an industrially developed area. The more the percentage rises beyond thirty percent, the more the area goes from industrially developed to industrially over-developed. In order to procure agricultural produce the industrially over-developed countries try to convert agriculturally predominant regions into their satellites. They feel the need to keep these industrially undeveloped countries under their control in order to serve as a market for their finished goods. If they do not obtain markets for their industrially produced consumer goods, they will have to suffer from economic recessions and growing unemployment.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: In this regard, there is no difference between communist and non-communist countries. All of them are equally aggressive in their approach. They are desperately searching for the wish-fulfilling cow, which they want to keep tied to their door, feeding it the minimum amount of fodder. Is it any wonder there are so many wars and conflicts in the world, so much war psychosis and sabre-rattling? Efforts must be made so that each and every country of the world can enjoy a balanced state in both agriculture and industry; otherwise, the socio-economic balance of the world is bound to be destroyed.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: The negative consequences of over-industrialization result in deterioration of personal, social and political health; due to the gradual psychic degeneration of both individuals and the collective, a kind of psychic epidemic may become rampant any moment which can endanger or jeopardize every expression of life. It may not happen today, but it will surely happen in the near future.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Where the industrial system (whether it is agro-industry, agrico-industry or non-agricultural industry) depends on outside labourers, the situation becomes precarious. The speed of psychic degeneration accelerates. Such a region will suffer from a chronic scarcity of food. The possibility of expanding the markets for their consumer goods will gradually become curtailed. As an example, we can look at Howrah, Hooghly, 24 Parganas and Burdwan. Since the labourers there are outsiders, the local people will never see good days. However developed or over-developed these areas might become, they will have to endure the ill effects of over-industrialization without being able to enjoy any of the benefits of industrialization. This sort of scenario can be seen daily in Howrah District. Moreover there are still many such areas in India where ninety percent of the population consists of farmers. There is no industry whatsoever in those areas. They are completely surplus labour areas. A balanced socio-economic structure will have neither surplus labour nor deficit labour. It cannot be permitted.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: The agricultural system should be built up similar to the industrial system; that is, the prices of agricultural produce should be determined by considering basic factors such as agricultural income, expenses and necessities. In other words, the farmers of Burdwan and Birbhum should not be forced to sell their rice at throwaway prices. Similarly, the farmers of Hooghly District should not be compelled to sell their potatoes at cheap prices, and the farmers of Nadia District should not be forced to sell their jute at low prices in order to pay off their debts.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Yes, Makarda is still some distance away. I remember now that old history of Makarda. Rich in scholarship and wealth, Makarda was once a center of Maháyána Buddhism. Just as Tamralipta (Tamluk) was a center of Maháyána Buddhism and an external port, so also was Makarda. Tamlukʼs Vargabhiimá is a goddess of the Buddhist period. Even though Makardaʼs Mákaŕcańd́ii (Márkańd́eyii Cámuńd́ii or Márkańd́eyii Vajratárá – both are canonized in Buddhist Tantric treatises) cannot exactly be said to be a Buddhist goddess; she is nevertheless a popular goddess from the Buddhist period.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: When the Bengalees abandoned Buddhism they kept Mákaŕdácańd́ii but gave her a different name. However, the fact that Mákaŕdácańd́ii is a popular goddess from the Buddhist period is suggested by its dhyána mantra [incantation for ideation] and by its similarity to the idol. It also clearly indicates that Makarda is not from the present period.
chapterTitle: Makarda – A Brief History of the Culture of Ráŕh

t: Navadviipa ( 1 ) → Nao-diia → Na-o-diiyá → Nadiiyá; or, Navadiipa → Na-o-diia → Na-o-diiyá → Nadiiyá.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: According to some, nine islands rose in ancient times, one by one, from the depths of the Bay of Bengal. The people of Ráŕh, axes and shovels in hand, sailed there in boats, cleared the forests thereon, and set up habitation. A conglomeration of nine islands – it was named Navadviipa (nava means “nine” and dviipa means “island”). Included in these are Navadviipa, Agradviipa (Áyadá – present Hooghly District) and Madhyadviipa or Májhdiyá (Krishnaganj Police Station of Nadia District).
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Some say that Raghunath Bhattacharya (Raghunath Shiromańi or Káná Raghunath), a talented son of Bengal, returned home after acquiring all the wisdom of Pakshadhar Mishra [a scholar and logician] of Mithila. The people of Bengal were delighted beyond measure at this. The pandits of Mithila would not allow anybody to copy their manuscripts on Navya Nyáya [new school of philosophy and logic], lest the pride of Mithila – the seat of Nyáya – be lost. Hearsay has it that Raghunath would copy one page of the manuscript every day and keep it hidden in the hollow of a tree. Thus he could bring along a copy of the entire manuscript when he returned. According to another opinion, Raghunath learnt the complete works by heart before he came back.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Naturally, his classmates used to treat this extraordinarily meritorious son of Bengal with envy. Raghunath had only one eye. His mates would ridicule him and say, “Indra has a thousand eyes; Shiva has three; all other humans and animals have two eyes; but our dear one-eyed friend, from which world do you hail?”
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Nevertheless, thanks to Raghunath Bhattacharya, Bengal occupied the top position in matters related to Navya Nyáya. A book [on logic] was written by Vishwambhar Mishra (Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev) also, who was the son of Jagannath Mishra. It is said that Mahaprabhuʼs treatise was even better [than one written by Raghunath]. It is said that Raghunath, on hearing this document read out to him, shed tears of sorrow. To console his friend, Mahaprabhu tore up his own manuscript and immersed it in the waters of the Ganges in Swarupganj. Thereafter he remarked, “Friend, I have sacrificed my document to the waters of the Ganges. Only your document will now survive. Stop crying.”
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: In any case, on Raghunathʼs return to his native land as a reputed pandit in Nyáya, the people of Bengal welcomed him by lighting nine large lamps on the bank of the Ganges. Raghunath was a product of Purvasthali in Burdwan District. In those days, Burdwan was spread across both shores of the Ganges. Even though the eastern bank was Samatat-Bagri, it was better known as Vauṋga-Ráŕh. Those nine lamps in Raghunathʼs honour were lit on the eastern bank. So thenceforth that eastern bank, instead of being called Vauṋga-Ráŕh, was called “Navadiipa” [“Nine Lamps”]. And in the course of time there evolved the present name “Nadiiyá” [spelled in English contexts “Nadia”]. As far as I can see, the name Navadviipa, signifying a group of nine islands, is more logical. But yes, whatever I have said about Raghunath is true.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture
