t: – These words were written by a poet of Nadia.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Yuddha karila Pratápáditya gáyer rakta kariyá sheś,
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Dhanya ámará yadi e shiráy tháke táder rakta lesh.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: [Pratapaditya shed his blood to the last drop while fighting. We deserve to feel proud if even a single drop of that blood is now flowing through our veins.]
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: The pandits of Mithila and Bengal without reserve decorated Raghunath with the title of “Shiromańi”. ( 2 )
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: In the opinion of some distinguished Vaeśńava personalities, Nimaichandaʼs [i.e., Chaitanya Mahaprabhuʼs] personality is comparable to the sun, even though we refer to him affectionately as cáṋd [the moon]. He is the focal point of, and surrounded by, other established and learned pandits. Nimaichanda is our ocean while all other learned pandits are shined and enlivened by the waves and ripples that flow from him. [So to some Vaeśńavas,] that is why this place is “Navadviipa”, ( 3 ) the assemblage of new wisdom”.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: It was in Navadviipa, on the moist soil of this same Nadia, that Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev, whose real name is Vishwambhar Mishra, was born in the charming atmosphere of the full-moon day in the month of Phálgun. Although presently Navadviipa is politically a part of Nadia District, geographically it belongs to Burdwan District in Ráŕh. However, this was not the case when Mahaprabhu was born. The city of Navadviipa was located on the eastern bank of the river Bhagirathi – in the direction where Swarupganj is today. As the Bhagirathi has changed its course and now flows along the east of Navadviipa, the city has shifted to the west of river and has become a part of Ráŕh. Both Shriipát́h Máyápur and Navadviipa were situated on the same side of the Bhagirathi. Máyápur [Mayapur] was part of the city of Navadviipa [, but remained on the east side of the river and hence became separated]. So those who say that Mahaprabhu was born in Mayapur are correct. Also, those who say that he was born in Navadviipa are not incorrect. ( 4 ) Jagannatha Mishra, Mahaprabhuʼs father, was a Brahman from a western Vedic family of the Dháká-Daksiń village in Habigunj of the erstwhile Sylhet District. His predecessor, Arjun Mishra, had come from Mithila to Bengal at the invitation of King Shyamal Barman.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Jagannath Mishra had two reasons for coming to Navadviipa. One of them was the fact that his wife Shachidevi was the daughter of Nilamvar Chakravorty, a resident of Navadviipa. It was Shachideviʼs desire that her husband become a permanent resident of Navadviipa. The second reason was Jagannath Mishraʼs fondness for bathing in the Ganges. He had moved to Navadviipa with the hope that he would be able to take his bath in the Ganges till the day he breathed his last. During his stay at Dháká-Dakśiń, all of his daughters died of smallpox. He came to Navadviipa childless. Vishwarup Mishra, his first son, born when he was quite elderly, mastered vast knowledge at a young age and left home in search of spiritual treasures. His second son, who was also his last child, was Vishwambhar Mishra – the one who adopted the sannyásin name of Shriikrśńacaetanya Bháratii, in short, Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev. His wisdom bloomed in his early youth. Like Raghunath Shiromańi, he also had in-depth knowledge of logic and philosophy. When Raghunath returned to Navadviipa as an expert in logic and philosophy, Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev was about the same age. Subsequently, Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev went on to study extensively subjects other than Nyáya philosophy and even propounded his own acintyabhedábheda tattva [theory of inconceivable difference in non-difference]. At the early age of eighteen, he gained reputation as a catuśpát́hii ( 5 ) pandit in Navadviipa in particular and across all of Bengal in general.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: In a place called Poŕámá Talá in Navadviipa, he debated and defeated Mahápańd́ita Keshavakáshmiiri, a Sárvabhaoma pandit ( 6 ) of India of those days. It must be remembered in this context that Navadviipa or Nadia was a seat of the Shákta doctrine before the appearance of Mahaprabhu. The founding goddess of the city of Navadviipa, Poŕámá, is a Tantric goddess. After the fall of Keshavakáshmirii, Vasudeva Bandyopadhyaya was acknowledged as the Sárvabhaoma pandit of India on the strength of his vast knowledge. He became known as Vasudev Sárvabhaoma.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Mahaprabhu visited Utkala [Odisha] several times at the invitation of Prataparudradev, the king. The major part of his later life was spent in Cuttack. During his journeys to Niilácala, Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadeva stayed in Vasudev Sárvabhaomaʼs residence on several occasions. Despite the fact that Vasudev Sárvabhaoma was a very learned pandit and much older than Mahaprabhu, he regarded the latter with deep respect and honour. Neither Keshavakashmiiri nor Mahaprabhu ever entered into a debate contest with Vasudev Sárvabhaoma, nor were they inclined to be in such a position.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: His [Chaitanyaʼs] first wife Lakshmidevi died of snakebite. She had been the daughter of the famous Pandit Vallabhacharya of Navadviipa (although this is disputed by some). His second wife, Vishnupriya, was the daughter of Pandit Sanatan Mishra, yet another luminary of Navadviipa. On the orders of Shriimat Iishvara Puri of Gaya, Shriimat Madhavendra Puri, his disciple, initiated Mahaprabhu with the mantra “Krśńa” and instructed him to do the sádhaná of madhura bháva [ideation of sweetness and pleasantness]. [In some opinions Iishvara Puri was the disciple of Madhavendra Puri]
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Though a recipient of worldwide fame, Vishwambhar Mishra, the darling of Navadviipa, was so moved by the miseries of living beings that he rushed to Kantakpura, or Kátoyá [Katwa], with the longing to sacrifice all earthly things and embrace the life of a hermit. This same Kantakpura or Katwa was a leading centre of wisdom of Ráŕh. It was here that Vishwambhar Mishra was initiated into sannyása [renunciation] by Keshav Bharati and adopted the name Shrikrishnachaitanya. During this period, Navadviipa was flooded with the lights of wisdom spread by Raghunath Shiromańi and with love for all creatures as preached by Mahaprabhu Chaitanyadev. This constituted a new recipe for life that inspired all of India. Neither Mahaprabhu nor Raghunath Shiromańi is alive, but their repository of knowledge is inextricably mixed with the life stream of Bengal. That is why poet Satyendranath Dutta has so appropriately said:
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Ámáderi ei kut́ire dekhechi mánuśer t́hákuráli.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Gharer cheler cakśe dekhechi vishvabhúper cháyá,

t: The luminaries who contributed to enhance the pride of Nadia are not just a handful. Phulia (Phulliká), located to the southeast of Nadia, was yet another centre where pandits and wise men lived. It is to this Phulia that Banamali Ojha, an inhabitant of Dhamarai (Dharmarájiká) of Dhaka-Vikramapur, came looking for an environment of learning. He was an extremely dhármika-minded person. His wife, Malini Devi, had the same love for dharma. Krittivas Mukhopadhyaya was their son. He had a vast knowledge of Sanskrit. His reputation did not remain restricted to Bengal, but spread across the whole of India. Hussain Shah, the ruler of Gaoŕa, had an intense desire to read the Rámáyańa in Bengali. However, the translation of Sanskrit into Bengali was not a matter that could be successfully tackled with a limited amount of knowledge. Hence he convened a gathering of the pandits of Gaoŕa. In this gathering, all the pandits without question acknowledged the fact that the wisest pandit was Krittivas of Phulia.

t: Nawab Hussain Shah extended his invitation to the same Krittivas Ojha to write the Rámáyańa in Bengali. He was no less than other an object of pride for Nadia and Bengal. He is a diamond-studded necklace adorning the Bengalee people.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Besides, is there anybody who does not know of Advaita Acharya [senior disciple of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu] (Shantipur), Krishnanada Agambagish (Purvasthalii in Burdwan), Jimutbahan Bhattacharya (Purvasthalii in Burdwan), and Devivar Ghatak (Birbhum)? Their places of birth may have been different – some may have been born in Burdwan and others may have been born in Birbhum –but Nadia was the seat of activity for all of them.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Col. Suresh Biswas, the person who gave pride to India by virtue of his bravery in war in South America [Brazil] and earned international acclaim, was a resident of Nadia.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: Sage Ramaprasad Sen [writer of devotional poetry on Kálii] belonged to Kumárhat́t́a or Halishahar [North 24 Parganas District]. However, his predecessors had migrated there from Goyás in Nadia. Rśi [and novelist] Bankimchandra may have lived in Kantalaparha, but his ancestors were from Chakdah in Nadia. They were a family native to the place.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

Roy from Krishnanagar), the famous author of modern Bengal, reputed poet [of rural Bengal] Yatindramohan Bagchi (Bagchi-Jamshedpur), and the fine litterateur Miir [Mir] Musharraf [Massaraph] Hussain Marhum from Kusthia (author of the Viśáda-sindhu) were all sons of Nadia.

t: When all the facts about Samatat in the ethnic life of Bengal come to be recorded, the contribution of Nadia will be written in letters of gold. This is the Nadia which educated people, even if they want to forget it, will not be able to forget. The dhármika mind has always remained attracted to the dust of Nadia.
chapterTitle: Nabadwip – an Especial Seat of Bengalee Culture

t: I had a close friend whose name was Kalikinkar Kahali, from Majdia in Nadia District. (Madhyadviipa → Majjhadiiya → Májdiá.) In ancient Bengal, a village surrounded by a river, canal or marsh was called diyá or dihá.) Majdia was then part of the Krishnaganj Police Station area, of the district subdivision of Chuadanga of the then undivided ( 1 ) Bengal.

Kalikinkarʼs father, Mukundalal Kahali, was an eminent homoeopath. Kalikinkarʼs mother was a great devotee of Krśńa, and on looking at Kalikinkar, one would think that he was a devotee of the goddess Kálii. It was impossible to elicit from him the name of Krśńa or any word related to Krśńa, even by mistake, and in these matters his presence of mind was very sharp. Once, I thought that whatever Kalikinkar might do, he would not be able to distort a historical truth or a universal truth. With an intention to trap him, I told him, “Well, Kalikinkar, my knowledge of geography is very poor. Can you tell me under which police station your Majdia comes?”
He at once replied, “Kaliganj… Kaliganj… Kaliganj.”

I said, “But Kaliganj is quite far from Majdia. Kaliganj Police Station is on the eastern bank of the river Bhagirathi, near the town of Katwa in Burdwan District. How can the village Majdia come under its jurisdiction?”
Pat came the reply: “Ours is Kaliganj number one, and that is Kaliganj number two.” [The actual name was Krishnaganj, which Kalikinkar could never bring himself to utter.]

I said, “Well, Nadia has been there since the time of the Pathans. I hear that once upon a time Nadia was under the jurisdiction of Chakla Jessore. Kasba is supposed to have been the district headquarters of Chakla Jessore. Later, Chakla Jessore split into two. One part continued as Chakla Jessore, and the other part was named Chakla Nadia. ( 2 ) I hear that Chakla Nadia was spread over a huge area, from Plassey in the north to the Bay of Bengal in the south; from the Bhagirathi in the west to the Padma in the northeast and to Jessore Chakla in the east. The district headquarters continues to be situated where it was in those days. I have been trying to remember the name of this town for quite a few days, but I am not able to recall it. Can you tell me the name of the district town of Nadia?”

I started scratching my head when he said, “Canʼt you even recall this simple matter? It is Kalinagar… Kalinagar… Kalinagar!” [The actual name was Krishnanagar, which Kalikinkar could never bring himself to utter.]...

I thought, let me catch Kalikinkar in another way. I said, “Kalikinkar, you must have heard that Hooghly is a district with a rich cultural heritage. It is well-nigh impossible to find the likes of it in terms of temple sculptures and fine aesthetic taste. Bankura-Manbhum (Purulia-Dhanbad-Singhbhum of the present time) has the greatest number of ancient temples. Mallabhum (the Vishnupur Subdivision of Bankura District) has the greatest number of temples. But it is difficult to find a match for the temples of Hooghly District in matters of delicate artistry and fine sensibility. Let alone the temple of Anantavásudeva, Hangseshwari of Banshbere and the Gupta Vrindaban temple of Guptipara, both the oldest church and the oldest mosque of Bengal are also situated in Hooghly District. The Imambara of Hooghly has a cultural heritage and the fame of Phurphurasharif has spread far and wide.

“The oldest college of Bengal is also in Hooghly, and the same is true about its press. The typefaces of the Bengali alphabet were first prepared by Panchanan Karmakar, a great son of the district. And who does not know about the chariots of Chandannagar and Guptipara? The chariot festival of Mahesh–Ballabhpur is a living legend. Moreover, there are so many beautiful fairs with different attractions in this district! There was a time when merchants from abroad came to participate in the Khunti Fair of Hooghly. The fame of the Gosaighat Fair crossed the Indian border and reached foreign lands.

“This is that Hooghly District! In the British period, a large proportion of Indian ICS officers came from this district alone. In the British period, when most districts in Bengal did not have a single college, Hooghly District had as many as four degree colleges. This is not a matter of any small pride. Mrs Chandramukhi Basu, the first woman M.A. of India, hailed from this district.

“Is that all, Kalikinkar? You know that after eating a dull, monotonous vegetable dish of shákcaccaŕi [a cooked, dry dish of greens] continuously for days together, one likes to have a change, to have some tasty dishes, and for that Hooghly offers excellent scope. Has anybody ever seen or heard of such delicious, mouth-watering delicacies? How fine is the artistry of the confectioners of this place! It is said that in ancient times the gods used to come to Hooghly District in human form, just to eat sweets. This is that Hooghly District! This district was part of Burdwan District until the Mughal period.”

I said, “Well, Kalikinkar, if I remember correctly, your maternal auntʼs house is in this district, isnʼt it? These days, doesnʼt your cousin [maternal sisterʼs son], Professor Sannyal live in his ancestral home? Well, at which station do you get down in order to go to your auntʼs home?”
He said, “Donʼt you know that my aunt lives in Chatra?”
I said, “But there is no station at Chatra; where do you get down?”
He said, “You can get down at Seoraphuli.”
I asked him, “Is Seoraphuli the nearest station?”
He said, “No, the nearest station is Srikalipur” [in fact the nearest station is Shrirampur, but Kalikinkar would not take the name of Rama].
I said, “Well, your cousin is an eminent professor. He has been doing research on the villages of Janai and Manad for a long time. I would like to meet him briefly. Could you tell me his name?”

The name of Kalikinkarʼs cousin was Krishnakishore Sannyal, but Kalikinkar said, “The name of my cousin is Báṋkát́hákur Syándel… Báṋkát́hákur Syándel… Báṋkát́hákur Syándel.” [Not only did he not take the name of Krśńa, he made a distorted pronunciation of the actual surname Sannyal out of sheer disdain]

I realized that however hard I tried, he would stick to his guns. Tel dáo siṋdur dáo bhavii bholbár nay [“No amount of oil and vermilion (gifts) can make a stubborn person give up their pursuit”.]...

The other day I was returning home after a morning walk. There were practically no people in the marketplace. Suddenly I noticed that Kalikinkar was returning home, carrying a huge cluster of káṋt́álii kalá ( 3 ) [a variety of banana] that he had just bought.
It dawned on me that Kalikinkarʼs mother, a great devotee of Viśńu, worshipped Satyanarayana every Sunday.
I asked him, “To which divine shrine are you going to so early at dawn, with a cluster of káṋt́álii kalá?”
He said, “My mother worships Satyakálii every Sunday, thatʼs why.” [Náráyańa is another name of Viśńu, of whom Krśńa is considered an incarnation.]...

Once Helaram Chatterjee, the famous Rámáyańa singer, came with his troupe from Bankura to our town for a Rámáyańa recital. All the people of the place were charmed by his presentation and rendition.

Immediately, a powerful committee was formed in the locality. The two local leaders, Radhikaranjan Roy and Radharaman Datta, took the initiative so that the Rámáyańa recital of Helaram could be continued there for quite some time. Kalikinkar was an expert in collecting subscriptions, so the responsibility of collecting subscriptions for this [event] naturally fell to him. One day, on seeing Kalikinkar moving from house to house with the subscription book, I asked him, “What are you collecting subscriptions for?”
“There is a committee, and I am collecting subscriptions at the request of the committee,” he replied.
“Who are the members of the committee, and what is the committee for?” I said.
“Kalikaranjan Roy and Kali Raman Datta are on the committee,” he explained.
“Please tell me what the committee is for?” I asked.

He said, “Helakali Chatterjee has come from Bankura. He is giving a first-class rendition of the Kálii-áyana [Kalikinkar used the word Kálii-ayana in place of Rámáyańa, because he would not utter the word ‘Rama’]. I am just collecting subscriptions for that.”...

I realized that it was impossible to catch Kalikinkar in a small net; so this time I cast my net very wide. I said, “You intimately know the Ráŕh region. You certainly know that the northern part of this very old Ráŕh region was known as Varddhamána Bhukti [bhukti means ‘district’] and the southern part was known as Dańd́a Bhukti.

“Dańd́a Bhukti has not received as much recognition in history as Varddhamána [Burdwan] Bhukti has, for various reasons. For some unknown reason, historians did not pay any great attention to Dańd́a Bhukti. If somebody wants to write the history of Dańd́a Bhukti they will see that there is so much material that if properly organized, one can write several Mahábháratas. As many famous people were born in this region, similarly there are also innumerable towns and villages of great cultural heritage here. Towards the end of the Pathan period Dańd́a Bhukti was renamed Hijli, and towards the end of the Moghul period its name was changed to Madinápur. When the British got the civil rights of Vardhaman, 24 Parganas and Chattagram, along with Madinápur, they renamed it Midnapore. In the course of time its Bengali name became Medinipur. The district, which is very large, has also made such a significant contribution to the art of town planning and civilization, not only to the entire Ráŕh region but also to the entire civilized world, that it is a veritable seat of human civilization. The sea that skirts it and the range of hills that borders the district, sloping from northwest to the southeast, led to a magnificent opulence of all kinds of earthly treasures. Starting with Kalidas, the great poet, many great people were born in this district. In the Buddhist period, Dantapurivihár of this district, the present name of which is Dáṋton, was built upon the place where a receptacle containing the relics of Buddhaʼs teeth – lay buried. It is here that Sarashanka, the most beautiful water tank, not only of the Ráŕh region but also of the entire Bengal, is situated.

“Káṋthi (Kanthiká), Tamluk (Támralipta), Chandrakona, Cheriaberia, Mahisadal, Kśirpai and Kheput́ [Káṋthi is Contai] are famous historical places, among many others. The district was in the forefront of the struggle for independence. Well, I forgot to name Nerhadeul, a very famous place of the district. I also forgot to mention Bogri-Krisnanagar. In Bengal there are a number of places named Krishnanagar.

“Of these, three Krishnanagars became famous: 1) Goarii-Krishnanagar, the headquarters of Nadia District; 2) Khanakul-Krishnanagar of Arambag Subdivision of Hooghly District; and 3) Bogri-Krishnanagar of Midnapur District.
I asked Kalikinkar, “Well, Kalikinkar, your father was an eminent physician, and I have heard that he used to practise in Krishnanagar. Which Krishnanagar was that?”
Without wasting any time Kalikinkar said, “All along my father practised in Káṋthi-Káliinagara.”
I realized that he was a deep-water fish; he could not be caught even in a very wide net...

It was impossible to tackle Kalikinkar. I thought, let me make use of a sentiment. One does not really [[shilly-shally]] with oneʼs fatherʼs name. The name of Kalikinkarʼs father was Dr. Mukundalal Kahali.
I said, “Kalikinkar, your father was an eminent physician, wasnʼt he?”

Kalikinkar said, “Does that need saying? Nobody had ever seen or heard of such a great homoeopath. A dose of Cina 200 administered by him could flush out one thousand worms from the body in one hour.”

I said, “When we refer to a doctor we either use his name or his title. For example, while referring to Dr. Arun Banerjee of our place, some used to refer him as Dr. Arun and some as Dr. Banerjee. By which name was your father better known?”
He said, “He was better known as Dr. Kahali.”
I asked, “How was his name written in the certificate?”
He said, “Ájebáje [meaning ”nonsense“, ”rubbish“] Kahalii… Ájebáje Kahali… Ájebáje Kahalii.” [“Mukundalal” is another name of Viśńu, of whom Krśńa is considered to be an incarnation.]
Kalikinkar at once left the place.

This banana, which originated in the Buddhist period, was used in worship and various rituals. In the next period, that is, in ancient times [the age of the Puranas] also, under its continuing influence, people preferred the use of káṋt́álii kalá in the worship of the mythological gods and goddesses. That is why a man who is very useful is described by the people of Hooghly as sarvaghat́er káṋt́álii kalá [a banana which can be used everywhere, in any kind of worship]. The káṋt́álii kalá is so called in the neighbouring region of Kolkata, because of its special kind of fragrance. In the Ráŕh region, particularly in Burdwan, its local name is guṋdhii kalá.

In South Bengal, in the slightly salty soil of south Midnapur and South 24 Parganas, the best indigenous banana is ciiniiságara. In Hooghly, Howrah, North 24 Parganas, Nadia and eastern Burdwan, the best indigenous bananas are cáṋpá and kanáibáshii. In the western Ráŕh region, banana is hardly cultivated at all, but with a little care, there can be a fairly good yield of ciinii cáṋpá. In Assam, East Bengal and North Bengal, all kinds of banana except ciiniiságara and ciinii cáṋpá will grow quite well. Martamán kalá (which came from the Martaman province of Burma), though of foreign origin, will grow very well everywhere in Bengal and Assam, except the western Ráŕh region. Because of its foreign origin, in East Bengal some people also call it saphri kalá.
In mid Bengal and North Bengal this very banana is known as anupama kalá.
In banana plantations, the land should not be crowded with saplings. The saplings of one land should be planted on another land of at least six milesʼ distance.

One should leave at least three clusters of banana while cutting the mocá [the banana flower, the cone at the end of the cluster of bananas]. While cutting the mocá one should also see whether the first bunch is properly developed.
Kavaca! Kavaca means rakśákavaca [safeguard, or an amulet used as a safeguard]; everyone knows this. For the people of the Burdwan River Basin, the Damodar Dam is also a kavaca!
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: It was the month of Jyaeśt́ha [mid-May to mid-June]. At that time Burdwan District was as hot a district as it is now. The lu [hot] winds blowing from the west were blocked to some extent by the Durgapur jungle. Still, it must be said that Burdwan, this crown jewel of Ráŕh, is hotter than other places in Bengal.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Midnight was upon me. It was as if the Mahákaola [the great spiritual master] was saying: “The mahánishá [great darkness] of your life has come. Throw off the earthly bondages and come out. Maybe it is not the new moon night (amánishá) but the full-moon night (púrńimá). The darkest, subtlest particles of the new moon night can be transformed into particles of moonlight. Cannot the new moon night of oneʼs life takes the form of the full moon? That terrible shadow of time that has trampled the human soul for so long, sometimes frowning outwardly, sometimes being wasted by the deep sense of ignorance, making the human being stumble on their path – is it eternal?” Truly, the Mahákaola was calling me.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I went out alone and found myself in the middle of the forest. To the south was the Damodar River and to the east was the Devidaha [big lake]. At that time this part of Burdwan District was vast marshland. Whatever it may be – pond, lake, marsh – the Devidaha does not have any comparison. The prehistoric Gáuṋguŕ [Gangur] or Behula River was a lost tributary of the Damodar River. The Behula of legend took the dead body of the imaginary Lakhindar on her lap, climbed on a raft and floated down the Gangur towards heaven. The Behula River has turned into the Devidaha of today.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I walked slowly and came to the edge of the Devidaha. The Devidaha that we are talking about was partially destroyed in the Damodar flood of 1913. It was swallowed anew by the Damodar during the time of the Second World War. The time that I am talking about was shortly before the Second World War.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: The Devidaha was created during the time when Shashanka was the king of Ráŕh. The Devidaha was not simply a large pond. Like the Damodar, Banka, Khari, Badai and other rivers, the vast waters of the Devidaha as well as the Gangur used to keep Burdwan District green with grain. Sugar cane was first cultivated in Ráŕh on both banks of the Devidaha while cotton was cultivated on its west bank. Historically, it can be seen that Burdwan District was the pioneer in sugar cane and cotton cultivation, the leading producer. The sugar cane there was sweeter than any place else. Unfortunately the farmers in Burdwan today are not so eager to cultivate sugar cane because sugar cane ties up the land for nearly the entire year, while if other crops can be grown on that same land then three harvests can be taken home [annually].
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: For the very same reason, the cultivation of both the mághii [winter] and caetii [spring] types of pigeon-peas (aŕahar dál) is fast diminishing in Burdwan. They are scarcely to be seen nowadays. Even though the Balagarh area of neighbouring Hooghly District was at one time considered the best for pigeon-pea cultivation, it bears mentioning that there also its cultivation has diminished greatly. Nowadays Purulia and Nadia Districts are preserving the standard of pigeon-pea production in Bengal. If some of the land in Purulia were not used for pigeon-peas, then it would remain barren for most of the year; thus, there is no recourse but to grow pigeon-peas there. And in Nadia the greater part of the soil is doṋyásh [mixed sandy and clayey soil]. Since there is very little clayey soil, many crops cannot be grown there. Still, in the Chakdah, Haringhata and Kalyani areas of Nadia the cultivation of both sugar cane and pigeon-peas (kandula – Kandulaḿ baladaḿ jiṋeyaḿ cośńaḿ tu hitakárakaḿ) is diminishing and kitchen vegetables are being grown in their place. Today Nadia District has turned into the worldʼs best district for growing vegetables. Of course, the traditional areas for growing potatoes have been Hooghly, Burdwan, Nalanda [Bihar] and Farukhbad [U.P.] Districts. The seeds that we import while sitting in Kolkata, such as the recently brought biliti tomato seeds from America, the difficult-to-get red radish seeds from Japan, the extremely long kuli eggplant seeds from China – some perhaps come from abroad but the better part of them are brought from Nadia Districtʼs Nagar-Ukhra, bought at bulk rate and stuffed into jute sacks.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: The variety of cotton plant which was known as deva-kápás in Burdwan has the longest fibres and is suitable for making the finest thread. The climate of Burdwan is somewhat drier than that of the rest of Bengal, thus those areas which are wetter than Burdwan used to buy cotton thread from Burdwan for weaving fine cloth. Cotton does not grow well in wetter climates; the cotton is subject to insect attack. However, these wetter climates are more suitable for weaving fine cloth. Thus Burdwan was not as famous for the weaving of cloth as it was for the production of cotton. This is not Burdwanʼs fault; its weather is to be blamed. This situation continued unchecked up until the time of Akbar.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I went and sat under a huge silk-cotton tree on the western bank of the Devidaha. Behind me stretched a vast, dense jungle. This jungle stretched up to my village in one direction, and to the Damodar River in the other. It does not do justice to simply call it a jungle – it was a dense jungle. There were large snakes in the jungle, not large but medium-sized tigers, wild boars, and the niilgái and krśńasár varieties of antelope. The roaring of tigers could be heard at night from the courtyard of my house.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I was sitting on the western bank of the Devidaha, a short way from the village of Pátun, the village of Maharshi Patanjali, the propounder of Seshvara Sáḿkhya philosophy. Patanjali had not been satisfied with the Sáḿkhya philosophy of Kapil. Kapil did not say anything clearly one way or the existence of Parama Puruśa though he accepted His existence. Patanjali openly acknowledged His existence.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I sat and thought for a while about Patanjali. On the other side of the Devidaha I saw six or seven wild boars drinking water. A short distance from me was a large crocodile, half in and half out of the water; he seemed to be staring in a certain direction.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I was alone and solitary. I didnʼt see any other living creatures in the vicinity, nor did I hear any tiger roars. A short distance away ran the ruined remains of the Badshahi Road, the same road that Pathan Badshah Shershah constructed at the beginning of the Mughal era, with only a few skeletal traces left to identify it. Burdwan was then the capital of the province of Bengal. Badshahi Road used to connect Burdwan to Delhi in one direction, and in the other direction it connected to the principal port of the time, Saptagrám or Sátgáoṋ, to which the Portuguese gave the name Port-de-Grandee – it extended south along the Bhagirathi till Shyampur, and on the other bank it used to go via Jessore to Dhaka Districtʼs Suvarnagram (Sońárgáoṋ). At that time Hooghly was part of Burdwan District.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: How busy Badshahi Road used to be! Gazing in the direction of the road, I thought back to how many horse-carts used to travel along it at one time, how many marriage processions, how many richly ornamented, newly-married brides, how many funeral bearers – the finality of the human beingʼs existence is reduced to ashes and those ashes were left to float in the waters of the Bhagirathi. Today the Badshahi Road is abandoned; some can recognize it if they see it, and some cannot.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: This is the Burdwan District about which Maharaj Vikramaditya had said: “I must get the possession of Burdwan District, without which the learned society will never be established in my kingdom.”
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I was sitting alone on the western bank of the Devidaha. Silently I started reciting to myself:
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Kál-sáyarer váluká-beláy base base pal guńi,
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Mane bhávi yadi cetaná-viińáy tava kathá kichu shuńi.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Dúr theke ese dúre bhese jáy se viińár tár ańuke nácáy
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Se maháchande paramánande kalpaná-jál buni.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Kivá áse jáy yadi ekvár palake dáṋŕáo sumukhe ámár
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Máni náhi kona sádhaná ámár d́aki bháve anurańi.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: [On the sand-duned shore of the sea of time I am sitting counting the moments,
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I wonder if I might hear something of You on the lyre of consciousness.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: From the distance it comes, into the distance it floats, that lyre making the particles dance,
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: In that universal rhythm, in that supreme bliss I weave the net of imagination.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: What would happen if once You would stand in front of me for a moment,
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I know I havenʼt accomplished anything, but I am calling You, and in my ideation there is reverberation.]
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: I looked up. It was a moonlit night. I couldnʼt see the stars. They had become lost in the light of the moon. The lesser light becomes lost in the greater light. The light of the firefly becomes lost in the light of the hurricane lantern. The light of the hurricane lantern becomes lost in the light of the hyáják [gas light]; the light of the hyáják becomes lost in the light of the sun.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Na tatra súryo bháti na chandratárakaḿ
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Nemá vidyuto bhánti kutoʼayamagnih;
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Tameva bhántamanubháti sarvaḿ
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: Tasya bhásá sarvamidaḿ vibháti.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: [Before that effulgent Supreme Entity, neither the sun shines, nor the moon nor the stars. Nor does the lightning flash, what to speak of fire. In Parama Puruśaʼs light all other entities shine. His effulgence illuminates all luminous entities.]
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: The awareness of Burdwan becomes lost in Ráŕh-awareness, Ráŕh-awareness becomes lost in Bengal-awareness, Bengal-awareness becomes lost in universal awareness, universal awareness becomes lost in Your footsteps, the Unknown Eternal Traveller.
chapterTitle: From Ráŕh Awareness to the Awareness of Supreme Consciousness

t: ÁCÁRYA m. or ÁCÁRYÁ f.: Spiritual teacher qualified to teach all lessons of meditation.

AHIḾSÁ: One of the points of morality: to refrain from purposefully inflicting pain or hurt on anybody by thought, word or action. Atharvaveda. The last Veda, composed approximately 3000 years ago, older than the Jain scriptures.
ANANDA MARGA: Path of divine bliss; ÁNANDA MÁRGA PRACÁRAKA SAḾGHA.
ÁNANDA MÁRGA PRACÁRAKA SAḾGHA: The socio-spiritual organization founded by Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar to spread the ideology and spiritual practices of the path of bliss.
ÁRYYÁVARTTA: Lit., “Land of the Aryans”; northern India, which the Aryans at one point occupied.
AVADHÚTA m. or AVADHÚTIKÁ f.: Literally, “one who is thoroughly cleansed mentally and spiritually”; a monk of an order close to the tradition of SHAEVA Tantra. AVADHÚTIKÁ, Nun of the same order.

AVIDYÁ: Ignorance; centrifugal, or extroversial, force; force of repulsion from the Nucleus Consciousness; aspect of the Cosmic Operative Principle which guides movements from the subtle to the crude.

BAULS: A psychology based on Jain TANTRA (which is another name for SHAEVA Tantra) gave rise to the Baul psychology. The Bauls were devotional singers whose devotion seemed to onlookers almost like madness.
BUDDHA: One who has attained bodhi, intuition. Lord Buddha, the propounder of Buddhism, appeared approximately 2500 years ago.

DÁYABHÁGA: A system of inheritance in which the heirsʼ right of inheritance is subject to the discretion of the father, who has the right to disinherit any of the children. Another feature of this system is the rights of inheritance for women.
DEVII: A goddess, a female deity.
DHARMA: Characteristic property; spirituality; the path of righteousness in social affairs.
DHYÁNA MANTRA: A Sanskrit verse listing the attributes of a deity, to be used for visualizing that deity in meditation.
DIGAMBARA, NIRGRANTHA: Unclothed.
GAOŔIIYA VAEŚŃAVA DHARMA: The Bengalee Vaishnavite religion.

GONDWANALAND: According to the anthropologists this great Super continent had a life of around 520 million years or more making it perhaps the most important geological structure of the last billion years.
JAIN: Literally, a follower of the Jain religion introduced in India a little more than two thousand years ago; also a title or surname in India.
KAYASTHA: A caste.
KIIRTANA: Collective singing of the name of the Lord, sometimes combined with instrumental music and with a dance that expresses the spirit of surrender.
KŚATRIYA: Written as kśatriya, a person whose mentality is to dominate over matter; written as “Kśatriya”, a member of the second-highest caste in India.
KULIINA: Of noble descent.
LIUṊGA (LINGA): A cylindrical, aniconic image of Lord SHIVA tracing its origins to phallus worship.
MAHÁBHÁRATA: “Great India”; the name of a military campaign guided by Lord Krśńa around 1500 BCE to unify India; the epic poem written by Maharshi Vyasa about this campaign.
MANTRA: A sound or collection of sounds which, when meditated upon, will lead to spiritual liberation. A mantra is incantative, pulsative, and ideative.
MAUṊGALKÁVYA: Poetic works by different thirteenth- and fourteenth-century poets, aimed at establishing the glory of certain gods and goddesses
MELBANDHAN: The creation of groups made up of persons having similar defects and virtues. Within such a group, no one could be discriminated against.
MITÁKŚARÁ: Mitákśará entails the heirsʼ equal rights of inheritance, not subject to the fatherʼs discretion.
MOKŚA: Spiritual emancipation, non-qualified liberation.
PARAMA PURUŚA: Supreme Consciousness.
PURÁŃA: Mythological story with a moral import; educative fiction.
RÁŔH: The territory, mostly in modern-day Bengal and Jharkhand, stretching from the west bank of the Bhagirathi River to the Parasnath Hills.
RGVEDA: The oldest Veda, composed over the period between fifteen thousand years ago and ten thousand years ago.
RŚI: One who, by inventing new things, broadens the path of progress of human society.
SADÁSHIVA: See SHIVA.
SÁHITYA: Literature; all those literary manifestations of the popular mind that always move along the path of welfare.
SÁMVEDA: Sáma means “song”; the song portions of three Vedas collectively made up the Sámaveda. So the Sámaveda is not a separate Veda.

SANKARACHARYA: One of the greatest philosopher of India 1300 years ago, born at Kaladi of South India. He is famous for his commentaries on the classical Upanishads, the Bhagvat Gita and the Brahma Sútra of Badaryan on which he based the doctrine of pure monism.

SANSKRIT: SAḾSKRTA. The classical language of India. It first emerged during the Post-Shiva period, and as a spoken language it began to be supplanted by Prákrta prior to the Krśńa period. Although not a spoken language today except in very limited circumstances, it is still important for its vast literature, especially spiritual literature. Sanskrit and English are the languages of the world that have the richest vocabularies. Sanskrit pronunciation was perfected by non-Aryan Tantrics in such a way that each of the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet constitutes one acoustic root of Tantra.
SHAEVA DHARMA: Shaivism; the theoretical or philosophical side of spirituality as taught by Lord Shiva.
SHAEVA N: Shaivite, a follower of Lord SHIVA.
SHAEVA, SHAIVITE ADJ: Following or pertaining to Lord SHIVA and his teachings.
SHAEVA TANTRA: Shiva Tantra; the applied, or practical, side of spirituality as taught by Lord Shiva.
SHIVA, SADÁSHIVA: A great Tantric guru of 5000 BCE who guided society while His mind was absorbed in Consciousness.
SHÚDRA: Written as shúdra, a person with a mentality of physical enjoyment only, a member of the labourer social class; written as “Shúdra”, a member of the lowest caste in India.

TANTRA: A spiritual tradition which originated in India in prehistoric times and was first systematized by SHIVA. It emphasizes the development of human vigour, both through meditation and through confrontation of difficult external situations, to overcome all fears and weaknesses. Also, a scripture expounding that tradition.
VAESHYA: Written as vaeshya, a person of acquisitive mentality, a member of the capitalist social class; written as “Vaeshya”, a member of the second-lowest caste in India.
VAEŚŃAVA: Vaishnavite; pertaining to the Viśńu Cult or Religion.
VARŃÁSHRAMA: Four-caste social system.

VEDA: Literally, “knowledge”; hence, a composition imparting spiritual knowledge. Also, a religious or philosophical school which originated among the Aryans and was brought by them to India. It is based on the Vedas and emphasizes the use of ritual to gain the intervention of the gods.
VIPRA: Written as vipra, a person who controls others by his wits, a member of the intellectual social class; written as “Vipra”, a member of the highest caste in India.
YAJURVEDA: A VEDA composed over a period between ten thousand years ago and seven thousand years ago. There was no script at that time.
